News.title: Thailand declares flood disaster in Bangkok as torrential rain & storms leaves city under water & sparks mass evacuation
News.content:
Next

A BRIT holiday hotspot has declared a flood disaster after torrential rain left the city underwater and forced hundreds from their homes.

Thailand’s sprawling capital has been battered by almost 48 hours of relentless downpours sparking an emergency red alert.



Roads have been swamped, canals have overflowed and filthy floodwater has surged into homes and businesses.

Authorities declared all 50 Bangkok districts disaster zones on September 26 as the deluge brought parts of the city to a standstill.





Almost 300mm of rain has hammered the capital since the afternoon of September 24, with residents forced to wade through waist-deep water.

Around 980 people have been driven into temporary shelters, while 36 bedridden residents relying on life-saving medical equipment have been transferred to hospitals.

Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt urged residents to stay home as emergency crews battled to pump out the stricken city.

Vendor Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok told AFP: “The water keeps coming in. It’s hard to go out now. It’s like at my waist level now.



“I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now.”

The torrential rain has even flooded areas around Don Mueang Airport, with floodwater pooling close to parked aircraft at nearby Air Force Base 6.

Waterlogged roads around the airport have sparked travel chaos, with around 10cm of water reported across several entrance and exit lanes.

Passengers have been warned to brace for delays and allow an extra two to three hours to reach the airport as traffic crawls through the flooded streets.

And the devastating scenes have stirred grim memories of Thailand’s catastrophic 2011 floods.



Somkid added: “I think this time is worse than the 2011 flood.”

More than 500 people were killed and millions of homes damaged when widespread flooding devastated Thailand 15 years ago.

The latest deluge has seen at least 13 roads flooded.



The eastern parts of Bangkok have been hardest hit, with those living alongside canals facing the greatest danger.

“Our problem is that the canals are full,” Chadchart said.

“We are cooperating with nearby provinces and try to drain water out through other sides, minimising the amount that flows into Bangkok.”

The governor urged those in vulnerable areas to haul their belongings to higher ground as more rain threatened the capital.

“The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full,” he said.



“The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled.”

Bangkok’s pumping stations have been running at full capacity as authorities fight to shift the vast volumes of water.

They were pumping a combined 1,200 cubic metres per second as municipal workers desperately tried to keep drains clear.



Worker Kwan Nobnom said: “Our job is to make sure rubbish along the road doesn’t block the drains, so the water can drain away quickly.”

“We thought this year would be dry, so we didn’t expect the flooding to be this bad.”

In the On Nut neighbourhood, residents were seen frantically filling sandbags to defend homes and businesses from the rising water.

Elsewhere, the sudden deluge left commuters facing a treacherous journey to work.

Motorbike rider Samruay Nakkamnueng said: “I woke up to go to work and the street in front of my house was flooded.”



“I worried if my motorbike would be able to wade through floodwater this much.”

The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration’s disaster declaration gives local organisations special powers to respond to the crisis.

But Chadchart urged residents not to panic over fears flooded roads could trigger food shortages.



“The public don’t have to be panicked,” he said.

By mid-afternoon on September 26, the governor said the crisis had “stabilised” – but warned it could still take days for the water to disappear.

“If more rainwater doesn’t fall in the area, it will be solved.”

“If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take 2-3 days to drain the floodwater,” he added.

But forecasters warned Bangkok could face yet more punishing rain.



September is the peak of the city’s rainy season, but this month has been dramatically wetter than usual.

Bangkok recorded 487mm of rain between September 1 and September 25, compared with an average of almost 269mm over the same period between 1991 and 2020.

Thailand’s Meteorological Department warned heavy rain was expected to continue across much of the country through Sunday.

A powerful low-pressure system over central Thailand was also strengthening monsoon conditions.

Disaster officials warned eastern, north-eastern and central Thailand could face flash floods, forest runoff, mudslides and overflowing rivers until September 27.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Bangkok is particularly vulnerable to rising water, with the low-lying megacity built on former marshland and sitting only around 1.5 metres above sea level.

Once dubbed the “Venice of the East” for its vast network of canals, the city is now battling to use those waterways to drain away the devastating deluge.

News.title: Woman, 26, who vanished two days ago is tragically found dead
News.content:

SAD DISCOVERY Woman, 26, who vanished two days ago is tragically found dead







Next

A MISSING 26-year-old woman who was last seen on Thursday has tragically been found dead.

Eloise vanished from Fleet, Hampshire, on Thursday morning with police announcing that she had been found dead.

Police had previously appealed for assistance locating Eloise after she disappeared.

People were urged to dial 999 immediately if they spotted her.





Eloise’s family have been informed and are being supported by specially trained officers.

Police said her death is being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.

A statement from the force said: “We are saddened to report that previously missing Eloise from Hampshire has been found and sadly declared deceased.

“It follows an appeal shared on Thursday 24 September to help find her.

“Her next of kin have been informed and our thoughts are with her family and friends during this tragic time.

“Eloise’s death is currently being treated as unexplained but not suspicious, and our officers will now continue their enquiries on behalf of HM Coroner.

“We thank the public for their concern and efforts to locate her.”

News.title: Boy, 12, rushed to hospital with fractured skull and broken ankle after being ‘hit by e-bike while crossing the road’
News.content:
'HIT AND RUN' Boy, 12, rushed to hospital with fractured skull and broken ankle after being ‘hit by e-bike while crossing the road’







Next

A BOY has been rushed to hospital with a fractured skull and broken ankle after he was reportedly struck down by an e-bike in a hit-and-run.

The youngster, 12, was hit by a Sur-Ron electric motorbike while crossing a road in Barnsley, South Yorkshire on Thursday, cops said.

The rider is said to have fled the scene without stopping to check on the victim.



His bike was later discovered but the rider has not yet been identified.



South Yorkshire Police said: “On Thursday 24 September, officers responded to reports of a collision involving a child and an electric bike on Houghton Road in Thurnscoe, Barnsley.”

“It is alleged that the child was crossing the road when a Sur-Ron bike collided with them. The bike fled the scene.

Our enquiries are ongoing and anyone with information is asked to get in touch.”



Dearne & District FC, where the injured boy plays, issued a statement following the incident.

They said: “The boy was involved in a serious hit-and-run incident involving an e-bike, close to the football cages towards School Street in Thurnscoe.

“He suffered a fractured skull and a broken ankle and is currently being cared for in the neurological department in Sheffield, where he is being closely monitored following a bleed close to his brain.

“His family are asking anyone who was in the area at the time, witnessed what happened, or has CCTV, doorbell or dashcam footage covering the area around 9pm to please come forward.



“The police are investigating and have recovered the bike involved.

“We are posting this at the request of his mum and would ask our community to please share this appeal as widely as possible.

“Our thoughts are with the young lad and his family, and we wish him a full and speedy recovery and hope to see him back on the pitch soon.”

They urged anyone with information about the incident to contact South Yorkshire Police.

News.title: Moment pregnant mum-of-two screams in terror as balaclava-clad thugs threaten her with knife in brutal crypto robbery
News.content:
Next

THIS is the chilling moment a pregnant mum screams in terror as a gang of balaclava-clad bursts into her home during a brutal crypto robbery.

The woman was held at knifepoint and her husband was beaten – with a substantial amount of cryptocurrency taken during the terrifying raid.



The CCTV footage shows the gang rushing towards the property in Smith’s Wood, Birmingham, at around 5.20pm on December 13 last year.

They burst through the door as the mum-of-two gives a blood-curdling screech.



The thieves demanded the couple hand over cash in crypto as they gave instructions to a fourth person on a video call.

The man was left with “significant injuries”, while his wife, who was just weeks from giving birth, was threatened at knifepoint.



The gang then fled the home having stolen the crypto currency as well as high-value watches, escaping in a BMW X3.

Crimestoppers are offering a £10,000 reward for any information which leads to the arrest and conviction of the offenders.

West Midlands Police say the attackers are all believed to be in their 20s and the incident “may have been a targeted attack”.

A force statement adds: “Due to wearing face coverings and hoods, accurate descriptions have been difficult, but one was described as a black man with a small diagonal scar beneath his left eyebrow.”



Alan Edwards, West Midlands regional manager at the charity Crimestoppers, said: “This was a young family, at home, weeks away from welcoming a new baby.

“What was done to them is hard to take in, and the effects are still being felt every single day.

“Four people planned this and four people know exactly what happened that evening.

“Others will know too: someone who was told about it afterwards, someone who noticed a friend or relative suddenly flush with money, or someone who saw a black BMW X3 in the area that Saturday.



“That scar under the eyebrow may be the detail that brings a face to mind.

“We understand that speaking up about something like this feels daunting. That’s precisely why our charity exists.

“We are not the police. We never ask for your name, we can’t trace your IP address, and you will never be asked to give a statement or go to court.

“In nearly 40 years we have never broken that promise.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“If this has been sitting with you, please pass it on to us to help keep our communities safe. You can help this family without ever saying who you are.”



Information can also be passed to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: How Mexican cartels are expanding bloodthirsty drug empire worldwide with super meth labs, gang-alliances & grim tactics
News.content:
EMPIRE OF SIN How Mexican cartels are expanding bloodthirsty drug empire worldwide with super meth labs, gang-alliances & grim tactics







Next

MEXICAN cartels are advancing at a terrifying pace with industrial-scale meth labs, criminal alliances and a deadly new drug on the market.

The world’s most vicious gangs are evolving with new tactics to expand their bloodthirsty empire across the world.



As their reach spreads far beyond Mexico’s borders, experts warn “unprecedented” levels of violence will follow.

Over the past decade, Mexican criminal groups have expanded their operations far beyond their borders.



While dominating the cocaine trade in Europe, cartels are developing new markets in Australia, New Zealand, Asia, Africa and the Middle East.

But they have turned to the production of a much more deadly drug – a new, potent crystal meth.

Rafaella Liptschitz, criminal network specialist at the New Lines Institute, told The Sun: “Cartels continue to adapt and become more resilient.

“As enforcement pressure intensifies in one area, these groups diversify production, spreading operations so that a bust in one country does little to disrupt the trade as a whole.



“Constant adaptation, be that through supply chains, trafficking methods or production locations, makes keeping up with them extremely difficult.”

‘Super’ meth labs churning out tens of millions of pounds of product have sprung up across Europe and Africa.

Mexico’s most notorious cartels – the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG) – are outsourcing their highly skilled cooks.



The drug chemists partner with local criminal groups and teach them how to create a lethal version of the drug.

Five Mexicans appeared in a UK court earlier this month accused of conspiracy to produce meth after police arrests.

It’s alleged they were part of a criminal syndicate making the drug at a meth lab on a remote farmland near Furnace End in Warwickshire. They all denied involvement.

Meth use in the UK has gone up by 61 per cent between 2021 and 2025, according to the amount detected in the country’s waterways.

The rise coincides with the Taliban’s crackdown on heroin production – leaving room for Mexican kingpins to exploit a gap in the market.



Rafaella said Mexican cartels now appear to be treating Europe as an “operational hub” rather than a “destination market”.

“Europe’s diverse criminal landscape allows cartels to integrate their operations into preexisting ecosystems relatively easily”, she added.

A report by the United Nations in June revealed that global meth trafficking is up by 13 per cent and new routes through Africa have opened up markets.



Police in South Africa have raided at least five meth facilities in the past two years. In each case, they arrested Mexican workers.

Last month, police uncovered a multi-million-pound meth lab on a farm outside Musina, in Limpopo province, near the border with Zimbabwe.

Officers said they found cauldrons filled with chemicals, vats of product ready to heat and drugs worth around £27million, as well as “an undisclosed amount of cash”.

Two Mexicans were arrested, along with two Zimbabweans and a Malawian.

All appeared in court a week later on charges of drug manufacturing, possession and money laundering.



Rafaella said: “Instead of cartels relocating leadership, they transfer production knowledge to local groups.

“This sets up a low-risk, high-reward structure that lets Mexican cartels plug into established criminal networks without owning the operation outright.

“So, a lab bust or arrest does little damage to the organization.



“This is not new, but is becoming more prominent abroad.”

South Africa appeals to Mexican cartels for several reasons, Rafaella said.

The country’s strategic and porous borders allow for easy transportation while busy ports offer access to established trade corridors with little enforcement.

Meanwhile, widespread corruption allows cartels and local criminal networks to operate untouched.

The scale of these meth labs and the frequency they are appearing suggests South Africa has “shifted” from a “transit country” in the global meth trade to “an emerging production site”, Rafaella said.



And it has spread far further across the continent, with similar sites raided in Kenya, and Nigeria, she added.

In May, Nigeria conducted one of its largest ever drug busts, with raids in Ogun and Lagos states.

Ten suspects, including three Mexicans, have been charged with operating an illegal drug lab, producing 2.7 tonnes of meth, and drug trafficking.



The presence of Mexican cartels in Africa demonstrates “the growing prominence of their franchise” and “just how global the drug trade is becoming”, Rafaella said.

Both the Sinaloa Cartel’s and CJNG’s Asian connections have now expanded to Chinese and Indian suppliers of fentanyl.

And in the past decade, the Sinaloa Cartel has formed methamphetamine trafficking routes and money laundering in Canada and the Middle East.

Meth production sites linked to Mexican cartels have also appeared across Europe.

Labs have been raided in the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain and Britain.



Rafaella said: “Spain has become a critical node in Sinaloa and CJNG’s European operations, as cartels use the country and its ports as a key gateway for meth and cocaine trafficked across the Atlantic. “

Meanwhile in Australia and New Zealand the Mexican cartels have recently surpassed the long-established Chinese criminal groups.

Around the world, the expansion of drug trafficking gives rise to increased drug use.

To avoid processing huge volumes of cash in many different currencies, cartels pay their local partners in drugs.

At the same time, regional gangs are forced to whip up consumption for profit.



The expansion of meth use across Europe has devastating effects.

Formed into large crystals – highly desirable to addicts – the meth produced by Mexican cartels is incredibly potent.

With little effective treatment, unlike for opioid use, the strain now flooding European markets is tied to horrifying death rates.



In the United States, it has already killed tens of thousands of people.

As Mexican cartels spread across the world, they are leaving a bloody trail of violence.

Rafaella said: “The violence tied to Mexican cartel expansion in South Africa mainly takes the form of targeted killings.

“A crime intel officer set to testify in an ongoing commission looking at police corruption has been assassinated, a state witness was killed in a big cocaine case in the Western Cape, and a businessman is on trial for allegedly financing several assassination attempts tied to police corruption.

“This style of going after witnesses, informants, and officials rather than public displays of violence differs from the often more visible cartel violence seen in Mexico.



“But the underlying dynamic of cartels using violence to discipline local partners and prevent defections is similar to what’s driving some of the low-level violence in Europe’s growing meth markets.”

The Mexican cartels’ arrival often offers local criminal groups with the capacity to increase their firepower.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If established criminal networks feel threatened by the Mexican cartels’ expansion, the competition could erupt into “unprecedented levels of criminal violence”.

“The concern is that as local drug markets expand, that violence could escalate toward the more overt, turf-driven violence we see in Mexico”, Rafaella said.

News.title: Shocking moment raging inferno rips through ferry off coast of Brit holiday hotspot sparking frantic evacuation
News.content:
Next

THIS is the jaw-dropping moment a huge inferno rips through a ferry off the coast of a British holiday hotspot sparking a frantic evacuation.

Shocking footage showed towering plumes of smoke billowing from the flaming vessel north of Mykonos, Greece.



Emergency services safely rescued 29 people from the burning 530ft truck and passenger ship, operated by Blue Star Ferries.

The raging blaze was tackled in an “extensive firefighting operation”, according to the Hellenic Coastguard.



Though the cause of the inferno which broke out on Friday is currently unclear.

In the extraordinary footage, a massive fireball can be seen tearing through the stationary Blue Carrier 2 vessel.



Other clips show the aftermath of the horror, with firefighting teams and smaller vessels working to beat the flames and rescue those on board.

The ship was later abandoned once the 28 crew members and one passenger, a truck driver, were saved.



At least five coast ​guard vessels and two firefighting speedboats assisted the recovery operation.

Authorities say the fire on board the ship has now eased.

Salvage crews are now focusing on stabilising the inferno so they can access the vessel and launch a probe into the ordeal.

Firefighting teams were still battling the flames on Saturday.

It comes after a spate of wildfires in Greece this summer which swallowed hectares of land and left towns completely scorched.



And in 2024, crew on a high-end yacht hired out by holidaymakers appeared in court over fireworks they allegedly lit on board that sparked a forest fire.

The raging wildfire is thought to have ravaged the pine forest in the port city of Piraeus on Hydra island, not far from the Greek capital Athens.

It is believed that cruise workers lit fireworks to entertain the holidaymakers, before igniting the fire in Hydra’s only pine forest.

The damage demanded the attention of several firefighters, according to climate minister Vassilis Kikilias who stressed that it took six planes to put it out.

News.title: Harrowing new bodycam footage reveals moment cops fatally shoot knife-wielding woman after deadly Times Square stabbing
News.content:
Next

NEW bodycam footage released by cops shows the final moments before a knife-wielding woman was shot dead in Times Square.

Pamela Cisneros, 49, can be seen brandishing two kitchen knives as NYPD officers repeatedly beg her to drop the blades.



The mum-of-three had stabbed two strangers in the heart of Manhattan on August 31 – killing one.

Footage released on Friday evening shows cops chasing after Cisneros before desperately trying to talk her down as she holds the blades in front of her chest.



“Put the knife down,” Officer Ryan Brito told Cisneros.

“Come and get me,” she replied, before Officer Francis Gagliano said: “I don’t want to get you.”

READ MORE IN WORLD NEWS KNIFE ATTACK Two tourists rushed to hospital after being stabbed near Acropolis

Cisneros then made the haunting admission: “I’m tired of this world already. Tired of this s**t.”

Brito replied: “I get it, I understand … I understand, but why? What’s going on?”



As the tense stand-off continued, the cops repeatedly urged Cisneros to calm down and breathe.

Brito desperately tried to appeal to her, saying: “I get it. The world is hard. Especially New York City. I know New York City is hard. Trust me, we all suffer.”

He then asked: “You believe in God?”

Cisneros replied: “No. Not anymore.”



She then warned the officers: “You’re going to have to kill me. Yes, you are.”

“Either that, or I’m going to kill all of you.”

Brito pleaded: “Listen, I know you’re going through a lot, but it’s not worth it. It’s not worth it. I promise you.”

More cops raced to the scene and repeatedly ordered Cisneros to surrender the knives.



But she vowed: “I’m not dropping anything.”

The horrifying footage then shows Cisneros swinging the two blades in circles at her side as officers deploy tasers in a frantic attempt to bring her down.

But the electric shocks appear to have little effect and Cisneros suddenly charges screaming towards the cops.

Officers Joseph O’Connor and Steven Darcy then fire three rounds, sending Cisneros crashing face-first onto the pavement.



She was rushed to hospital but pronounced dead.

Cops said Cisneros first pulled two knives from a red Target bag before attacking 68-year-old Tak Kam.

He was stabbed in the abdomen after leaving the subway near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue.

Cisneros then raced towards 42nd Street and plunged a knife into Bank of America executive Erin Piacenti, 32.



Erin, a new mum who had recently returned to work following maternity leave, was killed in the savage attack.

Just days earlier, the University of Pennsylvania graduate had celebrated her baby daughter’s baptism.

Cisneros then fled towards an NYPD substation, where officers confronted her clutching the two blades in front of her chest.

Months before the Times Square horror, Cisneros posted a rambling message about religion and the “end times”.

In the disturbing November 30, 2025 post, Cisneros warned about the “diminished [sic] love of people to the point of stabbing others for no reason”.



She added: “You can read it for yourself in the Holy Bible that warns about the end times.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police said Cisneros had a documented mental health history, including a previous suicide attempt.

She had earlier been described by police as “emotionally disturbed”.

News.title: Cyclist, 24, dies after ‘hit and run’ in early hours of the morning as cops launch manhunt for moped driver
News.content:
ROAD TRAGEDY Cyclist, 24, dies after ‘hit and run’ in early hours of the morning as cops launch manhunt for moped driver







Next

AN e-bike rider has died in a horror suspected hit-and-run crash in the early hours as police launch a manhunt for a moped driver.

Emergency services were scrambled to North Kensington, London, in the early hours this morning.

A section of the road has been sealed off as emergency services work at the scene.

Bystanders are said to have discovered a seriously injured man on the road and alerted police.





Paramedics battled to save the 24-year-old cyclist’s life but he was tragically pronounced dead at the scene.

His next of kin have been informed.

Police have since launched a manhunt for a moped driver with CCTV suggesting the vehicle was involved in the crash.

The moped driver failed to stop at the scene with detectives now attempting to track them down.



Images from the scene of the fatal collision show an e-bike abandoned on the pavement with a police forensic tent set up nearby.

Detective Chief Inspector Phil Wilkins, investigating from Hammersmith and Fulham CID, said: “Our thoughts are with the man’s family at what is a very difficult time.

“We have launched a full investigation and are working hard to get answers and trace the moped driver.

“As part of this, we’re urging anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen the e-bike or the moped to get in touch with us as soon as possible.



“If you have any information that could help, please come forward.”

News.title: Clubs seek legal advice after Man City found guilty over financial rule breaches
News.content:
Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation after Manchester City were found guilty of the vast majority of 115 breaches of financial rules they had been accused of by the Premier League.

Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. BBC Sport has been told that the club will appeal.

The news that City had been found guilty was broken by the Athletic,, external which reported that 114 of the 115 counts were upheld.

It came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months since a hearing by an independent commission concluded.

No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.

BBC Sport has been told the independent panel has ruled, and the majority of the charges have been upheld.

Manchester City were accused of a wide-range of rule breaches which centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.

The seismic decisions have left a huge number of questions about what will happen next, what City's punishment might be and how the current season will be affected.

And one possibility emerging is that rival Premier League sides may take legal action for compensation, claiming they have been impacted by City's actions.

A number of sides, prior to Friday's news, had already started seeking advice over whether they would have a case for financial compensation.

One source, who held a senior executive position at one Premier League club before moving to another, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.

However, another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league.

Such a move is not unprecedented. In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley Â£35m after they broke profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) over a three-year period.

Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.

Everton have appealed, with sources saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.

Meanwhile, it also emerged that:

Other Premier League clubs have been formally told about the independent panel's decision. A select group of club directors were informed by email and had to sign a non-disclosure agreement before they could read the document, a source told the BBC. It is not yet known when the decision of the panel will be announced officially.

Manchester City deny wrongdoing but being found guilty on the most serious charges means they could be looking at a points deduction serious enough to relegate them, large fines or even expulsion from the Premier League

A sanctions hearing will need to take place to decide the punishment. That has not happened yet and could take months.

An appeal would then take place - and while it is possible the punishment is not made public until after that, there remains the possibility that any sanctions will be communicated before any appeal takes place

An appeal process could mean the uncertainty surrounding the case continues to cloud the top flight

It is understood a number of City players do not have relegation release clauses in their contracts in the event of the club losing their Premier League status as a result of any sanctions

Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

News.title: The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City
News.content:
Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".

Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".

"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."

Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.

"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.

"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."

It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.

The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.

Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.

Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.

It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.

Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.

"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.

"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.

"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.

"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."

Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".

He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.

"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.

"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."

In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.

News.title: Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference
News.content:
Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that."

During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones".

Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July.

It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era.

It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans.

Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong".

Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet.

Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.

She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.

In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British".

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."

Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".

Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".

The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.

She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."

Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here.

But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.

But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.

The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this week.

Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.

She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

News.title: E-motorbikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
News.content:
Electric motorbikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes and e-motorcycles last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

Six forces responded to say some of the vehicles they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

E-bikes and e-motorcycles have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.

News.title: Joshua fight at risk over promoter row, says Fury
News.content:
Tyson Fury says his long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in December is in jeopardy because of a row between rival promoters.

The bout was announced earlier this week following years of failed negotiations, with the pair set to fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The event, which will be broadcast on Netflix, was confirmed as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC president Dana White, but this appears to be the sticking point.

Eddie Hearn, Joshua's promoter, has been at odds with White in recent months, and says the UFC head's involvement is a breach of their contract.

Fury says Matchroom promoter Hearn's reluctance to work with White is putting the fight in doubt.

"Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight. They're saying they're not going to fight now," Fury posted on Instagram.

"It's mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. He's making up a million different things and threatening we're not going to fight.

"Now you've got Turki Alalshikh finding alternative real men who will fight at the drop of a hat. Eddie Hearn has cost us the biggest fight in boxing history."

Hearn has been publicly feuding with UFC president White since the launch of Zuffa Boxing earlier this year.

Speaking to IFL TV, Hearn said White's involvement in the promotion of the Fury and Joshua fight "ain't happening", despite Netflix's news release.

"Dana White cannot be involved with this fight promotion. Netflix clearly didn't get the memo. No-one talks to each other," said Hearn.

"Then Netflix say the fight is in conjunction with Dana White. Now we have to go through that process and deal with it. It's a little bit annoying but as I've shown through the UK battle that we won, we stand by our contracts."

Fury's promoter Frank Warren said White was influential in securing the deal with Netflix after the fight was confirmed.

Fury's claim the bout could be off follows his post on social media earlier this month suggesting that Joshua, 36, was backing out of the fight, before calling for a third match-up with Oleksandr Usyk.

There was no official statement from Hearn or Warren in the news release sent out by Netflix to announce the fight.

BBC Sport has contacted Matchroom, Warren's company Queensberry Promotions, The Ring and Netflix for comment.

The dispute between Hearn and White is the latest stumbling block following years of failed negotiations around the fight.

In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American.

Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.

Fury and Joshua finally signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, with the date and venue confirmed this week.

News.title: Bangkok declares disaster as heavy rains spark flooding
News.content:
Days of almost continuous heavy rains have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital, with the city's governor declaring it a disaster-affected zone.

Almost 300 millimetres (11.8 inches) has fallen over the period, and more is expected in the coming days, according to Governor Chadchart Sittipunt.

Videos from Bangkok show cars trying to navigate roads that have been entirely submerged by the floodwaters, with some vehicles appearing stranded.

News.title: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
News.content:
And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.

But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting â a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says.

"The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now.

"The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."

Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine.

"The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."

Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women.

"I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."

Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been â and continue to be - weaponised.

"We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"

Scanlon too is a little baffled.

"For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't.

"I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?

"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

News.title: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on them
News.content:
"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.

She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help.

"These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.

Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.

Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves.

"Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'"

"Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."

News.title: Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

The Athletic , externalis reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count.

The Premier League declined to comment.

Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way.

Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added.

BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings.

Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the independent panel's decision and have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim.

News.title: Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says former business secretary
News.content:
A cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer has said Andy Burnham's government is not focused enough on boosting economic growth and needs to act with "more urgency".

Speaking to the BBC two months after being sacked in Burnham's cabinet reshuffle upon entering office, Peter Kyle said he wasn't making a "criticism" but "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government".

"If the destination means prosperity, it means freedom for people to do new things, and it means security for people and families, then why wouldn't we put our foot down and get there quicker," the former business secretary said.

It comes as Labour prepares to gather in Liverpool for its annual conference.

Burnham will address the conference on Tuesday and has said his speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role."

He has previously said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth" stressing his belief in the importance of devolving powers to local areas.

Giving regions and nations more control would, he has argued, create the conditions for "good growth in every postcode".

Kyle served as science secretary and later business secretary in the Starmer government, but has now returned to the backbenches as the MP for Hove and Portslade.

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said the government should be willing to take decisions that involve "short-term" pain in order to deliver economic growth, suggesting a delay to expanding workers' rights.

"We might need to look and have honest conversations with unions about how we sequence some of the rights going forward in order to make sure that we get growth into the economy in the shorter term," he said.

The government's Employment Rights Act was passed in December 2025 but some of the changes are not due to come into force until next year.

The former minister also suggested introducing a "tax growth test" which would measure the impact of each tax on the economy and asking government experts to review "obstacles" to growth.

Asked if there was enough focus on growth in the government, Kyle replied: "I don't think there is and that isn't a criticism - it is pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government.

"I think we need to up our ambition, I think that we need to act with more urgency when it comes to economic growth."

Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, but faces rising debt costs and warnings of slower economic growth.

According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the UK economy is expected to grow by 1%, slightly less than the 1.1% previously forecast.

Responding to Kyle's comments that the government needed to act with more urgency on economic growth, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy suggested that the prime minister was moving faster than his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I think the the reason, frankly, that we had a change of leadership at the start of this year is because we all felt that people need to feel the change in their lives that we promised in 2024 much more quickly."

She added that she believed Burnham was "impatient for change, and he thinks big about the sort of change that the country needs".

News.title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process".

During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses.

Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind.

An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029.

Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be.

"All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead."

News.title: UK ticket holder wins 'life-changing' £111m EuroMillions jackpot
News.content:
A UK ticket holder has won Friday's Â£111m EuroMillions jackpot, National Lottery operator Allwyn has confirmed.

One mystery player matched all five numbers â 11, 12, 15, 38, 49 â plus the two Lucky Star numbers â 10 and 12 â to scoop the major prize.

Allwyn's senior winners' adviser Andy Carter said it was "fantastic news for a UK EuroMillions player" who has secured the "life-changing" sum.

It marks the third time a UK winner has claimed the jackpot this year.

On 10 March, one UK winner took home a Â£181m jackpot - the third-largest in UK National Lottery history - while two UK-based winners shared a Â£125m jackpot with a French player in April.

"Be sure to check your tickets and get in touch if you think you might be tonight's lucky winner," Carter urged.

The record for the largest EuroMillions prize for a UK player currently stands at Â£195m - won by an anonymous player in 2022.

EuroMillions draws are held every Tuesday and Friday night across nine European countries.

Tuesday's jackpot is now at an estimated Â£14m.

News.title: Weekend of mixed UK weather with sunshine before showers arrive for some on Sunday
News.content:
A deep area of low pressure is forecast to approach from the Atlantic next week bringing a spell of windy weather.

This potential storm may also bring heavy rain to places, especially in the west, whilst some places further east could stay dry.

Many drought affected parts of England and Wales - where significant rainfall is still needed - may stay largely dry throughout the next week.

Before the arrival of wind and rain, though, some bursts of warmth will lift temperatures above average, possibly reaching the low-20s Celsius at times in south-east England.

News.title: 'Our wedding present left us gutted': Couple join dozens in car seller dispute
News.content:
Newlyweds Amber and Nathan Cooper spent all their wedding present money on a Â£7,000 Citroen C4 to take them on their dream honeymoon.

But as they made their way to Cornwall in August 2025, it lost power and began to roll backwards leaving them stranded on the A30, near the Jamaica Inn in Bodmin Moor, they told the BBC.

When they returned it to Trade Centre UK two weeks later, they discovered it needed a new engine, clutch and gearbox.

But a year on, they are still fighting for an apology and their money back.

News.title: Coroner appeals to families linked to jailed surgeon
News.content:
A coroner investigating the deaths of people treated by the jailed breast surgeon Ian Paterson has appealed for 106 more patients' families to make contact.

Inquests are currently being heard into the deaths of 70 women, to see if Paterson's treatment or care caused an unnatural death.

Paterson was jailed in 2017 after being convicted of wounding patients by way of botched and unnecessary operations and given a 20-year prison sentence.

The inquests' coroner, Judge Richard Foster, said he was recently notified of the deaths of a further 106 patients who were in their lifetime treated by Paterson for breast cancer, but he said he had not been told of their medical cause of death.

The list of 106 names, including six men, appears on the investigation website, external asking next of kin to contact the solicitors to the inquests Higgs LLP.

The law firm told the BBC: "We are simply seeking cause of death information to assess whether the deaths of these former patients of Mr Paterson will be investigated."

The disgraced breast surgeon worked with cancer patients at NHS and private hospitals in the West Midlands over 14 years.

At his trial the court heard that Paterson's technique involved leaving some breast tissue behind, preserving patients' cleavages, which breached national guidelines.

Investigations have so far found 106 patients died between 1995 and July 2026.

Others had surgery they did not need - some even finding out years later they did not have cancer.

The surgeries caused serious lasting physical and physiological harm to all the victims. One woman was unable to breast feed her baby as a result.

Paterson is due to be automatically released halfway through his sentence in 2027, before the inquests in Birmingham are due to conclude.

News.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

It is a brave new world for the Labour Party as its delegates head to Liverpool for their annual conference.

A summer of dramatic change was summed up by one senior minister who half joked: “This will be the first conference in three years where we won’t be talking about whether Andy Burnham will make a bid to become leader of the party.”

There is a sense too of what a difference a year makes.

Last year Mr Burnham arrived in Liverpool making his ambitions abundantly clear and ended up being mocked and leaving with his tail between his legs.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham finally has the job he has coveted for years (Toby Melville/PA) ( PA Wire )

It only took 10 months for him to finally get elected back to parliament and replace the not-at-all missed Sir Keir Starmer as leader and prime minister.

Now as Labour delegates arrive the talk is not of a leadership contest but whether Mr Burnham will call an early election - an idea which he tried to “knock dead” in his pre-conference broadcast interviews.

Despite that fairly emphatic statement, many MPs including his own ministers do not completely believe him.

“There are calculations being made,” said one minister. “How much are the Tories and Reform cancelling each other out?”

Another noted: “We appear to have pulled back all those votes we have lost to the Greens. Zack Polanski looked like the right leader for the Greens when Keir was in charge but the wrong one now.”

The Independent reported recently senior Labour figures suggesting that a comfortable win in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, called because of Sir Keir’s decision to quit as an MP after being dumped by his party, will be used to decide whether an early election is triggered.

One minister repeated the suggestion in the run up to the conference: “That is definitely part of the calculation. But of course it is a risk because when the margins are so narrow things can flip quickly.”

open image in gallery Sir Keir Starmer’s departure creates an opportunity in the forthcoming byelection ( PA )

The main issue for them appears to be whether the slide for Reform in the last year where they have dropped into third place in some polls and around four or five points behind Labour represents something more permanent or whether they could see a recovery.

“There are still concerns about those red wall seats,” noted one senior figure. “At the moment we seem to be likely to win in those seats because of tactical voting but you cannot rely on that.”

Among those still very nervous about a Reform assault on the red wall is chancellor John Healey who barely held on in 2019 to his Yorkshire seat. Foreign secretary Ed Miliband in Doncaster and Yvette Cooper in Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley also had scares in the same election.

But whether there is an early election or not the mood is undoubtedly more positive for Labour.

“Everyone is feeling more cheerful,” said one MP.

“Spirits have been lifted,” added another.

“We just feel like we have a fighting chance now where before with [Starmer] it was just hopeless.”

The most important change is communication in all its forms.

open image in gallery CChancellor John Healey barely held onto his seat in 2019

“Starmer and [former chief of staff Morgan] McSweeney just managed to find the worst way of communicating everything,” said one minister.

“We made a statement on cancelling winter fuel when we could have made one on saving the triple lock but saying the rich would not get their winter fuel to afford it.

“The welfare debacle could have been sold as an increase not a cut. It was all so badly done.”

Then there was the fact that “Starmer just didn’t or maybe couldn’t speak to anybody.”

“He’s really not missed,” another MP noted.

The by-election for his seat in Holborn and St Pancras has also underlined what many suspected.

“Look at Rishi Sunak. He’s stuck around and makes contributions. You can just see what Keir Starmer was in it for now that he is just shuffling off straightaway.”

All this appears to be different with Mr Burnham who is busy communicating on social media with videos on pub snacks and buses or playing the guitar as well as talking to his MPs and ministers.

“It makes such a change,” said one veteran MP.

“Those videos may be fun but he is always making a serious point with them,” added another.

The only people Mr Burnham appears to not want to speak to as much is journalists, with still only one press conference as prime minister in almost three months.

But as one MP put it: “Speeches and press conferences didn’t help Keir Starmer much. Actually quite the opposite.”

The next few days in Liverpool though will tell us whether this fresh optimism is surface deep or more deeply rooted in a party that can sniff a resurgence whenever the next election is called.

Taylor Swift has set two new Spotify records following the arrival of her latest single and extended album.

Data from the streaming service confirms that the 36-year-old pop star became 2026's most-streamed female artist in a single day. Her new single, Patient Zero, which dropped on Friday, also secured the title for the most-streamed song by a female artist in a single day this year.

The releases mark her first musical output since marrying NFL player Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden in New York in July. In the track Cleveland! - named after Kelce's hometown - Swift directly responds to detractors of their romance. The four newly added compositions on Life Of A Showgirl: The Encore also include Pink Clouding and Babylon.

Critical reaction to the extended record has been lukewarm. The album was awarded two stars by The Independent, The Telegraph, and The Guardian, with the latter describing it as: "It’s like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer breathlessly flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love."

Swift has released her first music since marrying Travis Kelce ( Getty )

Conversely, The Times handed down a four-star rating, calling the songs a "reminder that when it comes to taking diaristic details and making them palatable for the pop mainstream, nobody does it better".

Rather than being unreleased material left over from the original 2025 album, the additional songs were written after the initial release became a hit.

Swift is set to debut the music video for Patient Zero - featuring actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson - at Sunday's MTV Video Music Awards. She will also receive the inaugural MTV Artist Director award at the ceremony, an accolade recognising musicians who direct their own videos.

These latest achievements build on a milestone-filled year for Swift, who was named the most streamed artist in Spotify's nearly 20-year history earlier in 2026.

In June, she also achieved a historical milestone by becoming the youngest woman inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.

Swift was also in attendance to watch Kelce’s Kansas City Chiefs pull off a dramatic overtime win against the Indianapolis Colts last weekend, with footage emerging online of the pop star celebrating wildly at the end of the thrilling game.

Donald Trump taunted Iran as he labelled the Strait of Hormuz “Trump Strait” after Tehran proposed a deal to open the key waterway within a week if the US meets certain conditions.

In a post on his Truth Social platform in the early hours of Saturday, the US president shared a picture of a map, with the shipping route labelled with his own name.

It comes after Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi presented a seven-day plan involving a ceasefire to American negotiators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week. The conditions for Washington largely echo the ones agreed to in the June deal that fell apart.

They stated that Tehran would reopen the key waterway and resume talks on its nuclear programme but only if the US lifts its naval blockade, waives oil sanctions and observes a ceasefire that includes Lebanon.

open image in gallery Donald Trump's Truth Social post is his latest example of international ‘rebrandings’ ( Truth Social )

Lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as waiving sanctions on oil sales, would allow Tehran to ship out more of its crude and help its economy as its currency hits record lows and inflation soars.

Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday that the deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.

"If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and ⁠reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he said.

The White House said it was engaged in “constructive discussions” via mediators, but a Wall St Journal report cited US officials as saying Trump was sceptical that Iran would meet his demands.

Trump’s Saturday Truth Social post is the latest example of him coming up with his own names for locations to attempt to make a political point.

open image in gallery Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 31, 2026 ( Reuters )

He posted a map on Truth Social of New Mexico earlier this month, but the word Mexico was crossed out and replaced with America.

‘Naming’ the southwestern state on the US-Mexico border as New America was reminiscent of an executive order he signed early in his second term, in which he changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

In that January 2025 executive order titled “Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness,” Trump also changed the name of North America’s tallest peak, Denali in Alaska, back to Mount McKinley.

Trump’s controversial naming of America’s geography didn’t stop there. The president signed an executive order late last month changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America amid an escalating trade war with Canada.

Despite Trump repeatedly suggesting Canada become the nation’s 51st state, he recently told Fox News, “They think they’re a state, but they’re not a state. Why should we be subsidizing Canada?”

Saturday morning media duties and training for the Republic of Ireland were both delayed ahead of their controversial Nations League match against Israel in Debrecen, Hungary.

Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player had been scheduled to speak to journalists at 10.15am local time, but a UEFA official announced roughly 15 minutes prior that the session was moved to 12.30pm local time, following training.

It was subsequently confirmed that the squad would be 20 minutes late for their 11am practice, though shortly before 12pm local time they had still not arrived at the Nagyerdei Stadium.

Uefa officials could not explain the cause of the delay. The team had previously arranged a meeting on Friday to discuss matters, amid reports of a potential player statement prior to the press conference.

Nations failing to meet their obligations face potential warnings or fines from Uefa.

The Press Association has contacted Uefa and the Football Association of Ireland for comment.

open image in gallery Jason Knight does not believe the game against Israel should go ahead ( PA )

The disruption follows Thursday’s 1-0 defeat to Kosovo in Pristina to open the Republic’s campaign.

Speaking after that match, midfielder Jason Knight said: "Look, it’s difficult. I don’t think the game obviously should be going ahead but it is going ahead. We’ll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we’ll get our thoughts as a group and go from there.

"I’m quite experienced. None of us have gone through this scenario before but I’d like to think I’m experienced, thick-skinned and I can get through most things and that is what I will try and do.

"I’ll try and focus on the football as much as I can. I’ll give my view and my thoughts on it (the Israel games) when I see fit, but I’ll be trying to focus on the football as much as possible."

Last weekend, Ireland boss Hallgrimsson said his team would be will be “playing against genocide” when they faced Israel.

It brought a furious response from the Israel FA on Monday, who wrote on social media: “We’re not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we’re playing against the coach who embodies them”.

The Irish taoiseach Micheal Martin called the comments from the Israel FA “unacceptable” and said they “should be withdrawn” while speaking with reporters when attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

“We're very clear and I think [UN secretary general] Antonio Guterres said it again this morning, he has never in his lifetime seen the level and scale of death and destruction as he witnessed in terms of the Israeli government's war on Gaza in the aftermath of the horrific Hamas attack preceding the war,” Martin said.

“Our manager is saying the exact same thing. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands.”

Russian attacks killed four people across Ukraine Saturday, officials said, as the aerial war between Moscow and Kyiv intensifies.

Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones while front-line progress has slowed, some 4½-years after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

“It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day. If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday morning.

He listed “numerous strikes on residential homes” in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, and the Odesa, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions.

Two women in Zaporizhzhia died when they were trapped beneath the rubble of their destroyed home, Zaporizhzhia’s regional military administration said. A separate Russian attack on the city of Sumy also killed two people, local officials said.

Ukrainian drones target Russian refineries

Zelenskyy appealed at the United Nations earlier this week to countries to starve Russia of revenue through sanctions and trade bans, denying Moscow the money it needs to prolong the war. But despite years of diplomatic efforts, there is no sign of a breakthrough in ending the war.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses. A Ukrainian drone attack on the southern Krasnodar region killed three people and wounded two, local officials said Saturday.

Writing on Telegram, regional Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said that a Ukrainian attack sparked fires at two industrial sites, but did not give further details. Russian media outlets later reported that a local oil refinery was targeted in the strike.

Russian attacks spark fires in Kyiv

Elsewhere in Ukraine, two people were injured in the Kyiv region overnight after a Russian drone attack caused a fire at a warehouse in the Boryspil district. Russian drones also hit several districts in the Ukrainian capital itself, injuring four and damaging residential and office buildings, officials said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its attack on Kyiv had damaged a data center that supported both cellphone internet services and Starlink satellite communication systems.

Oasis musician Noel Gallagher has expressed his "shock" following news that Manchester City have been found guilty on almost all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules.

Reports on Friday claimed City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges issued by the Premier League in February 2023, allegations the club consistently denied.

Speaking on the Let Me Talk podcast, the prominent City supporter called the decision "quite sad" for fans and squad members.

"A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because only that the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.

"So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players."

Gallagher said Sergio Aguero’s title-winning goal can’t be taken away from the fans ( Getty )

When asked whether the verdict alters historic moments such as Sergio Aguero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher added: "Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw – they won it on the pitch.

"Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch.

"Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans. We were there, we know what we saw.

"Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt."

Meanwhile, former City chairman David Bernstein has admitted the club faces a “drastic” punishment if their appeal fails.

Urging swift action, Bernstein said on Times Radio: "First of all, the timing of this I think is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already.

"So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because…you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable.

"The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster. Not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial.

"I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty.

"All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that."
