Do we know Lamine Yamal? “No. Not at all. No one,” he insists. “Only my inner circle know what I think, the way I am. People don’t have a clue – not a clue, Not. A. Clue.” Why? “I grew up in a barrio where the less people know about you, the happier you are, the quieter your life. Obviously I like a footballer’s life, but I would also like to live in peace, a normal life. The nearest I can get is for people to know as little as possible. If I post something, I need to know I can handle what comes. At first it annoyed me to read things because I didn’t understand it. My mum would read something, call me and say: ‘Son, what’s this?!’ That affected me but it doesn’t affect me now.

“There are times I enjoy the pressure. I enjoy going on to the pitch, when a lot is expected. Then there’s a different kind of pressure which is nothing to do with what people say, nothing to do with football; it’s life. I don’t feel pressure in football. I will never lie at home thinking: ‘I played really badly, I didn’t win the Ballon d’Or, we didn’t win the league.’ It’s responsibility: I have my family. I’ve suffered, struggled with them, we’ve been through bad times and now that we’re enjoying life, I have to continue. If I have played football all these years, it’s because I love football but also for them. I know life is much longer. I have to look after my family, my little brother.”

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal in full flight against Argentina in the World Cup final. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

“In football there’s no fear,” he adds. “I saw my mum struggle so that I could play football. I’ve seen my dad go round the streets collecting scrap metal so I could eat. That’s fear. Now if I had a son, I could look after him. If my mum or my dad need anything, I can help. I don’t have that fear now and that’s the only fear I could have in life.”

So, play the game. Your way, as always, made in Rocafonda, the hard barrio whose postcode Lamine Yamal signals with every goal. Besides, he insists, fun is underrated in football. “Barcelona give you good things but you also need something of your own, your roots,” he says. “Barcelona gave me control, understanding, IQ. In the park there’s no IQ: you go at your opponent, then go back again. I have that. If I hadn’t come from where I came from and been at La Masia, I wouldn’t have come out like this.

“The thing is, I love football. I don’t play for money, I play because I love it. Players who obsess over goals or assists don’t enjoy it. I play for the fun: to dribble, to play one touch, two touches, to make a teammate who hasn’t scored score. For the fans’ happiness. To hear the olés. I play for that. I enjoy it. I get home and I say: ‘I’ve had a great time.’ If every player did that, we would enjoy it much more.

“At the World Cup, you heard it, felt it: when I got the ball, they would stand up, one after the other, all along the row. Like they were saying: ‘Let’s see if this guy is what they say he is.’ At the Camp Nou, people know I’m going to go at someone. That feeling, that expectation, is something you can only experience in sport, being a player like me. It’s like there’s something inside that makes you feel more powerful than anyone and I hope it’s there until the day I retire. There’s a surge around you and you feel like Superman, you feel like Spiderman. You feel spectacular.”

Sports.title: How do England beat Spain, or even score against them? The data suggests crosses
Sports.content:
England are about to face the hardest challenge in international football, maybe at any level of the game. They are going to try to score against Spain.

Spain conceded one goal in eight games on the way to winning the World Cup while allowing their opponents 2.37 expected goals, a mere 0.30 per 90 minutes played.

Thomas Tuchel has said he hoped his side “became for 10 minutes more like Spain” to comfortably dominate possession when the heat was on. A fine aspiration for those situations, but it is not an approach that will help England unlock the Spanish backline. The pass masters cannot be toppled that way. The solution may lie elsewhere within the same Tuchel press conference.

Tuchel spoke of how English fans and players prefer chaos. “There is no heritage of: ‘Oh, let’s control around the middle line. Let’s do a deep buildup and then bring them out’,” he said. “It’s just like: ‘Come on. Let’s kick the ball into the opponent’s box and fight with them’.”

And this is how England can beat Spain. Granted, it requires a little more nuance than Tuchel’s simple summation. But not much. The two defeats Spain have suffered in the Luis de la Fuente era help prove the point. Both occurred in the UK.

The first was in Euros qualifying at Hampden Park in March 2023, with Scott McTominay scoring both goals in a 2-0 win for Scotland. “For me, this is not football,” Rodri said after enduring the home side’s combative, time-wasting approach. No, pal, and that is why it worked. Nobody can out-football Spain; alternate methods are required to win. McTominay’s second saw him crash the penalty box to fire home after David García failed to clear a Kieran Tierney cross.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s only competitive loss under Luis de la Fuente came thanks to two goals from Scott McTominay, the second from a cross. Photograph: Robert Perry/EPA

When Colombia beat Spain 1-0 in a friendly at the London Stadium 12 months later, it was again a delivery from the left flank which did the damage. And again, there was a Premier League past-and-present vibe with Luis Díaz crossing for Daniel Muñoz to score.

These moments carry positive confirmation bias as they occurred in losses for Spain. They look important because they were. While no side beat them this summer, teams relied on crossing to fashion even vaguely decent opportunities.

The stats for the chances they allowed highlight this superbly. The average value of a shot is 0.1 expected goals. It can vary slightly from season to season or between competitions, but as a rule of thumb it works. Across 750 minutes this summer, Spain conceded just six chances that Opta deemed to be of greater value. Lowering the bar to 0.07 xG still only finds 10 shots that were worth more. The eight teams Spain faced had to work for a collective average of 75 minutes for an opportunity that had a better than one-in-14 likelihood of becoming a goal. It was very hard graft.

It is remarkable that the highest value shot they allowed in the tournament occurred in the 121st minute of the final. A match Spain utterly dominated from start to finish might have gone to penalties had Giuliano Simeone fired under the crossbar rather than over it. The move for his chance originated from a corner, as did the cross that presented Cape Verde’s Diney Borges with a 91st-minute opportunity to deliver a titanic upset in Spain’s first game.

Charles De Ketelaere’s goal for Belgium, the only one Spain conceded, was set up by a Timothy Castagne cross. It was one of the four Opta-defined big chances the Spanish allowed at the World Cup; all of them headers, all set up via deliveries from wide areas.

Cristiano Ronaldo had a relatively high value effort in the last-16 Iberian derby after a cross to the back post had been headed back towards him in the six-yard box. It was a better chance than any France produced in the semi-final. Their highest value attempt was rated at just 0.06 expected goals. It came from a corner.

There seems little other way to produce even a shot against Spain. Cape Verde, Saudi Arabia and Uruguay all tried to score from within their own halves, so starved were they of goalscoring opportunities.

Crosses seem to work though, at least relatively speaking, perhaps because Spain’s key defensive players are unaccustomed to facing them too often. Pau Cubarsí’s Barcelona conceded the second fewest crosses per game of the 96 clubs in Europe’s big five leagues last season. Athletic Bilbao, featuring the other two-thirds of Spain’s first-choice combination of goalkeeper and centre-backs (Unai Simón and Aymeric Laporte), were joint-ninth. Cubarsí and Laporte each contested fewer than four aerial duels per 90 minutes; many centre-backs in the Premier League won, let alone contested, more than that. Balls in the air are a much bigger part of the game in England, where ‘they kick the ball into the opponent’s box and fight with them’, to re-quote Tuchel.

In an age of tactical sophistication, crossing is deemed too inefficient. It is very old-school, leaning heavily on English football stereotypes. But we are not plotting out the development programme at St George’s Park for the future of the game, we are trying to see how England can score in one match against the meanest defence in international football.

If Trent Alexander-Arnold is keen to get back into Tuchel’s good books, delivering a trademark cross onto the head of Harry Kane against Spain would be a strong starting point. There may be no other way for him or England to prosper against the world champions.

Sports.title: We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights
Sports.content:
It couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of City had come to an abrupt end when more than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.

Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learned there were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken has come home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.

After all, this is a club that believes schadenfreude starts at home. We brag about our failings. Other songs we sing include “Empty seats at home” (to the tune of the Beautiful South’s Rotterdam) because we can’t sell out our tickets and “Is This the Etihad?” (to La donna è mobile from Verdi’s Rigoletto, natch) at deathly quiet away grounds.

It’s not about tempting fate. Nor is it hubristic irony – we can’t sell out despite winning all these trophies. It’s simply an acceptance that one way or another we’ll always be City, always suffer from Cityitis, and come the day, despite our endless UAE riches, we’ll do a City.

And that day has come. We don’t know what our fate, or sentence, is yet. When I interviewed Wayne Rooney recently he suggested we would have 60 points docked, making it virtually impossible for us to avoid relegation.

It could be worse, of course. We could lose all eight trophies we won in the period (2009-10 to 2017-18) we flouted fair play, including three Premier League titles and our record-breaking centurions season when we won with 100 points in 2017-18. To me, that would be disproportionate and would in effect mean the Premier League eating itself.

But is the verdict itself unjust? City will say yes because they don’t want anything as petty as fair-play rules thwarting their bid for global domination. The lawyers will say yes because they’re paid to do so. Many fans will say yes because they’re fans. But some of us believe we’re bang to rights.

Everton and Nottingham Forest have been docked points for lesser offences, so it would be embarrassing if City had got away with it; an undeniable case of one rule for the rich. Despite City’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed. Although it appears this is not the end because City intend to appeal.

View image in fullscreen The 2017-18 Premier League title may be one of eight trophies that Manchester City fear losing. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Our behaviour has been pretty outrageous at Dodge City. Failing to provide accurate and up-to-date financial reports, concealing salary details and bonuses, inflating sponsorship revenues and failing to cooperate or supply requested documents during the investigation all feature on the charge sheet. We used lawyers to royally take the piss. And when it comes down to it, that is not very City. After all, this is a club founded in 1880 as St Mark’s (West Gorton) by members of St Mark’s Church of England for humanitarian and social rescue purposes to serve the deprived area of east Manchester, where Shameless was filmed a century later.

So what happens next? We may lose trophies. We will almost certainly get relegated. We almost certainly lose our best players and say ha det bra to Erling Haaland, the great Nordic God of goalscoring (having said that he may stay just to see how many he could get in a Championship season). And we start building again.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If the very worst happens, and we lose all those trophies, at least we still have our anni mirabiles when we did the unprecedented domestic quadruple (2018-19), and treble including the Champions League (2022-23). There was barely a whiff of scandal in these years. We were simply obscenely wealthy, brilliantly run and managed by the world’s numero uno Pep Guardiola.

And plenty of positives will come out of our disgrace. The biggest being that justice is done. But there is so much more. City may get to play in the Championship where we enjoyed some of our finest moments (“We’ve got Kevin Keegan 100 goals a season,” sung to the tune of Let’s All Do the Conga a mere 24 years ago). League One? Halcyon days. For City fans of a certain age and disposition, beating Gillingham in the playoff is our top footballing memory. League Two? Thrill of the unknown. The only way is up, as the song goes.

Ticket prices come down, allowing regular civilians back into the Etihad. Prices become so low that we fill the ground. Fans begin to realise Wembley visits and winning trophies are to be treasured. Pep has already gone so there’s no danger of losing him. We learn some humility and stop coming over all sullen because we’ve only won the League Cup and FA Cup in one season.

Perhaps the biggest positive is that rather than simply pulling out the chequebook and signing the world’s best, we learn to think imaginatively. I noticed the God of Bermudan goalscoring Shaun Goater this year left his job coaching Aston Villa Women. He’s only 56, never relied entirely on pace, and I bet he’s a free agent.

Sports.title: Burnham’s booze ruse is a non-starter: just keep doing your drinking in the pub | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I don’t believe any child should eat gravel for breakfast. That’s why we’ve launched the National No Gravel Breakfast initiative. Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I think everyone should have access to sitting on a chair no matter if they live in the north or the chair-rich south. Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I don’t think pensioners should be required to stab themselves in the hand with cocktail sticks. Unless that’s what they want. In which case I will personally do this for them.

Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I believe in a mother’s love, the laughter of baby horses and beautifully crisp and gooey churros straight from the pan. Unless you don’t want those. In which case I believe you have that choice and I will fight for it. Or not fight for it. Whichever.

In the absence of a manifesto or an actual election campaign, it feels like the best place to experience raw, unfiltered Burnham-ism, to really get a handle on his vision as mid-season firefighting prime minister, is the videos on his LinkedIn page. Which are pretty good and, yeah, he seems nice, and like he generally agrees with me, so that’s fine.

This is not a criticism of Burnham. It seems a pretty clear-sighted strategy on his part, mainly because politics is ridiculous now. Keir Starmer is widely seen as perhaps the worst prime minister of all time, the man who lost control of immigration and did something terrible to the economy. Reality: immigration went down under Starmer. The economy is sluggish but not terrible. Starmer was above all a terrible communicator, choosing to make every public statement in that fussy, nasal upwards-register, like a notably dull and pissy professional angler explaining at great length why your waterproof trousers are inadequate.

View image in fullscreen The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has a pint in a pub, which is a much better place to have a pint than a football stadium. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

Burnham does seem to have a more state-of-the-art understanding of presentation. Most notably of the fact he must perform two simultaneous roles. First, the public one, which is basically a cover job, a way of stopping people reflexively hating him, as they must now hate all politicians in the end. Meanwhile any actual politics, the usual hard choices and compromises, will have to be Trojan-horsed beneath that. This may seem undesirable, but it’s a choice we have forced on these people, and a method that might actually allow him to at least get something done before he is inevitably chewed up by the rage and stupidity of the digital hive mind.

It is in this context that his comments this week about drinking in the stands at football must be interpreted. By now Burnham’s off-the-cuff response to a question has been sliced and diced and generally dismissed. It is worth adding some further context, pointing out exactly why this is not just a pointless idea but a bad one. But the most interesting part of his most significant engagement so far with football, the great public megaphone, is what it says about Burnham himself.

First up, this is just a dead issue. Burnham was just re-stating a long-held personal opinion, not making policy, or expressing any real intention to do anything. He’s in a period of ambient electioneering. In his mind this is an easy issue, a free hit, like saying yes we must have more chocolate at Christmas. It won’t actually happen. Alcohol has been banned within sight of the pitch since the late 1980s, and with good reason. I love drinking. I’m a fan, a cheerleader, a devotee. I love the softness, the booze-haze, the first three drinks, that delicious transition from sober towards something else that is always the best part, the bit you keep chasing across all the lost drinks that must inevitably follow. But really, come on.

Of all the many problems facing the nation, insufficient access to alcohol really doesn’t seem like a hot-button issue. Currently the average urban centre has 60 booze outlets per square mile. Maybe if you’re spending your days skipping warily between a shotgunned bottle of Oyster Bay in the Nisa local and the five-minute walk up the road to the Meatbag and Carrot, it would genuinely help if you could stagger into Loftus Road for a pint of warm Foster’s on the way. But nobody really needs to be more drunk at football. And if you really must drink, it’s not that hard to smuggle in the gin flask.

View image in fullscreen Fans can drink in their seats in the top two divisions of women’s football, but there is little indication that the men’s professional game will follow suit. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

Young people also don’t really drink. And many people who already feel excluded; new fans, women in particular, feel doubly uncomfortable around a pissed-up football crowd. As a final hard pass, within three minutes of re-legalising this, someone somewhere is chucking a pint in the air. No thanks.

The most interesting part of all this is that Burnham chose booze and football as an obviously tribal issue, choosing to introduce the idea of “discrimination”, as though people who want to drink at football are a lobby group, an oppressed section of society, or even any kind of identifiable demographic. Hang on, you can drink at the opera! Well, yes, but you also can’t sing songs at the opera, do the Poznan or call people wankers. Different environments have different rules. And plenty of people at the opera will have hot-footed it there from consuming the Premier League. What was the point again?

If we really are going to make this an-us-and-them issue I can kill it right here on Burnham’s own terms. This is a bad idea because it would help to close down pubs, and shovel money instead into the pockets of clubs owned by hedge funds. You might say buying a couple of pints in sight of a football pitch isn’t going to change pub culture. But that’s not how it works. That minor prohibition has helped create a culture of external football drinking, and this is one of the few physical match-day elements to exist outside football’s corporate force field.

Pubs are great and vital places. I love all of them. Urban pubs with flat felt roofs. Pubs with mock-Tudor cream cheese wall-coverings, unlike any other building known to man. Pubs that sell obscure brands of pub-only crisps. Crucially, pubs still provide a third space, a place where people can meet, where men actually speak. And they thrive around football grounds.

An amazing and deeply cheering fact: there are 174 active pubs within a one-mile radius of St James’ Park. Molineux has 50 pubs, Portman Road 29. Arsenal 33. When Andy Burnham sits down at Everton with Mark Carney and feels annoyed he can’t buy a £9 Peroni, he is also just a 15-minute walk from 23 public bars that survive purely on selling liquid to thirsty people.

All pubs operate on fine margins. Matchdays are their rush hour, guaranteed mega-rounds, a captive footfall. Why would you divert even the tiniest bit of that money to the wildly commodified institutional leisure facility up the road? Also, just to kill this once and for all, you can imagine how awful the fully realised Premier League experience will be? In related football news, it also emerged this week that Manchester United are literally selling off the pitch, just fully giving up on irony and leaning into it. We’ve hollowed this place out, chucked the bentwood chairs on the fire, sold your memories back to you. Yeah we can do a pub. Another round of deliciously fruity Yorke and Cole Witbier sir? Why would you put more money into this, and not into a place with a furry carpet that still performs some kind of authentic social function?

So much for all that. It won’t happen. The police don’t want it. Burnham was just re-sharing a personal opinion. But it does tell you something valuable about his reflexive way of thinking. The idea that this is a vital cultural issue is pure 1980s, from a time when to be interested in football was to be dismissed as a thug, an unwanted emissary of the undeserving working class.

View image in fullscreen Would the prime ministerial joint visit to Hill Dickinson really have been improved by a warm, overpriced pitch-side lager? Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

This is not the case now. Instead, football is the cultural imperialist, out there inflicting itself on everything else, always, always selling. And this is also a first very obvious example of playing to a base that exists most vividly only in his own cultural milieu.

There has been a successful projection of the new prime minister as fresh and novel, a figure from the outside. Which is not bad going for a Blair-era spad who will be 57 in January, the same age as Jacob Rees-Mogg and Woodstock.

But football is always telling you things. The response to that slight false note, a wider head-scratch over what is essentially a non-issue, is useful information. Time for a drink and a rethink.

Sports.title: Gary Lineker's podcast empire records soaring profit worth nearly £10MILLION after landing mega-money Netflix deal - as former Match of the Day presenter nets £1m payday
Sports.content:
Gary Lineker's podcast empire records soaring profit worth nearly £10MILLION after landing mega-money Netflix deal - as former Match of the Day presenter nets £1m payday

The podcast empire fronted by Gary Lineker has recorded a sensational £10million profit following a deal with Netflix – with the former England forward pocketing £1million from the success.

Financial records show Goalhanger Podcasts Ltd recorded £38million in revenue in 2025, with £5million paid out to shareholders – up from just £36,000 in 2024.

The firm behind his The Rest Is Football show with Alan Shearer and Micah Richards is also responsible for hits The Rest Is History; The Rest Is Politics, hosted by Rory Stewart and Alastair Campbell; and The Rest Is Entertainment with Richard Osman and Marina Hyde.

Goalhanger, so named as a nod to the former England striker's football career, continued to boom in popularity after Lineker stepped down in 2025 from his 26-year tenure on show Match of the Day and his £1,350,000 salary.

It is understood the company makes around two-thirds of its revenue from advertising while also increasing the number of paying subscribers, which is now around the 250,000 mark.

Netflix also struck a deal with Goalhanger to stream its The Rest Is Football podcast during the World Cup. Lineker fronted the show with Shearer, Richards and Joe Cole.

Gary Lineker (centre) has pocketed £1million after his podcast empire made £10m in profits

Financial records show Goalhanger Podcasts Ltd recorded £38m in revenue in 2025

The agreement has since been extended for two years.

The Rest Is Football has more than seven million monthly streams. Last year, it had more than 667million plays on audio and video across 13 shows.

The company said it has 'exceeded its own expectations in audience reach, engagement and financial performance, establishing a strong foundation for future expansion'.

It added: 'The company's partnerships with Spotify, YouTube and Apple have expanded our reach and we continue to work closely with platforms to understand how we can meet our audiences and advertisers where they are.'

Lineker's career shift from Match of the Day followed significant controversy over politically opinionated social media posts, notably a controversial Instagram post concerning Zionism that featured a depiction of a rat – an image historically associated with antisemitic motifs.

He continues to work in presenting, and is currently hosting celebrity challenge show The Box on ITV.

Goalhanger, which employs 80 people in its London HQ, is owned by the ex-footballer alongside Tony Pastor, a former controller of sport at ITV, and former journalist Jack Davenport.

Lineker holds an equity stake of at least 25 per cent, according to Companies House, which funnels into his estimated net worth of £30million.

Lineker presents The Rest Is Football with BBC pundits Micah Richards (left) and Alan Shearer

The company, founded in 2018, entices more than 750 million listeners to tune into the catalogue of shows – which boomed in popularity during the pandemic.

As the franchise continued to boom, Los Angeles-based investment firm The Chernin Group (TCG) bought a minority share in January this year. Greg Bettinelli, a partner of the firm, is now a director in the business.

TCG, which is led by media mogul Peter Chernin, is behind the production of blockbuster films including Planet Of The Apes and The Greatest Showman.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua in chaos as Gypsy King claims rival wants to pull OUT of  £150m Cardiff mega fight just over 24 hours after bout was confirmed
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury’s heavyweight blockbuster with Anthony Joshua has been thrown into chaos after the Gypsy King claimed his rival is pulling out of the Cardiff contest.

In a dramatic escalation a little over 24 hours after their £150million bout was confirmed, Fury took to Instagram to say the fight is now in jeopardy owing to a feud between Joshua’s promoter Eddie Hearn and the UFC’s Dana White.

White, who runs Zuffa Boxing alongside Saudi Arabia’s boxing supremo Turki Al-Sheikh, has been billed as the main promoter for the heavyweight showdown and had fought for the contest to take place in New York City.

Hearn, who successfully wrestled the fight back to Cardiff, has claimed that the contract Joshua signed stipulates that White cannot be involved in the contest.

In an expletive-laden Instagram video, Fury claimed the fight has been cancelled because of Hearn's ego – and that he is 'making up a million different things'.

He said: 'Breaking News: Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight they are saying he is not going to fight now.

'They're little s*** house cowards, mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego, he's making up a million different things and threatening that "we're not going to fight" you little coward.

'AJ pull your finger out you white flag, yellow-bellied coward. You know now we're coming home, now I'm coming home the Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales.'

Tyson Fury announced the news in a video on social media

Fury and Joshua's fight was due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair were set to meet for a press conference next week on September 30

Fury exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight in April 2026

Fury went on to call Joshua a 'body-building sausage'.

He also claimed that Al-Sheikh is now looking to find a new person to fight Fury at 'the drop of a hat'.

Fury continued: 'So I hope [Hearn and Joshua] are happy you little cowardly b*******, I've never seen anything like [Hearn and Joshua] you pure s*** houses and this is mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. What a little p****.'

The 38-year-old then posted a mocked up poster of himself and light heavyweight champion David Benavidez, hinting that the 29-year-old American could replace AJ in the Cardiff contest.

Fury and Joshua, 36, are due to meet on September 30 in a pre-fight press conference, but Hearn warned that White – who he labelled a ‘loser’ and a ‘soppy t**’ after the fight was confirmed – must not be present at the London face off.

But Fury now claims that this latest demand could see the fight unravel. In a stinging response, Al-Sheikh also threw his weight behind White by posting a photo of the American smoking a cigar on Instagram.

It is understood that both men would have pocketed around £75million for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil.

Hearn had also succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York.

Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff.

The event, broadcast on Netflix, was expected to take place around 2am to accommodate a US audience.

This is a breaking news story. More to follow.

Sports.title: Football finance expert reveals why a points deduction is 'the most likely' punishment for Man City, whether Liverpool and Man United can claim 'robbed' Premier League titles and the compensation can of worms that awaits
Sports.content:
Football finance expert reveals why a points deduction is 'the most likely' punishment for Man City, whether Liverpool and Man United can claim 'robbed' Premier League titles and the compensation can of worms that awaits

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire has revealed the 'most likely' outcome for Manchester City following their charges is a points deduction.

City and their fans, despite an almost-certain appeal, are nervously awaiting punishment after they were found guilty on the vast majority of their 115 charges around financial irregularities against the Premier League.

A number of cards are on the table, including financial punishments, a loss of points and the stripping of titles.

As is relegation, which could come into play if City are dealt a heavy deduction this season. And that, according to Kieran Maguire, is likely.

'There is no doubt a points deduction would be the most likely outcome in the view of many,' Maguire said on TalkTV. 'We have seen them before for Nottingham Forest and Everton for breach of the financial limit rules. So that is feasible.'

It remains unclear what sort of punishment could be handed out, though, and things could yet get worse for the eight-time Premier League champions.

“A POINTS DEDUCTION WOULD BE THE MOST LIKELY OUTCOME.”



Football finance expert Kieran Maguire explains the possible scenarios for Manchester City after they were found guilty of a huge number of financial rule breaches in a bombshell judgment.@CharlieRowley18 @KieranMaguire pic.twitter.com/91E8mlaKD2 — Talk (@TalkTV) September 26, 2026

A football finance expert has warned Manchester City will likely face a points deduction after their guilty charges - pictured, City striker Erling Haaland

'If you take a look at the Premier League handbook,' Maguire added, 'it says the recommendations are as broad based as you want them to be. Anything from a fine, to a points deduction, to expulsion from the league.

'Also, it could be that the titles won during that period will be taken away, though you can't retrospectively have the joy that winning a match and title brings from a fans' perspective.'

In that case, a number of clubs could find themselves up on their major honours, with the likes of Manchester United and Liverpool set to benefit if City are stripped of titles.

A number of former United players have taken to social media to suggest they should now have more trophies to their names, while City also won the likes of the League Cup and FA Cup in the period of which they have been charged.

David De Gea, for example, posted on X: 'So…… Let's talk. How many Premier League titles have I won then?'

De Gea played for United from 2011 to 2023, winning the league title in the 2012-13 season.

If City were to hypothetically be stripped of their recent titles, though, he could be quids in.

Man United finished second in the Premier League in the 2011-12 season – the year De Gea joined the club, were then also runners-up in the 2017-18 campaign, in which De Gea played 37 of the 38 league games, and the 2020-21 season, with the Spaniard featuring in 26 league matches.

Former Man United players Rio Ferdinand (left) and David De Gea (right) have called for City to be stripped of titles

Rio Ferdinand was also keen to state his case, posting on X: 'Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet.'

Former United manager Jose Mourinho, meanwhile, said in 2024: 'We won the Europa League and finished second in the Premier League. I think we still have a chance to win that league. Maybe they punish Manchester City with points, we win that league. And then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal.'

Some have also likened the situation to that which faced Juventus 20 years ago. In 2006, the Italian giants were relegated, given a 30-point deduction and were stripped of two top-division titles after they were found to have been involved in conduct amounting to sporting fraud.

A can of worms could therefore be opened, and clubs will no doubt be eager to claim what they believe is theirs – whether that be in trophies or money.

Maguire pointed to the fee Everton were ordered to pay Burnley after they were found guilty of breaches in the 2021-22 season, which the Clarets argued helped Everton stay in the Premier League at their expense.

'Then there is a separate issue where clubs who have lost out on titles could put in financial compensation for not getting into Europe,' Maguire added. 'For loss of prize money

'We do have a precedent where Everton were told they had to give Burnley £35million for a single breach in a single season.'

Sports.title: Noel Gallagher pleads for Man City NOT to be punished with club facing threat of relegation as superfan opens up on his 'shock' after learning of bombshell 115 verdict
Sports.content:
Noel Gallagher pleads for Man City NOT to be punished with club facing threat of relegation as superfan opens up on his 'shock' after learning of bombshell 115 verdict

Oasis superstar and Manchester City fan Noel Gallagher has pleaded for mercy after his club were found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 financial charges levelled against them.

Gallagher, alongside brother and bandmate Liam, is a big City fan and regularly attends games with his sons.

He is also close friends with former manager Pep Guardiola, and went into the club's dressing room after they won the 2018-19 Premier League title.

Gallagher has been left reeling after it was revealed that City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 financial charges against them - casting doubt on the legitimacy of their trophy-laden spell under the club's Abu Dhabi ownership.

The Oasis songwriter revealed he has been left in 'shock' by the verdict, but implored football's decision-making bodies not to punish the supporters or players for 'whatever goes on in the boardroom'.

'A little surprised because only that the club has assured us all along that they would vehemently deny any of these charges,' he said on the Let Me Talk podcast.

'So it was a bit of a shock to find out we've been found guilty of all but one but really overall quite sad really, sad for the fans and for the players.

🎙️ LET ME TALK: THE CHARGES



Join @SamLee, @DomFarrell1986, Noel Gallagher, and @DavidMooney to discuss:

🔹 City found guilty

🔹 What does this all mean?

🔹 What next?

🔹 Feelings about the past decade now



🎧 Sign up to listen in any podcast app: https://t.co/WZJtHxW1Yn pic.twitter.com/71uDfU2Tch — Let Me Talk (@LMTPod) September 26, 2026

Noel Gallagher, a close friend of Pep Guardiola, says the fans and players should not be punished after City were found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges

'Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw: they won it on the pitch. Whatever goes on in the boardroom it's nothing to do with the supporters or the players, the players won the game and won that (2011-12) title on the pitch.

'Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that's nothing to do with the fans. We were there, we know what we saw. Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.'

City are set to appeal the decision but any punishment is now expected to follow, with some fans calling for the club to be stripped of the trophies they won at the time.

There had initially been confusion around the time period that the charges relate to, with the initial offences ranging from the 2009-10 season to the 2017-18 campaign.

There are then further charges surrounding failure to comply with the investigation, which range from December 2018 to February 2023.

It remains unclear what any punishment could be, though the threat of relegation appears a legitimate possibility.

Gallagher joked a fortnight ago that his 'heart is full of pride' after his 15-year-old son flipped his middle finger at Man United fans during City's derby win at Old Trafford.

Sonny Gallagher celebrated alongside his brother Donovan, 18, and their Oasis rockstar father Noel, 59, in the stands 62 minutes into the game, with City a man down after Phil Foden's red card.

The teenager flipped off rival fans in the stands and jeered as star striker Haaland netted in the second-half what later proved to be the winner.

Sports.title: The clubs who could seek compensation as Premier League sides consider legal action after Man City found guilty of vast majority of rule breaches - and what happens next: Key questions answered
Sports.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations.

The competition accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.

The long-awaited verdict has now been reached with the belief it is a victory for the Premier League, despite Man City having strenuously denied the charges.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation.

Daily Mail Sport's Mike Keegan provides answers to the key questions, including the next steps, Man City's expected appeal and how serious the punishment could be.

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 Premier League rule-break charges

WHAT DOES IT MEAN?

This cannot be viewed as anything other than an overwhelming victory for the Premier League.

To see Manchester City found guilty of the ‘vast majority’ of the 115 charges is an outcome that Richard Masters will no doubt see as vindication for what has been a costly, long-running legal battle in which the stakes were incredibly high.

It is safe to assume that had the tables turned the other way, the chief executive would have been in P45 territory.

More important than that, those who City feel were the key protagonists, the so-called ‘Red Cartel’, will also feel vindication.

To put it simply, Manchester City have been found guilty of cheating their way to success between 2009 and 2018, a period when they dominated English football.

The verdict cannot be viewed as anything other than an overwhelming victory for the Premier League and its chief executive Richard Masters

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

There has been no statement from the Premier League, while City’s only says that the process remains ongoing and is subject to strict confidentiality.

What is clear is that City will appeal. What is not clear is whether the sanction will drop before any appeal.

WHAT ARE THE PUNISHMENTS?

Take your pick. Hefty points deductions, potential relegation and transfer bans are all on the table. Rule W51 in the Premier League handbook states ambiguously that ‘such other penalty as it shall think fit’ is an option.

There is, however, a scepticism among some, based on a lack of noise from many of the other clubs and the lenient punishment recently handed to Chelsea that whatever penalty lands will not see City stripped of titles or relegated. ‘They’ll get a slap on the wrist and ordered to pay legal costs and not much else,’ one exec predicted.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation

HOW DOES AN APPEAL WORK?

In all likelihood City will appeal and recent cases tell us that they tend to be dealt with expeditiously.

An appeal board would be set up, appointed by the chair of the panel and, again, featuring three people. Some feel that this would be an exercise in the Premier League marking its own homework.

At this early stage, it is worth an assumption that City could argue the panel was not impartial. The bad news for them, however, is that this is a high bar to clear.

Unlike City’s case with UEFA, it cannot go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (who overturned UEFA’s findings).

WHAT ABOUT COMPENSATION?

Last year, in a move believed to have been instigated by former Arsenal chief executive Tim Lewis, the Gunners, Tottenham Hotspur, Liverpool and Manchester United served legal notices reserving their right to take action.

Should the verdict stand, they will then seek damages for a wide variety of issues. The most costly claims are likely to come from those who say they missed out on Champions League qualification during the period in question thanks to City’s law breaking. But the scope would not end there.

Clubs could also, for example, argue that as a result of the breaches they were unable to sign a calibre of player that would have allowed them to be more successful on the field. Some believe £200m would not be out of the question, but that remains to be seen.

Ex-Arsenal chief executive is understood to have instigated a move last year that saw the Gunners, Tottenham, Liverpool and Man United served legal notices reserving their right to take action

WHAT ABOUT THE INDEPENDENT FOOTBALL REGULATOR?

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Regulator declined to comment when contacted by Daily Mail Sport. However, David Kogan will be well aware of the situation.

The IFR was brought in for a variety of reasons, not least to ensure that those owning the nation’s football clubs were fit and proper to do so. The IFR would have the power to force City’s owners to sell, but such a scenario is viewed as unlikely.

DIDN’T CITY TRIUMPH OVER THE PREMIER LEAGUE RECENTLY ON SPONSORSHIP RULES?

They did, with three senior judges deeming the rules unlawful. As a result, a series of amendments were made. City again launched a legal challenge, but surprisingly came to an agreement with the Premier League in September. Those cases, however, were always separate to the 115, as it became known.

Sports.title: Former Man United star David De Gea echoes Rio Ferdinand's calls for Man City to be STRIPPED of 2011-12 crown after 115 charges verdict: 'So, how many Premier League titles have I won?'
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United players are continuing to weigh in on Manchester City's guilty verdict with the Premier League – and David De Gea is keen to know how many Premier League titles he may end up with by the time it all comes to a head.

A guilty verdict has been delivered on the vast majority of City's 115 rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations. The competition accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.

City are set to appeal the decision but any punishment is now expected to follow, with some fans calling for the club to be stripped of the trophies they won at the time.

There had initially been confusion around the time period that the charges relate to, with the initial offences ranging from the 2009-10 season to the 2017-18 campaign.

There are then further charges surrounding failure to comply with the investigation, which range from December 2018 to February 2023.

With potential punishments on the line, former players are now looking to see what retrospective success may now come their way – including De Gea.

David De Gea (left) has echoed Rio Ferdinand's calls to strip Man City of trophies following their guilty verdicts

'So…… Let’s talk,' he posted on X. 'How many Premier League titles have I won then?'

De Gea played for United from 2011 to 2023, winning the league title in the 2012-13 season.

If City were to hypothetically be stripped of their recent titles, though, he could be quids in.

Man United finished second in the Premier League in the 2011-12 season - the year De Gea joined the club, were then also runners-up in the 2017-18 campaign, in which De Gea played 37 of the 38 league games, and the 2020-21 season, with the Spaniard featuring in 26 league matches.

Rio Ferdinand was also keen to state his case, posting on X: 'Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet.'

Ferdinand's United came second to City in the 2011-12 season, which saw Sergio Aguero score a last-minute goal against QPR to win the league ahead of the Red Devils.

The win marked City's first-ever Premier League title, and they would go on to claim seven more top flight titles, plus a plethora of other trophies.

Former United defender Gary Neville has also previously called the case a 'disgrace' and 'stain on the game', while ex-midfielder Paul Scholes had formerly said a guilty verdict would 'be bad for the integrity of Manchester City'.

Sports.title: Rodri issues defiant response to Man City being found guilty of vast majority of Premier League rule break charges as former star insists he 'believes' in the club despite verdict
Sports.content:
Former Manchester City captain Rodri insists he 'believes in the club' and their success cannot be taken away after they were found guilty of the vast majority of their Premier League rule break charges.

Rodri, whose seven-year spell at Man City ended in the summer when he moved to Barcelona, became the first individual associated with the club to speak following the bombshell news on Friday.

Daily Mail Sport understands Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 charges by an independent panel.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties and even relegation.

Points deductions could even be applied onto previous seasons, raising the chance that City will be stripped of their Premier League titles.

When asked about the verdict ahead of Spain's Nations League match against England on Saturday, Rodri reiterated his belief Man City will be found innocent.

Rodri has insisted Man City's success cannot be taken away from them despite the club being found guilty of the majority their Premier League rule break charges

The former Man City captain insisted he believes in the innocence of the club amid the verdict

The midfielder referenced a previous 2020 decision which saw Man City banned from the Champions League and fined by UEFA for a breach of financial rules, which was later lifted on appeal by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9million.

'We have faced something similar in 2020 if I remember correctly, a similar process, a different accusation but similar process.

‘In the first instance we were found guilty but we believed in the club and the innocence the club maintained, and in the end we ended up being acquitted.

‘I believe in the justice system and I believe in the innocence of the club.’

When asked whether he had been given assurances by the club of their innocence, Rodri added: 'They always tell us the confidence of their innocence and when you look in someone’s eyes and they are talking in that way – and we have the example of 2020 the process was the same and at the end nothing happened – we were very calm in this way.

'We were never a team that was nervous about these kind of things. I am not going to say it is normal but some teams go through these situations and it is part of football today.

'Everyone has to follow the rules and for me that’s great. They always expressed the confidence they never did anything wrong and we believe in that, and that’s the thing.

'We will believe the club. I have been there and I know how they work and how they cooperate.'

Rodri insisted Man City's success was 'deserved' and the result of hard work from the players and staff

Rodri won four Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, three Carabao Cups and a FIFA Club World Cup during a glittering spell at Man City under Pep Guardiola.

When asked whether he it hurt that Man City's achievements have been questioned, Rodri insisted the success of the players and staff during that period cannot be taken away.

'For us, the players, it is a different thing. For you guys there are all kinds of opinions but we always tried to think in a positive way,' Rodri said.

'When you live daily in that club and all the people that worked hard all these years to have all the success we have had, not only Pep [Guardiola] and the players, but from the owners to the guys that work daily, what we did they cannot take it out of us.

'It is not something that is paid by money, it is paid with effort and partnership, being shoulder to shoulder every day.

'We had a lot of success over the years and I can tell you that everything was deserved and I am glad I could live one of the best eras in English football.'

Man City are set to appeal the verdict.

A Manchester City spokesperson said: 'The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

'The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'

The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal

Man City, who have always strongly denied wrongdoing, were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.

Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.

The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period.

A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.

The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.

City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.

The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

Sports.title: Inside Alejandro Garnacho's Aston Villa struggles: The doubt over who really signed him from Chelsea, ominous signs behind the scenes that won't please Unai Emery - and how Argentine can still win him over
Sports.content:
Inside Alejandro Garnacho's Aston Villa struggles: The doubt over who really signed him from Chelsea, ominous signs behind the scenes that won't please Unai Emery - and how Argentine can still win him over

Surely it cannot be happening again. Aston Villa have already spent one season paying a substantial salary to a loan player they did not want. Would they really repeat that mistake?

‘Harvey Elliott’ is the name people remember when they look at Alejandro Garnacho’s situation at Villa Park. The same terms – loan with a conditional obligation to buy – and the same lack of playing time.

By last autumn, Unai Emery had decided he did not wish to sign Elliott permanently and therefore, under the terms of his loan agreement, he was able to make just nine appearances across that campaign before going back to Liverpool.

At that stage of his Villa career, Elliott had played 118 minutes, even though he joined the club only at the end of the summer 2025 transfer window. Garnacho arrived at Villa Park and has featured for only 31 so far.

The £43million transfer next summer, as detailed in the loan arrangement with Chelsea and which will happen if certain targets are hit, is already looking unlikely.

There is still plenty of time for Garnacho to alter the course of this story. Villa play two friendlies during the break, one of which is against Sevilla in Spain on October 2. Garnacho owes it to himself to attack this training camp with all his heart. The rest of his time at Villa may depend on it.

Alejandro Garnacho has had a miserable start to life at Aston Villa, featuring for just 31 minutes so far this season

‘We are delighted with Alejandro,’ said Unai Emery at Garnacho's unveiling. ‘He is so talented.' But that positivity already feels like ancient history

Why Garnacho?

Not long after the final whistle in Aston Villa's 3-1 win at Coventry on September 16, Garnacho was heading out of the CBS Arena and en route to the Villa team bus. With Emery making changes for the Carabao Cup clash, many had expected Garnacho to start. He did not even make it on to the pitch.

Any player would be disappointed in that situation, especially one with nearly 200 senior appearances and eight caps for Argentina before the age of 23. It is also understood there were no compulsory post-match exercises as the players were due to train the following morning.

Generally, though, constant application is the route to Emery’s heart as the Spaniard demands ‘serious, mature, responsible’ players.

Emery may not be pitchside after matches but nothing escapes him.

His backroom team will tell him exactly what happened during the post-match running drills: which exercises were performed, which players gave their all, which – if any – were slacking off.

Garnacho was left on the bench at Tottenham three days later, too, and may not even have made the squad had Brazilian winger Alysson been fit.

The attraction of Garnacho is obvious. Even though he struggled at Chelsea last season, between 2023-25 he scored 21 goals and had 17 assists for Manchester United. Emery has wanted an incisive wide attacker ever since he came to Villa and on the face of it, Garnacho ticked the boxes.

Yet the nagging doubt remains: was Emery truly desperate to sign him, the way he was desperate to bring in Morgan Rogers in January 2024, or Marco Asensio on loan a year later, or Nicolas Jackson this summer?

If Emery were, it seems surprising that he would then promote academy prospect George Hemmings above Garnacho and sign off on the £50m deal for Ibrahim Mbaye, who can play on either flank. Not to mention his early-season backing for Alysson.

Not long after the final whistle in Aston Villa's 3-1 win at Coventry on September 16, Garnacho (pictured the week before) was heading out of the CBS Arena and en route to the Villa team bus

Garnacho stayed in his tracksuit at Tottenham three days later, too, and may not even have made the squad had Brazilian winger Alysson been fit

Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and Chelsea counterpart Behdad Eghbali are also thought to enjoy good relations though Emery laughed off suggestions last month that the two clubs, both on the naughty step with UEFA for breaching financial rules, would ever help each other.

‘They want to kill us, and we want to kill them,’ he said. ‘They signed Morgan and Emiliano Martinez to kill us.’

The facts are these: Garnacho joined Villa from Chelsea on July 23, two days after Rogers had moved in the opposite direction for a record £117m. Chelsea and Villa traded four players this summer alone, with Martinez moving to Stamford Bridge along with Rogers, and Jackson joining Garnacho in the West Midlands. Set-piece coach Austin MacPhee swapped Villa for Chelsea, too.

Clubs can deal with one another as they see fit but unless Garnacho starts to play regularly, we will always wonder about the exact circumstances that led him to Villa.

Can Garnacho turn it around?

After Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho, Garnacho is the third player to lose his way at United and turn up at Villa on loan not long afterwards.

The spell at Villa Park in the second half of 2024-25 revived Rashford’s career. Though he could not help Villa qualify for the Champions League, he did enough under Emery to earn a year’s loan at Barcelona and make the England squad for the World Cup. Rashford is now playing for United again, which seemed impossible only a year ago.

On the flipside, Sancho started only nine Premier League games for Villa and is now without a club after leaving Old Trafford last summer. Reports in Russia this week said the 26-year-old was in discussions with top-flight club Krasnodar. Emery had really wanted Rashford; Sancho not so much.

Whose path will Garnacho follow? Playing for Emery can be exhausting but there are still relatively painless ways to impress him.

Emery has already ticked off Garnacho for dawdling on the touchline when preparing to come on

The Villa boss reignited Marcus Rashford's career after he fell out of favour at Man United. Can he do the same for Garnacho?

Lucas Digne, for example, won his boss over partly by turning up for extra sessions on his days off. ‘Continue working,’ said Emery when asked how Garnacho can force his way into the team. ‘Work, work, train, work.’

There is another simple rule with Emery: a player can catch the eye as much he likes on the ball but if he does not follow instructions when Villa do not have possession, he will not play very often.

Emery has already ticked off Garnacho for dawdling on the touchline when preparing to come on and has admitted Garnacho could have done better in his early appearances. These are not good signs.

Listening actively in meetings, both individual and collective, is also key. Emery will explain in painstaking detail what he wants from a player. If he does not deliver it, woe betide him.

Emery will not tailor his approach to young people with short attention spans. It’s his immersive way – repetitive training sessions, 90-minute video briefings, detailed tactical breakdowns – or nothing. With 12 major trophies to his name, why should he change?

After significant turnover this summer, Emery is relying even more on a cohort of senior players who have been at Villa throughout his time – John McGinn, Matty Cash, Tyrone Mings, Emi Buendia. They emphasise to new signings exactly what is needed to succeed at the club.

The smart ones listen and learn. There is no suggestion that Garnacho, a shy, quiet individual, is disruptive but clearly he is not doing enough to convince Emery and right now few at Bodymoor Heath can see a path to regular first-team football.

There is mitigation: Garnacho suffered a nasty facial injury during a pre-season fixture against Thai club BG Pathum United, which slowed his progress and meant he did not feature in the UEFA Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain. Playing on the wing for Emery is also the most tactically demanding role on the pitch and very few master it immediately.

Daily Mail Sport understands Garnacho scored the only goal in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Southampton yesterday. That won't do his cause any harm.

Garnacho’s career is still in his own hands – though Sancho’s tale should be fresh in his mind.

There is no suggestion that Garnacho is disruptive but clearly he is not doing enough and right now few at Bodymoor Heath can see a path to regular first-team football

How does the story end?

Watch Garnacho’s first interview at Villa and you will see a player who has lost his way and is fighting to regain it.

‘We are delighted with Alejandro,’ said Emery at the time. ‘He is so talented, young and he showed us his wish to help our project. We are really happy.’

Emery has seen what Garnacho can do. Cash was one of Villa’s best players last season yet when Chelsea hammered them 4-1 at Villa Park, Garnacho gave the right back a chasing. It was a reminder of what he offered during his best spells at United.

‘I was looking for a club to get confidence and to try to be the player I was in my first years at United,’ said Garnacho on the day he joined Villa. ‘I spoke with the manager and I think he will give me the confidence to be here and to help the team.’ Emery and Garnacho were filmed embracing during the video.

Since he crossed swords with former United boss Ruben Amorim, there has been far more focus on Garnacho’s mistakes than his talent – and this is partly his fault. He still has immense raw ability and Emery is exactly the type of coach who can unlock it, as long as they can find a common understanding.

Time is already running out. Daily Mail Sport revealed on September 21 that La Liga clubs are already following the situation, should the loan be cancelled in January. If that happens, it would feel like a huge missed opportunity, for Villa, Emery and most of all Garnacho himself. The ball is in his court.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.
