“There was Luka Binyat, who was a correspondent of Vanguard newspaper. For writing a piece, the government of El-Rufai arrested him and sent him to jail, where he stayed for almost a year,” he said.

He also referenced the case of 89 community leaders from Kachia Local Government Area who, according to him, were detained for over nine months in Kaduna Prisons after protesting the killing of their leader.

Mr Sani also highlighted the arrest and imprisonment of Islamic clerics from Zaria who protested against the retrenchments from the Kaduna State Civil Service, a lecturer at Kaduna State University named John Danfulani, and Leadership newspaper reporter Maida Joseph—all for criticising the state government.

He further alleged that members of the Islamic Movement in Nigeria (IMN) remained in detention for six to seven years facing murder charges following lethal clashes with security forces.

Turning to the security situation in Southern Kaduna, Mr Sani dismissed those defending Mr El-Rufai, claiming that most commentators lacked firsthand knowledge of the region.

“I went through the comments of people about what General Musa said, and if you look at it, 80 per cent of those who are commenting have never been to Southern Kaduna. They don’t know where Sanga is, where Kauru is, where Kachia is, where Kagarko is, where Banchiki is, where Kufana and Ozan Kuzeta are. So, they only read what they read on the pages of newspapers,” he said.

“But it is a fact that terrorists and bandits have been killing people in Southern Kaduna for over a decade without any intervention from the state government. Not only in Southern Kaduna. In Central Kaduna, where I come from, the state government did nothing.”

He accused the Mr El-Rufai administration of failing to support local security agencies.

“There was never a time when the government led by Nasir El-Rufai provided support for the police, the Army or the Civil Defence, or took any serious measure to end or stop that violence,” Mr Sani claimed.

Mr El-Rufai is yet to respond to the allegations.

Shehu Sani and Nasir El-Rufai

The political feud between Mr Sani and former governor El-Rufai is well documented.

Both politicians were in the All Progressives Congress (APC) when they took office in 2015; but their relationship quickly deteriorated over political control, patronage, and governance styles.

The feud reached a boiling point ahead of the 2019 elections when Mr Sani as a senator joined to block a $350 million World Bank loan requested by the Mr El-Rufai administration, arguing it would burden the state with unsustainable debt.

The move severely fractured the Kaduna APC chapter, leading to Mr Sani’s suspension from the party and his eventual defection to another platform after being denied the APC senatorial ticket.

Mr Sani is now running again for the Kaduna Central senatorial seat under the APC.

World.title: Six takeaways from Nigeria vs Madagascar as Super Eagles fight back for victory
World.content:
Nigeria’s 2-1 victory over Madagascar in their opening 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier at the Godswill Akpabio Stadium in Uyo was far more revealing than the scoreline suggested.

George Ilenikhena and Moses Usor, both making their senior Nigeria debuts, delivered the goals that rescued the Super Eagles after Clement Couturier had stunned the hosts with Madagascar’s 16th-minute opener.

Nigeria were made to sweat for the three points. Alex Iwobi thought he had levelled the contest, only for his effort to be ruled out after Akor Adams was penalised for a foul on the goalkeeper. The pressure continued to build before Ilenikhena struck just before half-time to restore belief inside a tense Uyo stadium.

The second half brought another twist, as Stanley Nwabali produced a crucial one-on-one save seven minutes after the restart before Chelle turned to his bench. Moses Simon came on for his 100th Nigeria appearance, while Usor entered for his senior debut.

The LASK forward needed just four minutes to announce himself.

After Oluwasemilogo Ajayi cleared a Madagascar corner, Usor collected the ball inside his own half, powered away from two defenders and smashed a left-footed finish into the near post to complete Nigeria’s comeback.

Tolu Arokodare later struck the post in the 74th minute, while Nigeria had to withstand late pressure before finally securing the points.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

For Chelle, the victory was more than three points. It offered a first glimpse of what Nigeria can become with new faces stepping forward, established players answering questions and a squad beginning to discover different ways to win.

PREMIUM TIMES looks at six major takeaways from Nigeria’s comeback victory

Ilenikhena delivers the dream debut

There was more than just a goal behind Ilenikhena’s equaliser.

Born in Lagos and raised in France from the age of three, the striker was eligible to represent both countries and spent months considering his international future before ultimately committing himself to Nigeria.

Chelle rewarded that decision with a senior call-up, and Ilenikhena wasted little time repaying the faith.

His first Super Eagles appearance ended with his first Nigeria goal, arriving at perhaps the most important moment of the night; seconds before half-time, when Madagascar appeared set to take their shock advantage into the dressing room.

His European pedigree had already provided plenty of evidence of his potential.

Ilenikhena made 51 appearances and scored 10 goals during his two seasons with Monaco, including a memorable Champions League winner against Barcelona.

Now, he has his first senior international goal to add to the collection.

Bassey cements his position as one of Africa’s standards bearer in defense

Calvin Bassey looked every inch the defender Nigeria needed when Madagascar tested the Super Eagles.

The Fulham centre-back was composed in possession, aggressive in duels and difficult to beat as the visitors repeatedly looked for opportunities to exploit Nigeria.

His performance was built less on spectacular tackles and more on positioning, anticipation and control.

Against a Madagascar side willing to absorb pressure and attack on the counter, Bassey consistently showed the authority to deal with danger before it became a bigger problem.

His Uyo performance further underlined why he has become such an important figure in the Super Eagles’ defensive structure.

Nwabali answers the repeated questions surrounding Nigeria’s No.1 spot

Stanley Nwabali entered the qualifier with questions surrounding his club situation, but there was little sign of rust when Nigeria needed him most.

The goalkeeper left Chippa United in February after requesting his release and subsequently spent months without a club before returning to the South African side in July.

Against Madagascar, however, the goalkeeper looked ever ready. Seven minutes into the second half, Nwabali stood tall in a one-on-one situation and denied the visitors what could have been a potentially devastating second goal.

That intervention proved crucial as Nigeria went on to complete their comeback.

Maduka Okoye has also featured for Nigeria this year, starting against Iran, Poland and Portugal, although the Udinese goalkeeper arrived late to camp this time around because of club commitments.

Okoye eventually arrived on Friday, but Nwabali’s latest performance has strengthened his claim to the starting shirt.

For the Super Eagles, having two goalkeepers capable of competing for the position can only increase the pressure for consistency.

Usor and Chukwueze’s battle for minutes upcoming?

Samuel Chukwueze gave Madagascar plenty to think about before making way. The winger’s direct running caused problems and he was one of Nigeria’s more dangerous attacking outlets during the opening half.

Then Usor arrived and changed the game, introduced alongside Moses Simon around the hour mark, the LASK forward needed just four minutes to turn his senior debut into another headline.

His goal had everything: strength to escape two defenders, acceleration to carry the ball from inside Nigeria’s half and the composure to drill a left-footed finish into the near post.

Usor’s club form had already made his call-up difficult to ignore. He produced 15 goals and 10 assists in 35 matches across all competitions for LASK last season, helping the Austrian club complete a league and cup double.

He also scored and provided an assist in LASK’s remarkable Champions League comeback against Celtic in August.

One debut does not settle Nigeria’s winger hierarchy, but Usor has certainly forced his way into the conversation. For Chelle, it means another dangerous attacking option from the bench, and more competition for Chukwueze and the other wide players.

Nigeria finally gets a glimpse of life without Osimhen

Victor Osimhen’s absence was always going to dominate the conversation around Nigeria’s opening qualifier.

The Galatasaray striker was ruled out of both September fixtures after suffering a muscle strain in his right thigh against Başakşehir, leaving Chelle without a forward who has scored 35 goals in 52 appearances for the Super Eagles.

Nigeria, however, found another route to goal; two debutants provided the goals as Ilenikhena levelled the contest before Usor completed the comeback. Arokodare also hit the post, while Ademola Lookman repeatedly threatened the Madagascar defence.

The performance certainly does not diminish Osimhen’s importance to the team, but it gave Chelle something equally valuable; evidence that Nigeria can find goals from different areas of the squad.

It also reflects the coach’s attempts to widen his options, as Chelle handed first senior call-ups to Ilenikhena, Isaac James and Arthur Okonkwo in September, while Usor joined the group after Femi Azeez’s injury.

For a team preparing for a demanding qualification campaign, that depth could prove significant.

Nigeria is learning to win the hard way again

Madagascar arrived in Uyo with a clear plan: defend compactly, frustrate Nigeria and attack when opportunities emerged.

For much of the first half, it worked, as the Barea took an early lead through Couturier and made life uncomfortable for the Super Eagles, forcing Nigeria to work for every opening.

But Chelle’s side gradually found a way back into the contest, as Ilenikhena’s equaliser changed the mood before Nigeria’s second-half substitutions added fresh energy to the attack.

Nwabali’s crucial intervention prevented Madagascar from restoring their advantage, while Usor’s goal completed a comeback that showed Nigeria could navigate a difficult match without everything falling into place.

It was not a flawless performance, but it was a victory built on resilience. And that may be one of the most important lessons from the night.

The bigger picture

Nigeria may have escaped Uyo with three points, but the real value of the night could lie in what Chelle discovered along the way.

Ilenikhena chose Nigeria and immediately delivered. Usor arrived for his first senior appearance and changed the game. Nwabali responded when the Super Eagles needed him, Bassey provided calm at the back, while the team found a way to win without Osimhen.

Those are significant pieces for a coach trying to build a squad capable of navigating a long qualification campaign.

But there is no time to admire the comeback.

Guinea-Bissau await in Morocco on Tuesday, and the pressure rises immediately. With co-hosts Tanzania already guaranteed a place at AFCON 2027, only the highest-ranked non-host nation in Group L will secure the remaining qualification ticket.

Nigeria have made a winning start; now Chelle’s new-look Super Eagles must prove they can turn that promising opening into momentum.

World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: In Kaduna, community peacebuilding offers way to stop disputes from becoming violent
World.content:
When two young people began arguing during a community activity in Kaduna, Mistura Hussain did not immediately try to determine who was right. Instead, the 18-year-old

Kaduna State University student listened to both sides, let them explain what had happened, and tried to keep the disagreement from becoming personal.

The argument eventually ended without a fight.

For Ms Hussain, the incident was a practical test of something she had learnt during a peacebuilding training organised by the Muslim Peace Network (MPN): that a disagreement does not have to become a conflict, and a conflict does not have to become violent.

“Before, we would argue over simple conversations, and it could become personal,” she said.

That kind of intervention may appear small, but in Kaduna State, where disputes over land, political interests, resources, identity and religion have repeatedly contributed to wider violence, peacebuilding organisations argue that preventing escalation can begin with how people handle seemingly ordinary disagreements.

Nigeria has for decades struggled with communal, ethnic and religious conflicts that have claimed lives, displaced families and deepened mistrust between communities. A report by the International Crisis Group identified political manipulation, poverty, unemployment, and ethnic and religious rivalries among factors that have fuelled conflicts in northern Nigeria. Kaduna has also experienced repeated interreligious violence linked to political, land and historical tensions, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The scale of violence remains significant. Between January 2024 and August 2025, the European Union Agency for Asylum, citing ACLED data, recorded 475 security incidents in Kaduna resulting in 951 fatalities. The incidents included violence against civilians, battles, riots, and explosions or remote violence.

But some of Kaduna’s worst episodes also show how a dispute over a specific issue can take on wider ethnic or religious meanings.

In 1992, for example, a dispute over the relocation of a market in Zangon-Kataf escalated into violent confrontations between Hausa and Atyap communities. Rotimi T. Suberu, a Nigerian political scientist and scholar of ethnic conflict, documented the crisis in his work on ethnic minority conflicts in Nigeria. According to his account, based on official estimates, 95 people were killed, 252 were injured, while 133 houses and 26 farmlands were destroyed. The violence later spread to other parts of Kaduna State.

A dispute over a market did not remain a dispute over a market.

Human Rights Watch later noted that the 1992 crisis was initially sparked by disagreement over the relocation of the market before the violence took on wider ethnic and religious dimensions.

The lesson is one that peacebuilding practitioners say remains relevant: disagreements can become more dangerous when they are interpreted through existing community divisions, rumours and mistrust.

That possibility remains a concern in communities such as Kakuri in Kaduna South Local Government Area, which has previously been identified as a Kaduna community where religious and other tensions could become flashpoints.

But Kakuri was not defined solely by conflict.

According to Hussain Makanjuola, Executive Director of MPN, Muslim and Christian youths in the community had been playing football together as part of efforts to strengthen their relationships.

Mr Makanjuola said those relationships were tested after anger spread following the killing of Deborah Samuel, a Christian student who was beaten and burned to death by fellow students at Shehu Shagari College of Education in Sokoto State on May 12, 2022. She had criticised classmates for posting Islamic religious messages in a WhatsApp group meant for academic discussions, with some students interpreting her comments about Prophet Muhammad as blasphemous.

He added that the incident became a source of anger among some Christian youths in Kakuri, who began retaliating against Muslim youths, and three people were killed before security personnel intervened.

The episode showed how a disagreement or misunderstanding, even when it begins outside a community, can quickly deepen existing tensions and threaten relationships within it, Mr Makanjuola noted. It also highlighted why peacebuilding efforts that build trust, communication and relationships before a crisis can help communities manage tensions and prevent disagreements from escalating into violence.

In another case, the West Africa Network for Peacebuilding (WANEP-Nigeria) reported that a Community-Based Reconciliation Committee in Kakuri helped resolve a feud between two families after the disagreement became serious enough to involve security authorities. The families eventually reconciled following mediation.

These experiences point to the space community peacebuilding seeks to occupy: helping people recognise tensions, open dialogue and resolve disagreements before they acquire wider religious or communal meanings.

Building relationships before conflict

Against this background, MPN has spent the past several years working with young people, religious leaders, women and community leaders in Kaduna.

Established in 2020 and based in Kaduna, the organisation uses peace education, interfaith dialogue, community mediation, and grassroots engagement to encourage residents, students, and religious, community, and traditional leaders to address disagreements before they develop into violence.

Its activities include the Community Initiatives to Promote Peace (CIPP), Peace Clubs in schools and a network of Community Peace Officers operating across six local government areas.

The organisation’s work is not limited to telling participants to “live in peace”. It focuses on building trust and giving people the confidence to address problems before they become sources of wider tension.

During its workshops, participants learn conflict prevention, tolerance, communication, and peaceful problem-solving. They learn to listen to opposing views, express their concerns without blaming others, and work with people from different religious and social backgrounds.

Some sessions use practical group exercises in which participants encounter disagreements and are expected to resolve them through discussion rather than confrontation. The exercises allow participants to practise the communication and problem-solving skills they may need when disagreements arise outside the training.

Between 2021 and 2025, MPN said its Peace Education programme reached more than 3,700 students in seven private schools in Kaduna, where it established Peace Clubs. The organisation also said its Community Initiatives to Promote Peace programme reached about 10 communities.

The Peace Clubs give students a space to discuss differences, learn communication and conflict-resolution skills, and interact with students from backgrounds different from their own.

Rather than learning about religious tolerance only as an idea, students are encouraged to practise listening, communicating, and working with people whose religious identities may differ from theirs.

MPN has also worked with religious teachers and community leaders.

In January 2023, the organisation organised a training for Arabic and Islamic teachers in Kaduna on peacebuilding and preventing religious extremism in schools.

Mr Makanjuola said MPN conducted 12 training workshops between 2021 and 2025 on different areas of peacebuilding, including sensitisation of religious and community leaders, women and youth engagement, and conflict prevention, adding that more than 600 people were trained.

The organisation’s Community Peace Officers operate across Kaduna North, Kaduna South, Chikun, Kagarko, Zaria and Igabi local government areas, serving as community-based contacts who can identify tensions, encourage dialogue and connect disputing parties with people who can intervene.

The idea is simple: intervene while a disagreement is still small.

From lessons to everyday relationships

The changes MPN is trying to encourage are not only about settling disputes when they occur. They are also about making it easier for people to interact before a crisis happens.

Maryam Ahmed, a 17-year-old Muslim student at Malika International School, said the peace education activities changed the way she interacted with students from other religious backgrounds.

Her experience points to another aspect of peacebuilding: reducing the distance that can exist between young people because of religious identity. Instead of approaching students from another faith mainly through assumptions about their religion, the activities gave her opportunities to interact with them directly and build relationships through shared experiences.

Other participants similarly described becoming more comfortable communicating with people from different faiths and backgrounds.

A 26-year-old Christian student at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, Monica Ishaya said the MPN training changed her perception of people from another religion, allowing her to see them as friends rather than as people defined by religious differences.

“I became more confident interacting with people from different religious and ethnic backgrounds,” she said.

Mariya Ahmed Tijjani, an MPN official who first participated in the organisation’s activities as a beneficiary before joining its staff, said dialogue challenged some of the assumptions she had about people from other religious backgrounds.

She said her experience showed her that people could disagree on religion and still maintain friendships and work together.

The approach extends beyond students.

MPN also engages religious and community leaders to help address misunderstandings, encourage dialogue, and use their influence within their communities to prevent disagreements from becoming wider religious or communal disputes.

Misbahudeen Muhammad Raji, an Imam (a Muslim religious leader) with the Nasirudeen Society of Kaduna State who has participated in MPN activities, said religious misunderstanding, ignorance and inflammatory interests could contribute to tension.

He recalled intervening when two motorcycle riders from different religious backgrounds exchanged abusive words in Rumi. Rather than letting the disagreement become a religious issue, he brought the parties together, encouraged them to listen to each other, and helped settle the matter.

In Chikun, Christian women’s leader Anna Yakub also recalled an incident in which a disagreement between community members began to create tension along religious lines. She said community members intervened, brought those involved together and opened a dialogue before the disagreement could escalate.

The examples illustrate how the lessons from peacebuilding activities can move beyond training rooms into everyday disputes in communities.

John Akor, senior pastor (a Christian church leader) of God’s Love Auditorium Church in Kaduna and a facilitator in some of MPN’s programmes, said religious leaders could play an important role because of the influence they have over their congregations.

Their involvement means peacebuilding is not confined to workshops. Participants can take the lessons into places where disagreements occur, including schools, religious spaces, families and neighbourhoods.

The approach is also consistent with the wider experience of peacebuilding organisations in northern Nigeria. A USAID evaluation of an interfaith peacebuilding programme found that training, dialogue and joint activities created opportunities for Muslims and Christians to interact, build relationships and improve perceptions of one another.

More recently, the United Nations reported that an Early Warning and Early Response system operating in Kaduna and Katsina had recorded 126 cases since its launch in August 2023, with 53 cases resolved within three months. The system relies on local collaboration to identify and respond to tensions before they develop into larger conflicts. The United Nations said the mechanism had also strengthened communities’ and local government peace committees’ ability to detect and respond to potential conflicts at an early stage.

The experience of AbdulPatai Adekunle Badmus, an official of the Interfaith Mediation Centre who attended some MPN workshops, offers another indication of how such interventions can influence behaviour.

Mr Badmus recalled a young participant from one of the organisation’s Peace Clubs who initially had little interaction with Muslim students but later became more comfortable around them and formed friendships.

Such changes matter because peacebuilding is not only about what happens when violence has already started. It is also about changing how people relate to one another before a crisis occurs.

Mr Badmus said the effects of such work can become more visible over time as participants carry the relationships and attitudes they develop into their schools, homes and communities.

Samson Auta, a conflict resolution expert and co-executive director of the Interfaith Mediation Centre, said community peacebuilding could strengthen the ability of people to identify tensions, communicate across differences and seek mediation before disputes become violent.

He explained that conflicts were often shaped by several factors, making it important for communities to have people who understand how to recognise tensions and respond early.

Mr Auta said MPN’s peacebuilding activities showed how conflict could be mitigated at the community level, but achieving stronger, longer-lasting results would require long-term commitment rather than short-term interventions.

Similarly, Obi Onyeigwe, an independent peacebuilding expert, said effective peacebuilding programmes could build relationships that continue beyond a single workshop, particularly when communities take ownership of mechanisms for resolving their own problems.

Beyond the work, resources remain a challenge

While MPN has expanded its peacebuilding activities across schools and communities, limited resources have made it difficult for the organisation to reach everyone who could benefit.

The organisation said it has continued some of its peacebuilding activities with limited funding, relying on partnerships and the commitment of community members and volunteers.

The challenge became particularly clear when the Kaduna State Ministry of Education approached the organisation about expanding its Peace Clubs in public schools across the state. The request raised the possibility of taking the peace education model beyond the seven private schools where the organisation had established Peace Clubs.

But MPN could not extend the programme to all public schools because it lacked the resources required for such an expansion.

The organisation has so far established Peace Clubs in seven private schools and reached more than 3,700 students through its Peace Education programme. Extending the model to hundreds of public schools would require additional funding, personnel and sustained support.

The same constraint affects its work with Community Peace Officers and community leaders, limiting how far the organisation can extend activities that depend heavily on local presence and regular engagement.

Community peacebuilding cannot replace security operations or address all the economic and political causes of violence.

But for the people participating in these programmes, the ability to recognise tension, listen to opposing views and intervene before a disagreement becomes a larger confrontation offers another layer of protection.

For Mistura Hussain, the lesson is now part of how she approaches disagreements. What once might have looked like a confrontation can now be an opportunity to listen.

And in communities where a small quarrel can sometimes acquire a much larger meaning, that change may begin with something as simple as learning that disagreement does not have to end in violence.

This reporting was produced under the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) SAIL+ Programme Fellowship.

World.title: AFCON Qualifiers: Chelle reflects on Madagascar win, warns Eagles ahead of Guinea-Bissau clash
World.content:
Super Eagles coach Eric Chelle has explained how he changed his team’s formation to overcome Madagascar’s compact defence in Nigeria’s 2-1 comeback win in their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying opener on Friday.

Nigeria fell behind after Ehsan Kari put Madagascar ahead in the 15th minute at the Godswill Akpabio Stadium, Uyo.

George Ilenikhena levelled in first-half stoppage time before fellow debutant Moses Usor completed the comeback in the 65th minute.

Chelle said Madagascar’s decision to sit deep made it difficult for Nigeria to penetrate through the middle, forcing him to alter his tactical approach.

From diamond to 4-2-3-1

According to the coach, Nigeria initially lined up in a diamond formation but struggled to find spaces against Madagascar’s low block.

“In the first half, we started with a diamond. I don’t know if you saw it. We started the game like that, and like I said, they put a low block; they were very compact inside, so it was difficult to bring the game inside,” Chelle said during his post-match press conference.

He explained that Nigeria initially tried to deal with the situation by shooting from distance before switching to a 4-2-3-1 formation to exploit the wider areas.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“So, we started with shots to manage that situation, and this is why, at the end of the half, you saw him on the line. After that, we passed into a 4-2-3-1 because when you play against a low block, you have to pass by the side, by the side, to make some crosses. This is why we changed the system.”

The change eventually helped Nigeria create more opportunities, with Ilenikhena restoring parity before Usor struck after the break.

Chelle admits room for improvement

Despite securing the three points, Chelle was not entirely satisfied with Nigeria’s performance.

“This game was not bad, but not good either. We made the first mistake, and that is why we conceded a goal,” he said.

“After that, we had a lot of chances to score, but technically we were not very good. This is why we had to chase the score and try to come back.”

The coach, however, praised the players for their response after going behind.

“But at the end, the state of mind was good. The state of mind was good; they gave everything for the jersey and the country.”

Guinea-Bissau next

Nigeria will now turn their attention to Guinea-Bissau, where they will play their second Group L qualifying match on Tuesday.

Chelle said the Super Eagles must quickly move on from the Madagascar victory and prepare for a different opponent.

“I’m happy because they found the solution. It was not easy. So now we have to forget this game and analyse what we did, and after that, we have a second game in Guinea-Bissau.

“This is not the same team. They have their strengths, their weaknesses. So I have to think about what we will do in Guinea-Bissau. I cannot tell you whether we will play with that system or not. We have to go first with our state of mind, and after that, we will play that game.”

Nigeria’s victory gives Chelle’s side an important start to the qualifying campaign, but the coach will now have to find another tactical solution against a Guinea-Bissau side he expects to pose a different challenge.

World.title: ‘It is a dream come true’: Moses Simon celebrates 100th Super Eagles appearance
World.content:
Super Eagles winger Moses Simon has described reaching 100 appearances for Nigeria as a “great privilege” and a dream come true after achieving the milestone in the Super Eagles’ 2-1 victory over Madagascar in Uyo on Friday evening.

The Paris FC winger came off the bench in the second half to make his landmark appearance, replacing former Sevilla striker Akor Adams at the Godswill Akpabio Stadium.

Simon immediately brought his trademark pace, directness and skill to the game, taking on Madagascar defenders and creating opportunities for Nigeria as the Super Eagles secured victory in their opening 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying fixture.

Speaking at the post-match press conference, Simon reflected on the significance of reaching the century mark and expressed his appreciation to the coaches who have trusted him with opportunities to represent Nigeria throughout his international career.

“Thanks to the coach for the opportunity. Thanks to every coach that gave me the opportunity,” Simon told reporters.

The 31-year-old admitted that reaching 100 appearances was something he never imagined when he first began his international career, making the achievement even more meaningful.

“Of course, this gives me joy and it is a great privilege to play for the Super Eagles,” he added.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

For Simon, however, the milestone is not the end of his international journey.

The Paris FC star reaffirmed his commitment to the national team, promising to continue giving everything whenever he receives another call-up.

“It is a dream come true. I never believed I would play 100 games but I believe one thing, whenever I am called up, I will be there to give one hundred per cent,” Simon concluded.

Simon’s appearance against Madagascar also placed him in an exclusive group of Nigerian footballers who have reached the 100-cap mark for the Super Eagles.

He now joins Joseph Yobo, Vincent Enyeama, Ahmed Musa and Alex Iwobi as players who have made at least 100 appearances for Nigeria.

Having celebrated a landmark moment in Uyo, Simon will now turn his attention back to the Super Eagles’ qualifying campaign as Nigeria prepares for its next Group L fixture against Guinea-Bissau on 29 September.

World.title: Osinachi Ohale retires from Super Falcons after 16 years
World.content:
Super Falcons defender Osinachi Ohale has brought the curtain down on her international career, announcing her retirement from football at the age of 34 after 16 years of representing Nigeria.

Ohale made the emotional announcement on Friday through a farewell statement on her Instagram page, ending a remarkable journey that saw her earn 86 caps, feature at four FIFA Women’s World Cups and compete at seven editions of the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations.

Her decision comes after Nigeria fell short in the race for qualification for the next FIFA Women’s World Cup, with the experienced centre-back having been part of the Super Falcons squad during the latest campaign.

Ohale admitted that walking away from the national team was one of the most difficult decisions of her career after spending more than a decade wearing the green and white.

“There are moments in life when words are simply not enough. Today is one of those moments,” she wrote.

“After 16 years of wearing the Nigerian jersey, representing my country, and giving everything I had to the beautiful game, I have made the very difficult decision to retire from international football.”

86 caps, four World Cups and seven WAFCON appearances

From her senior debut in 2010, Ohale became a constant presence in the Super Falcons setup, playing under different coaches and alongside several generations of Nigerian players.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Her international career took her to four FIFA Women’s World Cups; 2011, 2015, 2019 and 2023, while she also featured at seven WAFCON tournaments.

She leaves the national team as a five-time African champion, having been part of Nigeria’s title-winning squads in 2010, 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2024.

The 2024 WAFCON tournament was staged in Morocco in July 2025 after being postponed from its original schedule, with Nigeria reclaiming the continental crown by defeating the hosts 3-2 in the final.

Ohale was on the pitch that night and produced another memorable contribution to Nigeria’s title triumph.

She scored as the Super Falcons recovered from two goals down to defeat Morocco 3-2 in the final, adding another defining moment to a career already filled with major tournaments and trophies.

Australia 2023 remains one of her biggest moments

Among the many highlights of Ohale’s international career was her performance at the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand.

Nigeria faced co-hosts Australia in the group stage and produced a thrilling 3-2 victory, with Ohale scoring the Super Falcons’ second goal to help turn the game in Nigeria’s favour.

It was one of the standout moments of a tournament in which Nigeria advanced from a difficult group and reached the knockout stage.

But for Ohale, the memories go beyond goals, trophies and appearances.

“I have stood on the biggest stages in the world, representing Nigeria at four FIFA Women’s World Cups and seven WAFCON, and I am incredibly proud that we lifted the African title five times,” she wrote.

“But beyond the numbers and trophies are the memories that will stay with me forever, the tears, the celebrations, the difficult moments, the victories, the defeats, the friendships, the sacrifices, and every time I stood proudly with my hand over my heart and heard the Nigerian anthem.”

‘I would choose Nigeria every single time’

Ohale’s farewell message was as much about gratitude as it was about retirement.

Looking back on the journey from the young player who dreamed of representing Nigeria to becoming one of the country’s most experienced defenders, she reflected on the sacrifices that came with wearing the national-team shirt.

“I gave this jersey my youth, my strength, my sweat, my tears, and my heart. And if I had to do it all over again, I would choose Nigeria every single time.”

She also paid tribute to the people who shared the journey with her, including her teammates, coaches, technical staff, family, friends and the Nigeria Football Federation.

“To my teammates, coaches, staff, family, friends, Nigeria Football Federation and everyone who walked this journey with me, thank you. You became part of a chapter of my life that I will treasure forever,” she wrote.

The veteran defender also reserved special appreciation for the Nigerian supporters who followed the Super Falcons through their successes and difficult moments.

“To the Nigerian fans: thank you for believing in us, supporting us, celebrating with us, and standing by us through every high and every low. Your love made wearing this jersey even more special.”

‘The jersey will leave my shoulders, but never my heart’

Ohale’s international career ends with an impressive résumé: 86 caps, 16 years, four World Cups, seven WAFCON appearances and five African titles.

But as she reflected on the numbers, the defender made it clear that her greatest source of pride was simply having the opportunity to represent Nigeria.

“Today, I say goodbye to international football with no regrets, only gratitude.

“86 caps, 16 years, 4 World Cups, 7 WAFCON, 5 WAFCON titles.

“But the greatest achievement of all is knowing that I had the privilege to serve my country.”

She ended her farewell with a message that captured the depth of her connection to the Super Falcons.

“The jersey will leave my shoulders, but it will never leave my heart. Thank you, Nigeria, for allowing me to live my dream.”

A career that continues beyond the Super Falcons

Although Ohale has stepped away from international football, her club career continues.

The 34-year-old currently plays for Pachuca in Mexico, following an international club career that has also taken her to the United States, Sweden and Spain, including a spell with Alavés.

Her retirement therefore closes one chapter rather than bringing her football journey to an end.

For Nigeria, however, the departure of one of its most experienced defenders marks the end of a significant era.

From her first appearance in 2010 to her final years as one of the senior figures in the Super Falcons dressing room, Ohale was part of five African title-winning teams and represented the country on football’s biggest stages.

She leaves international football with 86 appearances, five WAFCON winners’ medals and four World Cup appearances, but above all, with the gratitude of a player who gave 16 years to the Nigerian jersey.

And in her own words, there are no regrets; only gratitude.

World.title: Tenth woman found dead in South Africa’s string of killings
World.content:
Deputy National Police Commissioner responsible for Policing, Lieutenant General Tabelo Mosikili (C) gives a press conference outside the Boksburg Magistrate Court in Boksburg on September 21, 2026 ahead of the first court appearance of three people accused of the murder of a woman whose body was found in the east of Johannesburg. South African police said on September 20 they had arrested three people over the killing of one of nine women found dead in a neighbourhood east of Johannesburg in a series of murders that have alarmed the nation. The discovery of the nine bodies in Kempton Park over two months has fuelled fear and anger, as authorities investigate whether a serial killer or killers were responsible. (Photo by EMMANUEL CROSET / AFP)

South African police on Saturday found another body in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, bringing to 10 the number of women found dead in the municipality over the past two months.

The discovery adds to growing concern over violence against women in a country long plagued by violent crime, while police work to establish whether the killings are connected.

The body was found in the Tembisa township, police said, without providing further details.

“At this stage, we can only confirm the discovery of the body. Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene,” police spokeswoman Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.

Local television station eNCA reported that the semi-naked body was found at a cemetery.

The nine other victims were mostly in their 20s and 30s, with some found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual assault.

The first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.

Two other suspects, women aged 31 and 38, were arrested in connection with the ninth victim and charged on Monday.

Police have said that case may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.

Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and the declaration of gender-based violence as a national disaster.

South Africa, a nation of 62 million people, has one of the world’s highest murder rates, with more than 60 killings a day on average.

AFP

World.title: Shettima tasks ECOWAS leadership on sub-region’s unity, integration
World.content:
Vice President Kashim Shettima has urged the new leadership of the ECOWAS Commission to prioritise regional unity and integration in advancing the progress of the sub-region’s people and economy.

Read Also: 2027: Election riggers should go to jail — Obi

Shettima stated this on Friday in New York, United States, when he granted audience to a delegation from the ECOWAS Commission.

The delegation was led by its new President, retired Gen. Birame Diop, on the margins of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

He also urged the commission to build bridges of friendship and promote programmes and policies that would significantly impact the lives and livelihoods of people across the sub-region.

Shettima also implored the new leadership of the sub-regional body to take private sector participation seriously in the execution of the Lagos-Abidjan highway project.

“Beyond your administrative duties, your leadership of the commission must make deliberate efforts to build bridges of friendship across the sub-region.

“ECOWAS should be at the forefront of our engagement with emerging blocs in the area such as the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).

“I urge ECOWAS under your leadership to champion the cause of regional integration and strengthen the bonds of unity and friendship among our people,” he said.

He congratulated the commission’s new president on his election, noting that he assumed office at a difficult time that would require greater synergy and cohesion among leaders and people of the sub-region.

Shettima assured Diop of Nigeria’s continuous cooperation and support.

“My boss, President Bola Tinubu, is a man of honour and conviction who will always support efforts aimed at advancing the transformation of ECOWAS as a regional body and the progress of the area in general.

He said Nigeria would continue to create the enabling environment for ECOWAS as a body to succeed and contribute meaningfully to the attainment of the vision and objectives set by its founding fathers.

Earlier, Diop eulogised Nigeria for the role it played in the establishment and sustenance of ECOWAS over the years.

He also commended Nigeria for its sacrifices towards the stability and prosperity of the sub-region in spite of the challenges.

Diop decried rising concerns regarding insecurity and lagging development across the sub-region.

He said the commission was facing unique challenges that required Nigeria’s direct intervention as a “big brother” to be successfully resolved.

He described ECOWAS as a tool for regional stability that should be encouraged and supported at all times.

The commission’s president anppea to other countries in the sub-region to cooperate with Nigeria to ensure inclusive development and a better future for the people of the sub-region.

The meeting had Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu; and the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of the Federation, Chief Lateef Fagbemi (SAN) in attendance.

Others are the Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Amb. Jimoh Ibrahim, and top officials from the ECOWAS Commission, among others.

Vanguard News

World.title: Iraq seeks exemption from US ban on Iran airlines
World.content:
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.

All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.

“The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures,” the prime minister’s media office said.

An exemption would allow flights to resume “for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians,” it added.

Iranian airlines mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran’s holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran and patients seeking medical treatment there.

Several Iraqis told AFP that enforcing the US sanctions has left them scrambling for solutions, with some fearing they would lose access to treatment in Iran or others stranded there with little choice but to take the more than 12-hour journey home by land.

Iraq has joined several countries including the United Arab Emirates in enforcing the US ban, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines would be “shut down” on Wednesday.

Relations between Iraq and neighbouring Iran, both Shia-majority countries, have long been close, due to religious kinship as well as political and economic interests.

Iraqi airlines stopped flying to Iran at the start of the Middle East war in February.

AFP

World.title: ‘I’m like three women’ — Ivie Atuwatse rules out polygamy for Olu of Warri
World.content:
Ivie Atuwatse III, wife of Ogiame Atuwatse III, the Olu of Warri, has opened up on the joys and challenges of being married to the traditional ruler, saying she takes pride in seeing people celebrate his achievements.

Ivie spoke in a recent interview with BBC News Pidgin, where she discussed life as the wife of the monarch and the demands that come with his position.

She said one of the things she enjoys most about the marriage is watching people appreciate her husband’s personality and achievements.

“The thing wey I like about being married to His Majesty is that, all the fame or the popularity wey him get, na say I get to see the world celebrate his genius, his swag also, cos me too I dey celebrate am,” she said.

“And when the world dey celebrate am, e dey ginger me more. I dey extremely proud of am as a human being, and to see that they also appreciate am dey give me much joy.”

However, Ivie admitted that the Olu’s responsibilities can sometimes make it difficult for her to have enough time with him.

“But on the other side, dem say food wey dey sweet sometimes flies dey like to chop from am,” she said.

“Sometimes e dey busy and it can be hard to want to share my husband with all the many different duties that he has, and so that can be equally difficult.”

She said they were learning to adjust to the demands of his position.

“And so, we are learning to navigate it because sometimes I just want him to myself,” she added.

The interviewer also asked whether she would accept another wife if the Olu changed his position on polygamy, having previously said he was not open to it.

Ivie dismissed the possibility, insisting that she was confident her husband would not change his mind.

“Firstly, His Majesty no go fit change him mind about polygamy. Make we just settle that one for there,” she said.

“Me alone, one me, I be like three women, so I dey alright for am.”

World.title: Soldiers rescue 14 kidnapped in Katsina, arrest terrorist logistics couriers
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

Troops of Operation Fansan Yamma have rescued 14 kidnapped victims, comprising 12 males and two females, while conducting a routine patrol operation in Katsina.

Lieutenant Colonel Aliyu Danja, Media Information Officer, said on Saturday that the victims were kidnapped from Anguwan Miko and Tafoki villages in Faskari Local Government Area.

Danja also said three terrorist logistics couriers were arrested in a separate operation by troops in Faskari Local Government Area.

He said, “On 24 September 2026, troops of Sector 2 intercepted three suspects travelling on a motorcycle in Faskari Local Government Area.

“Preliminary interrogation revealed that the suspects were conveying the sum of ₦2.7 million, suspected to be ransom money, alongside three mobile phones, for onward transfer to a terrorist kingpin through intermediaries within the area.

“The suspects and the recovered items are in military custody for further investigation.

“Similarly, on 25 September 2026, troops of Sector 2, acting on credible intelligence about the movement of terrorists in Faskari Local Government Area, established an ambush position and engaged the terrorists, forcing them to flee in disarray.

“Exploitation of the area subsequently led to the recovery of one AK-47 rifle, 30 rounds of ammunition and one motorcycle.

“In a related development on the same day, troops conducting a routine patrol intercepted and rescued 14 kidnapped victims comprising 12 males and 2 females.

“Preliminary investigation revealed that the victims had earlier been abducted from Anguwan Miko and Tafoki villages in Faskari Local Government Area.

“The victims were reportedly abandoned by the terrorists upon sighting the advancing troops.

“They were subsequently rescued and handed over to the Faskari Local Government authorities for further necessary action.

“The successes underscore the commitment of Operation Fansan Yamma to protecting the lives and property of citizens, rescuing persons held in terrorist captivity and denying terrorists and other criminal elements freedom of action across the Joint Operations Area.

“The Theatre Command commends the troops for their vigilance, courage and prompt response, and urges members of the public to continue providing timely and credible information to security agencies on suspicious movements and activities within their communities.”

World.title: Sokoto govt replies ADC on ₦25bn water works, 4.2MW solar project
World.content:
Gov Ahmad Aliyu of Sokoto State

By Musa Ubandawaki

Sokoto State Government has defended its investments and ongoing interventions in the water sector, dismissing claims by the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate, Hon. Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, over the state’s water supply situation.

The state Ministry of Water Resources, in a rejoinder signed by the Commissioner, said the government was implementing a comprehensive strategy aimed at addressing both the immediate and long-term water needs of residents across Sokoto metropolis and other parts of the state.

The ministry said claims that the government had failed to tackle the water crisis did not reflect the scale of interventions currently being undertaken, stressing that several major water projects were either under procurement, rehabilitation, construction or at various stages of implementation.

According to the ministry, the ₦25 billion earmarked for the rehabilitation of the Sokoto Township Water Works and the ₦5 billion provision for solarisation contained in the 2026 Citizens Budget were budgetary appropriations for multi-year projects and should not be interpreted as funds already released and expended.

“Government acknowledges that the water sector requires massive investment.

However, budget appropriation is not the same as cash backing. Releases are made in phases based on project milestones, procurement processes and available revenue,” the ministry said.

It explained that the ₦64.09 million reported as expenditure in the first quarter of 2026 represented early-stage mobilisation and consultancy payments, adding that further releases were being processed in the second and third quarters in line with the implementation timelines of the projects.

The ministry particularly pointed to the solarisation of the Sokoto Water Works as one of the administration’s major interventions, saying the contract for the installation of 10,000 solar panels with a projected 4.2 megawatts generation capacity was awarded in May 2026.

“Site clearing and procurement are ongoing. The project is designed to reduce dependence on the national grid and provide the power required to operate the water pumps on a 24-hour basis,” it stated.

Beyond the central water works, the government said it had also provided 42 solar-powered boreholes across Sokoto metropolis, including projects at Tudun-Wada Gebe, Tudun-Wada Old Cemetery, Bazza Area, Dallatu Road, Lamido Adama Road, Kofar Atiku and Shagari Close, among other locations.

The ministry further disclosed that six major water schemes—Tamaje, Old Airport, Gagi, Mana, Runjin Sambo and Ruga Liman—were at different stages of design, procurement and rehabilitation, with a combined projected capacity of 40 million gallons of water per day.

It clarified that the ₦14.1 billion associated with the six schemes represented their total projected cost and was not money already spent by the government, insisting that implementation would proceed in phases as the projects advanced.

On emergency interventions, the ministry said more than 120 kilometres of burst and damaged pipelines had been repaired across Sokoto metropolis within the last 18 months, while new booster stations had also been installed to improve water pressure, particularly in elevated areas.

The government acknowledged the hardship faced by residents who, according to the ministry, sometimes pay between ₦200 and ₦300 for a 25-litre container of water, but argued that its strategy was designed to address the structural causes of the crisis rather than rely solely on temporary interventions.

“Government understands the hardship of buying water at ₦200 to ₦300 per 25 litres. That is precisely why we are investing in long-term solutions rather than temporary fixes,” the ministry said, adding that the solarisation and reticulation projects were intended to improve water availability even during the dry season.

The ministry maintained that access to potable water remained a priority of Governor Ahmed Aliyu’s administration, insisting that the issue should not be reduced to political campaigns, while challenging Dan’iya and the ADC to support public sensitisation and protection of water infrastructure.

“Water is a fundamental right, not a campaign slogan. Governor Ahmed Aliyu’s administration will not politicize it,” the ministry declared, assuring residents that measurable improvements from the solarisation project and the six major water schemes would begin to emerge within the next 12 months.

The government also pledged continued publication of budget performance reports and invited stakeholders to visit project sites for verification, while urging residents to protect public water infrastructure and pay applicable water bills to support the sustainability of the system.

World.title: Iran proposes Hormuz plan, Trump reportedly refuses
World.content:
The United States had yet to publicly respond on Saturday after Iran offered a plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, though reports indicated that President Donald Trump had rejected the proposal.

The waterway key to the world’s oil supply is central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months, though new mediation efforts took place this week.

Iranian state media reported on Saturday that President Masoud Pezeshkian was on his way back to Tehran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York.

There he met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, according to the presidency, and said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”

Earlier in the week, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held talks with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel.

“Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN.

“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.

However, within hours of his comments The Wall Street Journal reported Trump had rejected the proposal, citing US officials familiar with the matter.

The report noted that the 80-year-old president was sceptical that Tehran would meet his demands and added he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely.

Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled “Trump Strait”.

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: “We will not cease punishing the US until Iran’s seven conditions are met.”

Iran’s plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon, according to Araghchi.

He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year.

– Hostilities in Yemen –

It notably calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.

On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.

Pezeshkian said in an interview with broadcaster CBS that the “process will begin from the very day they accept it”.

“We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan… if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before,” he added.

Mohebi told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear programme.

But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

World.title: 2027: Atiku’s victory will end rotational presidency — Shehu Sani
World.content:
Shehu Sani

A former Kaduna Central Senator, Shehu Sani, has said the victory of the African Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, in the 2027 election would mark the end of the informal rotational presidency arrangement in Nigeria.

Sani stated this on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday, while arguing that the South should be allowed to complete an eight-year presidential tenure before power returns to the North.

The former lawmaker said Atiku had a constitutional right to contest the election but maintained that political considerations should also be taken into account in determining the direction of the 2027 contest.

“I never said Atiku should not run. Constitutionally, he has the right to run for any election. But what I said was that the southern part of Nigeria should be allowed to have its eight-year tenure in office, just like the way the North has from 2015 to 2023,” Sani said.

He said candidates from the South, including the Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi, should be allowed to contest the election, alongside other southern aspirants.

According to Sani, the ADC should field Rotimi Amaechi, while the NDC should present Obi and the APM should field Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde.

“Let the South struggle it out and see who wins, and for four years. And when the tenure is done by 2031, the North shall have its unchallengeable opportunity to produce leadership of the country,” he said.

Sani acknowledged that rotational presidency was not provided for in the Nigerian Constitution but said political parties and leaders should consider the arrangement in the interest of equity, fairness and national stability.

“There are things that are not written in our constitution, but in the interest of justice, fairness, equity, and peace, we need to consider all these things here,” he said.

He argued that the arrangement should not be determined solely by population or electoral strength, noting that former President Muhammadu Buhari completed eight years in office between 2015 and 2023 without what he described as a serious challenge from the South.

Sani also said his position was not intended to prevent Atiku from contesting.

“The constitution has not stopped him from contesting the election. He can contest the election, but for me, that is my position and I’m not backing down on it,” he said.

Asked what an Atiku victory would mean for the rotational arrangement, Sani said it would effectively bring it to an end.

“If Atiku wins, it means that is the end of rotational presidency in Nigeria,” he said, adding that such an outcome could generate resentment in parts of the South.

Sani maintained that allowing the South to complete eight years would make it easier for a northern candidate to succeed Tinubu in 2031 without facing resistance from the South.

“But if we allow the South to have their eight-year term, by 2031, a Northerner takes over, there will be no challenge from Southern part of Nigeria,” he said.

World.title: APAMS Unveils 19th Office in Nigeria
World.content:
Founder and Chairman, APAMS Funeral Limited, Dr. Kevin Chukwumobi, has unveiled the company’s new Port-Harcourt office in Rivers State, further expanding its operational presence in the South-South region of Nigeria.

The new facility, located in Port-Harcourt, the Rivers State capital, becomes the 19th branch office of the funeral company and was officially unveiled on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, in a ceremony that also coincided with Chukwumobi’s 56th birthday.

The opening adds Rivers State to APAMS’ clientele base and growing network of operational locations across the country, as the company continues to extend its funeral and related services closer to clients in different parts of Nigeria.

Beyond serving clients in Rivers State, the Port-Harcourt office has been designated as the South-South Regional Headquarters of APAMS, from where the company’s operations in other South-South states will be coordinated.

The regional structure is expected to cover APAMS’ operations and expansion in states including Edo, Delta and Bayelsa, among others, providing a central administrative and operational base for the company’s activities within the region.

The choice of Port-Harcourt also gives APAMS a strategic presence in one of the South-South region’s major commercial centres and provides a base from which the company can respond more efficiently to the needs of clients across the region.

Speaking on the development, Chukwumobi said the opening formed part of APAMS’ continued expansion and efforts to take its services to more locations, while strengthening its ability to serve clients across the country.

The unveiling also continued a tradition associated with the APAMS chief executive, who has often used his birthday as an occasion to commission or unveil new business projects and offices, turning the celebration into an opportunity to mark another milestone in the company’s growth.

For APAMS, the Port-Harcourt office represents not only another branch in its growing network but also an important regional base for consolidating its presence in the South-South and supporting the company’s wider expansion plans.

The Port-Harcourt Office is located at Km. 3 East/West Road near Nkpolu Bus Stop, beside Conoil Petrol Station, Rumuigbo, Port Harcourt, River State.

Those that attended the event included Lady Nkem Chukwumobi,(Executive Director, Apams Funeral Ltd), Chief Pius Njoku, (Chairman Pillars Group), High Chief Dr Darlington Nwabunike (President, De Imperial Philanthropic Family & CEO Turo Africa Ltd), and Chief Nwabueze Umeh (Ofiafuluego Na Okija).

Others are , Chief Mike Agbasi (Ikenga Ukpor, Chairman, Heritage Group) Chief Anthony Maduka ( Chairman, Vegas Astoria Hotel Onitsha), Chief Felix Ojimba, (CEO Transtel Group), Chief Chinedu Okeke (Ekwe Ogidi, CEO Golden Tulip Hotel,Asaba) and Chief Izuchukwu Ubabuko (CEO, Ingoliment Gold).

World.title: Tinubu Belongs in League of Africa’s Transformational Leaders, Says Audu
World.content:
*PEBEC DG cites Mandela, Rawlings, says controversies cannot erase president’s political record

Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Director-General of the Presidential Enabling Business Environment Council (PEBEC), Princess Zahrah Mustapha Audu, has drawn a historical parallel between President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and former South African President Nelson Mandela and Ghana’s former leader Jerry John Rawlings, arguing that the controversies surrounding a political leader’s biography should not be allowed to erase the record of his political accomplishments.

Audu, who is also the National Publicity Secretary of the City Boy Movement, made the argument in a commentary in which she maintained that history ultimately judges consequential leaders by the institutions they build, the changes they introduce and the political transformations they drive.

Her intervention comes amid continuing public debate over Tinubu’s political record, his educational history and the economic reforms implemented by his administration since assuming office in May 2023.

Audu argued that the appropriate approach was neither to glorify the President nor to dismiss his entire political career because of disputed aspects of his biography.

“His certificates may be questioned. His biography may be contested. But his political accomplishments cannot simply be written out of history,” she said.

According to her, history does not demand that consequential political figures possess “immaculate biographies”, but records what they built, changed, defended or transformed.

She invoked Mandela’s political evolution as an example, noting that the former South African leader moved from imprisonment and armed resistance against apartheid to becoming the country’s first democratically elected president and a central figure in its transition to constitutional democracy.

Audu similarly referenced Rawlings, whose political career moved from military intervention and revolutionary government to elected constitutional leadership in Ghana.

She stressed, however, that the comparison should not be interpreted as equating Tinubu with either Mandela or Rawlings.

Rather, she said, the broader historical lesson was that political identities and legacies could evolve and should be examined across the entirety of a leader’s career.

“History rarely evaluates consequential political figures from a single chapter of their lives,” she argued.

On the long-running controversy over Tinubu’s educational credentials, Audu urged Nigerians to distinguish between allegations, disputed facts and matters established by available evidence.

She cited the 2023 litigation in the United States involving Chicago State University, noting that the university’s registrar confirmed that Tinubu attended the institution and graduated in 1979, while the dispute included questions over the provenance and authenticity of a particular diploma copy submitted to Nigerian electoral authorities.

Audu maintained that public officials should remain open to scrutiny, but argued that criticism should be confined to what evidence establishes.

“Political achievement cannot make legitimate questions disappear. Neither should legitimate questions be exaggerated beyond the evidence in order to invalidate everything that followed,” she said.

She contended that Tinubu’s political career itself constituted a substantial body of evidence that should form part of any assessment of his leadership.

According to Audu, Tinubu’s emergence as President was the culmination of decades of political activity spanning the Senate, the pro-democracy struggle, Lagos State governorship, opposition politics and the formation of the political coalition that produced the All Progressives Congress (APC).

She argued that whatever judgment Nigerians might make about his politics, his ascent could not reasonably be described as accidental.

“His career was constructed over decades of alliances, defeats, negotiations, institution-building, political calculation and electoral contests,” she said.

Audu further argued that formal educational credentials, while important, were not the only evidence of political ability.

“Achievement is also evidence,” she declared, pointing to decisions, institutions, political coalitions, administrative systems and electoral contests as part of the evidence through which a political leader could be assessed.

She went as far as describing Tinubu as potentially possessing exceptional political ability, arguing that his decades-long political survival and eventual emergence as President demonstrated capabilities that could not be explained by certificates alone.

A major part of Audu’s argument focused on the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms, particularly the removal of the petrol subsidy and the reform of the foreign-exchange regime.

She acknowledged that the reforms had imposed significant costs on Nigerians, with inflation, food insecurity and the rising cost of living becoming major concerns.

Independent assessments have similarly recorded both gains and significant social pressures. In its June 2026 Article IV assessment, the International Monetary Fund said reforms over the previous three years had strengthened Nigeria’s macroeconomic stability and resilience, while also warning that conditions remained difficult for many Nigerians. The IMF estimated poverty at 63 per cent and said 27 million Nigerians had faced food insecurity in late 2025.

The IMF also said the ending of fuel subsidies, cessation of deficit monetisation, tighter monetary policy and exchange-rate liberalisation had reduced fiscal vulnerabilities, rebuilt external buffers and improved foreign-exchange market functioning.

At the same time, the Fund called for stronger social protection, greater fiscal transparency and accountability, and reforms in areas including electricity, agriculture, infrastructure, security and human capital.

For Audu, the mixed record reinforces rather than undermines the need for a more nuanced assessment of Tinubu’s presidency.

“A reform may be economically consequential and socially painful,” she said, arguing that Nigerians should be capable of recognising both dimensions simultaneously.

Audu’s central argument was that Tinubu’s controversial biography and his political achievements should be examined together rather than treated as mutually exclusive narratives.

“History is not acquittal, history is accumulation,” she declared.

She cautioned against what she described as two opposing approaches: portraying the President as beyond criticism on one hand, and treating every controversy surrounding him as sufficient to invalidate his entire political career on the other.

“Biography should be scrutinised, his government should be criticised where evidence warrants criticism, and his achievements should be subjected to precisely the same evidentiary standard and commendation,” she said.

Her remarks echo a broader defence of the administration’s reform agenda. In July, the State House reported calls at a City Boy Movement national retreat for sustained public support and grassroots engagement around the Federal Government’s reforms.

Audu ultimately made the strongest claim of her intervention by declaring Tinubu “Nigeria’s greatest president to date”, a political assessment that remains her stated position rather than an independently established historical fact.

The broader question raised by her intervention, however, is whether Tinubu’s eventual place in Nigerian history will be determined primarily by the controversies surrounding his past, the immediate hardships associated with his reforms, or the longer-term institutional and economic consequences of his presidency.

World.title: Climate Crisis: ECOWAS Parliamentarians Warn of ‘Security Time Bomb’ as Land, Water Shrink
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

West Africa is facing a widening climate-driven crisis in which shrinking water resources, degraded farmland and changing weather patterns are increasingly fuelling competition for land, aggravating farmer-herder conflicts, displacing communities and deepening poverty, parliamentarians from the region have warned.

The warning came as lawmakers at the Second 2026 Parliamentary Seminar of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in Accra, Ghana, examined the increasingly dangerous intersection between climate change, environmental degradation, livelihoods, migration and regional security.

The discussions marked a significant shift from treating climate change principally as an environmental problem to recognising it as an emerging governance, humanitarian and security challenge requiring coordinated legislative and regional intervention.

The Nigeria’s presentation to the seminar revealed how environmental pressures are intersecting with population growth, agricultural expansion, climate variability, land degradation and changing migration patterns to intensify competition between farming and pastoral communities.

The report warned that disputes over crop destruction, land and water, encroachment on livestock routes, cattle theft and changing patterns of seasonal migration have contributed to persistent farmer-herder tensions across the country.

But it cautioned that the conflicts cannot be reduced to a simple confrontation between farmers and herders.

Communal tensions, banditry, organised crime, climate pressures and weaknesses in conflict-resolution mechanisms are also contributing to the crisis.

“In Nigeria, internal displacement has been linked to armed conflict, communal violence, farmer-herder conflict, banditry, terrorism, flooding and other disasters,” Nigeria’s presentation stated.

Citing 2025 assessments by the International Organisation for Migration, the presentation said more than 2.2 million people were internally displaced in the North-East, while over 1.3 million were displaced across the North-Central and North-West regions.

The figures underline the scale of a crisis that has moved beyond humanitarian relief into the areas of governance, development, food security, environmental management and national security.

At the centre of the crisis is a resource equation that is becoming increasingly difficult to manage: less predictable rainfall, declining water availability, pressure on productive land and growing populations competing for the same resources.

For farming and pastoral communities, the presentation noted, land and water are not merely economic assets. They are essential to survival.

As traditional grazing routes become blocked, agricultural land expands and water sources diminish, pastoralists are forced to alter movement patterns while farmers face increasing pressure to protect cultivated land.

Without effective mechanisms for dialogue, mediation and resource management, such environmental pressures can escalate into violent disputes.

This was reflected in Togo’s presentation, which detailed the country’s attempt to regulate transhumance and reduce conflicts linked to livestock movement.

Togo established its National Transhumance Committee in 1995 to monitor livestock movement, routes, animal health and disputes. However, changing environmental and security conditions have prompted the country to introduce a new 2026–2030 plan addressing farmer-herder conflict, pressure on land, climate change, security challenges, inadequate monitoring and weak enforcement.

The experience demonstrates that traditional systems for managing pastoral movement are increasingly being tested by environmental and demographic changes.

The seminar also highlighted how environmental stress can create a chain reaction extending from food production to displacement.

Cabo Verde’s presentation focused on water scarcity, warning in effect that the consequences of climate change are interconnected: reduced water availability affects agriculture, pressure on agriculture affects livelihoods, while deteriorating livelihoods can influence migration.

When displaced or migrating populations encounter communities already competing over scarce land and water, tensions can intensify.

For Nigeria, therefore, the challenge is not simply preventing people from being displaced but creating conditions that allow those already displaced to rebuild their lives.

The country’s presentation identified safe and voluntary return, local integration or relocation, access to land and housing, restoration of property rights, livelihoods, education, healthcare, documentation and participation in community life as essential elements of durable solutions.

This means that displacement policy cannot stop at providing food, temporary shelter and emergency assistance.
