World.title: Meeting in Mexico City, Sheinbaum and South Korea’s president pledge deeper ties
World.content:
Listen to this article

Visiting South Korean leader Lee Jae Myung and his Mexican counterpart, President Claudia Sheinbaum, agreed Thursday to deepen their bilateral relationship through a new roadmap focused on economic and financial cooperation, trade and technology.

In a joint press conference at Mexico City’s National Palace, the two presidents announced the signing of 17 agreements that included expanded cooperation in artificial intelligence, aerospace, energy, defense and supply chains.

Lee’s visit took place as Mexico seeks to diversify its economic relations amid international trade tensions and negotiations with the United States, its main partner, and as it promotes Sheinbaum’s Plan México to attract investment and increase national production.

During the press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that bilateral trade reached US $27 billion in 2025, pointing out that South Korea is one of Mexico’s top five trading partners worldwide, while Mexico is the Asian nation’s main partner in Latin America.

“The goal of greater complementary economic cooperation between our countries will generate shared prosperity and benefits for our people,” Sheinbaum said, adding that South Korean investment since 2006 topped US $11.5 billion.

Lee — the first South Korean leader to visit Mexico since 2010 — said both countries agreed to finalize the review of their reciprocal investment promotion and protection agreement, in order to strengthen economic ties.

“Mexico, the world’s 10th-largest economy and a hub of the global supply chain, is a highly important strategic partner for Korea,” Lee said.

The agreements signed range from economic and financial cooperation, to science and technology, as well as agriculture, security, intellectual property, culture, tourism and academic exchange.

Sheinbaum and Lee committed to promoting trade and investment and facilitating the integration of Mexican small and medium-sized enterprises into the supply chains of South Korean companies operating in Mexico.

Both governments also adopted a Mexico-Korea Action Plan 2026-2030 and will seek to complete the review of the agreement on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments “in the short term … in order to facilitate trade.”

Lee also announced talks to create a US $100 million credit scheme to facilitate Mexican companies’ acquisition of goods and services from Korean companies and to support South Korean firms operating in Mexico.

Yes, K-pop was on the agenda

At the same time, the two countries agreed to expand their cultural and educational exchanges, including the possibility of establishing a K-pop culture center in Mexico and a Mexican cultural institute in South Korea.

On that topic, Sheinbaum announced that K-pop superstars BTS will return to Mexico next year, adding that Stray Kids (a popular South Korean boy band) was to perform at Mexico City’s Estadio GNP Seguros on Friday.

Although BTS has not officially confirmed a return visit to Mexico, Sheinbaum said the group had accepted her proposal during their visit to the National Palace in May.

With reports from EFE, El Universal and Billboard

World.title: Tabasco homicides dropped over 50% since 2024, officials report: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Sheinbaum on tour: As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco.

As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco. 📉 Homicides down 54% in Tabasco : National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day.

: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day. 🚔 Over 6,500 arrests since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period. 🔻 La Barredora “greatly diminished” : Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.”

: Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.” 🗨️ Sheinbaum weighs in on Trump-Xi meeting: The president called Thursday’s meeting in Washington between Trump and Xi “very interesting.” She warned that rivalry between the two powers creates global uncertainty and reaffirmed Mexico’s preference for “peace and cooperation for development.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Villahermosa, capital of the Gulf Coast state of Tabasco.

Security officials presented data showing that the federal government has made significant progress in combating violence in the state, including through the arrest of alleged criminals accused of fueling it. Officials reasserted that the government’s security strategy is yielding results in Tabasco and across the country.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments on the meeting in Washington, D.C., on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum will join both leaders, and various others, at the APEC Summit in China in November.

Government reports 54% reduction in homicides compared to 2024 peak

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that the daily homicide rate in Tabasco in August was 1.6, a reduction of 54% compared to November 2024, the month with the highest murder rate —3.5 per day — since the current federal government took office in October 2024.

“Thanks to the strengthening of the national public security strategy and coordination with the state government, a reduction in this crime has been achieved,” she said.

According to the data Figueroa presented, the year-over-year decline in homicides in August was 16%.

Figueroa also reported that Tabasco has recorded an average of 10.3 high-impact crimes per day so far in 2026.

That figure represents a decline of 12% compared to 2025 and a reduction of 18% compared to 2024. Among the offenses classified as high-impact crimes are homicides, kidnappings, acts of extortion, violent robberies and rape.

More than 6,000 people arrested in Tabasco since October 2024

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that more than 6,500 people — 6,527 to be exact — were arrested in Tabasco between Oct. 1, 2024 and Sept. 15, 2026.

Data he presented showed that 2,053 firearms and 12.97 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period.

García Harfuch said that the arrest of “important targets” in Tabasco has had a “direct impact on the reduction of violence.”

He mentioned a number of the most significant arrests that have been made in the state, including that of a man accused of nine homicides.

García Harfuch: La Barredora has been weakened

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the current strength in Tabasco of La Barredora, a criminal group that was formerly allegedly led by ex-Tabasco Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena.

Bermúdez, who served as security minister in the state government led by former Governor Adán Augusto López Hernández, was arrested in Paraguay in September 2024 and subsequently extradited to Mexico, where he is in prison awaiting trial. López, a Morena party senator and former federal interior minister, has faced claims from opposition parties that he was also involved in La Barredora when the group was allegedly led by Bermúdez.

García Harfuch said there have been “a lot of arrests” of people linked to the criminal group. He subsequently praised the Tabasco state police for their efforts to combat organized crime.

“This organization is greatly diminished,” he said, referring to La Barredora.

“It’s practically split in two,” García Harfuch said.

Sheinbaum comments on Trump-Xi meeting

A reporter asked the president about the meeting on Thursday between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, noting that the latter stated that China and the United States must maintain a peaceful relationship and engage in “healthy” competition.

Sheinbaum described the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents as “very interesting.”

“… The idea of rivalry between two important nations such as China and the United States creates uncertainty in the world,” she said.

“And what Mexico has always sought is peace and cooperation for development,” Sheinbaum added.

She said that her government’s view is that economic competition shouldn’t create “rivalries between countries.”

Mexico has important economic relationships with both the United States and China. Mexico and the United States are each other’s largest trading partner, while China is a large exporter of goods to Mexico.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Cano’s ‘Malinche’: A musical that’s not all song and dance
World.content:
Just about every evening for the past year and a half, more than 1,000 people have made their way to El Frontón, a century-old Art Deco theatre in Mexico City’s small but historic enclave, Tabacalera.

There, the musical, “Malinche,” has been in full swing, having recently kicked off its second run on Aug. 15, with more than 80 cast members singing and dancing flamenco, urban, hip-hop and contemporary to the vision of Jesús Carmona, donning face paint, leather crop tops and fringed two-pieces in an auditorium seating 1,299.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MALINCHE EL MUSICAL (@malinchethemusical)

Created, written and directed by Nacho Cano, the show entered the Mexican theatre scene in March 2025 after a two-and-a-half-year run in Madrid, where it was housed in the IFEMA complex.

It wasn’t exactly Cano’s vision, who unsuccessfully pitched for a 30-meter Aztec-inspired pyramid in Hortaleza, but the venue was still kitted out with a small pyramid, cenotes, pyrotechnics and live bands, making a sizeable impression in Spain’s commercial theatre market.

Since its opening night, though, “Malinche” has faced backlash for what some consider historically insensitive depictions of the 1519 Spanish Conquest, including its retelling of Aztec emperor Moctezuma’s Christian awakening.

The controversy surrounding “Malinche” requires a discussion that centers not only its account of the titular Nahua woman, but also the political background of those who paved the way for its success.

Navigating the history and identity of Malinche

Much of popular art cannot be separated from its contemporary political milieu, both socially and geographically, and Nacho Cano’s work is no exception.

It was just seven years ago that then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador sought an apology from Spain’s King Felipe VI over the colonial treatment of Indigenous Mexicans. After he failed to deliver such an apology, the king was subsequently excluded from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s inauguration, though he has since acknowledged that “there were significant abuses.”

Often described to those who don’t know her as the “Mexican Pocahontas,” it is widely understood that Malintzin, Doña Marina (her Christian name), or Malinche was an Indigenous woman who became Hernán Cortés’ interpreter and thus played a critical role during Spain’s conquest. Around 14 years old when she met Cortés, Malinche would eventually give birth to their son.

In no uncertain terms, Malinche’s history has been written for her. There is no surviving account from her own voice, only skewed and holey Spanish and Nahuatl accounts of the conquest. As an interpreter pushed into slavery, a potential informant of the Cholula massacre, or a willful lover — depending on who you ask — Malinche’s story becomes warped and warbled on the tongues of many.

A contested icon across modern political agendas

Like any cultural paradigm, scholars have attempted to categorize her perception and presentation both temporally and by groups supporting varying ideologies.

A traditional nationalist slant views Malinche as a traitor, “La Chingada,” taking on an Eve-like persona in her betrayal of the nation for the conquistadors, ultimately facilitating the tragic end of the Mexica. Others stress her victimhood not only at the hands of her oppressors but also in her literary portrayal as a traitor.

Here we see, through the abstraction of Malinche, the reduction of the female to a single narrative. Her portrayal even inspired the neologism “malinchista,” which refers to those favoring foreign cultures and ideals.

Meanwhile, feminist and Chicanx discourse have outlined Malinche’s dynamic representation in alignment with varying political agendas and strived to empower her agency. Many view her as a victim of colonial patriarchy who, as scholar Gloria Anzaldúa described it, exists beyond the “traditional/treacherous binary,” and chose to “be a survivor” who “cast her lot with the Spaniards to ensure survival of a race.”

Other postcolonial scholars take on such subaltern perspectives but question Malinche’s true autonomy, often highlighting the backdrop of religious colonial values of benevolence that Malinche was constructed and demonized against.

Acutely relevant, a pro-Hispanic and contemporary transformation of the narrative sees Malinche much like Disney portrays Pocahontas — a young woman whose love for the heroic Western explorer enabled the birth of the mestizaje, making her the “mother” of Mexico.

And so enters Nacho Cano, creator of “Malinche.”

Nacho Cano’s path from pop star to controversy

Ignacio “Nacho” Cano is a former member of the popular band Mecano, a luminary of Spain’s ’80s music scene and one of the biggest Spanish pop stars of the time. The band’s debut album sold 1 million copies in Spain alone, and they have since sold more than 30 million records worldwide.

Cano went on to develop the wildly influential “Hoy No Me Puedo Levantar,” a musical exploring Madrid’s post-Franco countercultural movement, La Movida, and one of the most financially successful Spanish musicals to date.

Despite his status as a 20th-century pop idol, Cano also established himself as a controversial political figure. He’s an avowed ally of the right-wing president of the Community of Madrid and People’s Party, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who presented him in 2021 with the Order of the Second of May.

Ayuso herself was described by Politico as being in a “nationalistic showdown with Mexico.”

Such political dissension stems from her admiration of Cortés and defense of the Spanish Conquest as a civilizing mission, perhaps most notably at this year’s “Celebration of Evangelization and Mestizaje in Mexico.”

Sheinbaum has rebuked Ayuso’s characterization of the “conquest as salvation,” while Ayuso has been dubbed by Morena party members “the heir to the Spanish Falange,” a far-right fascist political movement founded in Spain in the 1930s.

Cano has similarly argued that “without Cortés there would be no Mexico,” a sentiment reflected in the feathers and flashlights of his extravagant musical production.

Divided perspectives and powerful corporate backing

In July 2024, Cano was arrested for alleged improprieties and poor working conditions for the performers in Madrid’s “Malinche,” including undocumented immigrants. The charges were dropped the following year, with Cano insisting that left-wing leaders led an alleged coordinated attack.

Beyond the show itself, Cano offers viewers a more detailed insight into the 10-year process behind his play in the 2021 Netflix documentary, “Making Malinche,” a name whose very essence speaks volumes. Malinche is once again a woman methodically remade and reduced, this time to an unwavering, consensual lover.

In an interview with El Mundo, Cano argued that Mexico’s history has been told “deliberately poorly,” and claimed in the documentary that his work is more historically accurate.

The overarching narrative he perpetuates is that Malinche was not a betrayer, but a woman whose passionate love for a Spaniard gifted humanity the New World.

We have seen a correlation between Malinche’s shifting portrayal and shifting Mexican cultural identity, as critics argue Cano has both sanitized and romanticized the violent reality of Spanish conquest.

Left-wing critics have argued the musical erases Indigenous trauma and experience in its “perpetuat[ion] of a Eurocentric narrative,” describing it as a “spectacle of postmodern Falangism.”

On the other end of the spectrum, conservative critics have chided Cano for doing a disservice to Catholicism, accusing him of not pushing far enough “an authentic ode to the history of Spain, against ideological revisionism and the Black Legend,” a reference to a school of thought that suggests “anti-Catholic” and “anti-Spanish” narratives deliberately position the Spanish Empire as singularly motivated by cruelty and greed.

However, these are not the only reasons many people in the left-wing community have boycotted “Malinche.”

The champions of ‘Malinche’

Ricardo Salinas Pliego, a Mexican television magnate and chairman of Grupo Salinas whose net worth is estimated to be US $5 billion, is responsible for bringing “Malinche” to Mexico and promoting it on his network, TV Azteca. His wife, María Laura Medina de Salinas, served as an executive producer during its opening in Mexico last year, after falling “in love” with it in Madrid and “form[ing] a synergy” with Cano, according to José Manuel Azpiroz, the director of communications at Salinas’ Grupo Elektra.

What’s more, the show is officially “presented” by Banco Azteca, part of Salinas’ conglomerate.

Much like Cano, Salinas is no stranger to controversy, having been accused of tax evasion to the tune of US $3 billion while also flirting with a presidential run.

Once labeled “the newest face of the Mexican new right,” he is an outspoken critic of Sheinbaum and supporter of the National Action Party (PAN), with a political temperament that follows in the footsteps of Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Salinas and Cano also have close ties to Juan Miguel Zunzunegui, a Mexican historian and avid rejector of the Black Legend. He defends the Spanish empire and upholds a history that dismisses Indigenous suffering and denies the mass violation of women.

In an interview with El Mundo, he said, “[t]he Spaniard who thinks they did horrible things in America does so out of ignorance.”

Cano recently wrote the prologue to Zunzunegui’s book, “Hernán Cortés,” and Zunzunegui is involved in the current run of “Malinche,” making a special appearance as Spanish friar and translator Jerónimo de Aguilar.

Turning historical violence into a love story

Malinche’s representation has been utilized as a vehicle to express specific sociopolitical ideologies within Mexican society, both at home and abroad. The question now is why proponents of “Malinche” feel a desire to promote a history of colonial violence as a love story that’s couched in consent and results in creation?

Some have asked a similar question of Disney’s romanticization of colonial relationships in its 1995 adaptation of “Pocahontas,” with the understanding that depicting a “mutually satisfying encounter” legitimizes what they describe as the violence of Western history.

“Malinche” too warrants consideration as part of a broader ideological posture seeking to sublimate Spain’s imperial legacy. However, with its second season running through January 2027, its popularity, devoid of nuanced conversations about who gets to write and rewrite history, speaks for itself.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: TV Azteca Took a US$290 Million Loan From an Offshore Bank Before Filing
World.content:
MEXICO · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened. TV Azteca took a facility of up to US$290 million from AlterBank in January, weeks before seeking bankruptcy protection. — Who reported it. Armando.info and El Faro published the investigation on 24 September, and Proceso summarised it the next day. — What AlterBank is. Outlets describe it as an offshore lender registered in Saint Lucia with three employees. — Who is named. Proceso names two Venezuelans, Augusto César Castillo Chávez and Tomás Hernández, as the men behind it. — The company answers. TV Azteca says the financing was legal and that the money went to its tax bill in Mexico. — The creditors answer. Bank of New York Mellon has gone to a United States court, calling the deal a possible fraudulent transfer. — Why it matters. Mexico’s second broadcaster owes creditors about 24 billion pesos, roughly US$1.4 billion, and is restructuring under court supervision.

Mexico’s TV Azteca borrowed from an offshore bank registered in Saint Lucia weeks before it sought bankruptcy protection. The facility ran to as much as US$290 million, about 5 billion pesos.

The investigative outlets Armando.info and El Faro published the finding on 24 September. The broadcaster says the loan was legal and that the money paid a tax bill.

An Elektra store, part of the same Grupo Salinas as TV Azteca, which is not in the insolvency cases (Photo: Werther mx, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Investigation Says

The two outlets traced the lender, AlterBank, to Saint Lucia, a Caribbean island of about 180,000 people. El Imparcial, summarising the work, described a financial entity with three employees.

Proceso, the Mexican weekly, named two Venezuelans as the men behind the bank: Augusto César Castillo Chávez and Tomás Hernández. It reported that both have been linked to President Nayib Bukele’s government in El Salvador.

El Siglo de Torreón, reporting the same investigation, said Hernández had been identified as an adviser to that government. It also reported claimed links to companies tied to alleged corruption in El Salvador’s pandemic spending.

None of that has been tested in court. No charge has been reported against AlterBank, against the two men or against TV Azteca over this loan.

Armando.info reports on Venezuela from exile, and El Faro is a Salvadoran outlet that now works from Costa Rica. Both have published on Bukele’s government before, and both are read as critical of it.

The Timing

The facility was agreed on 29 January 2026, according to the specialist service BankruptcyData. Repayment was due in July, creditors told a court in Miami in June.

TV Azteca asked a Mexican judge for concurso mercantil, the country’s bankruptcy procedure, in September. Five of its subsidiaries, including the online-casino permit holder Ganador Azteca, filed separately on 18 September.

That sequence is what interests the creditors. Money arrived from an unfamiliar lender shortly before the company sought protection from the creditors it already had.

The broadcaster has also asked a New York court for recognition of the Mexican case. That step, known as Chapter 15, stops American creditors seizing assets while the Mexican process runs.

What the Company Says

TV Azteca’s position, as reported by El Siglo de Torreón, is that the financing was legal and legitimate. It says the proceeds went to meet obligations with Mexico’s tax authority, known as the SAT.

BankruptcyData reported a different emphasis, saying the facility was obtained to stop the seizure of the broadcaster’s assets. The two accounts are not necessarily in conflict, because a tax debt can trigger a seizure.

It is not clear how much of the money was actually drawn. The reports describe a maximum facility rather than a confirmed transfer of the full amount.

The Creditors’ Case

Bank of New York Mellon, which represents bondholders, has gone to a United States court over the transaction. Its filing raises the possibility that the loan was a fraudulent transfer, a legal term for moving assets out of creditors’ reach.

Creditors first raised the AlterBank facility in a complaint filed in Miami on 2 June. The company has since sought protection in New York as well, to shield the Mexican restructuring from American lawsuits.

A fraudulent-transfer claim is an allegation, not a finding. Courts on both sides of the border will decide whether the January deal stands.

Who Ricardo Salinas Pliego Is

TV Azteca belongs to Grupo Salinas, the conglomerate of Ricardo Salinas Pliego, one of Mexico’s richest men. His businesses run from broadcasting to retail and banking, and he is a vocal critic of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

He has spent years fighting the tax authority in court over bills he disputes. Those cases are separate from the bankruptcy, but they are the backdrop to a loan the company says went to the SAT.

The group has also lost ground in its core business. Mexican advertising has moved to streaming and social platforms, which hits the second broadcaster harder than the first.

What to Watch

The first question is documentary: which accounts the US$290 million passed through, and what security the lender took. Creditors will press for that in the United States, where disclosure rules are wider.

The second is whether Mexican regulators look at AlterBank at all. Nothing published so far shows a Mexican authority examining the lender.

The third is the restructuring itself. A judge who treats the January facility as suspect can reorder the queue of creditors waiting to be paid.

For viewers and staff, none of this changes the schedule yet. Concurso mercantil is designed to keep a company trading while the arguments go on.

World.title: Ecopetrol Fracking Return and Offshore Push as Colombia Reserves Fall
World.content:
COLOMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened. Ecopetrol’s incoming president said on Friday that Colombia has oil reserves for 7.4 years and gas for 5.9. — Who he is. Joaquin Gutierrez Caballero managed President Abelardo de la Espriella’s election campaign and has no background in oil. — The reversal. He said Ecopetrol will apply what he called responsible fracking and keep exploring offshore, undoing the previous government’s stance. — The production problem. Ecopetrol pumped 705,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day between April and June, its weakest quarter in four years. — The offshore prize. Sirius, a deepwater gas find 77 kilometres off Santa Marta, holds more than six trillion cubic feet of gas. — The opposition. Former president Gustavo Petro blocked fracking in office and called it the worst foolishness, saying water is worth more than gold. — What comes next. Courts have already suspended Ecopetrol’s two fracking pilot wells once, so a restart would face fresh legal challenge.

Colombia’s state oil company has a new president, and his first speech was a warning. Joaquin Gutierrez said the country has only 7.4 years of oil reserves left and 5.9 years of gas.

He also promised what he called responsible fracking, a method the previous government refused to allow anywhere in Colombia. He said offshore exploration in the Caribbean would continue, with the Sirius gas discovery at its centre.

Ecopetrol’s Barrancabermeja refinery on the Magdalena river, the company’s largest plant (Photo: Yesid Ferney Patiño, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Colombia’s New Oil Chief Said

Gutierrez spoke on Friday at the ceremony that handed him control of Ecopetrol. Semana reported his phrase that he had not come to dress up reality for anybody.

El Colombiano quoted him describing a narrow energy horizon for the country and calling the reserve figures derisory. He put proved reserves at 7.4 years for oil and 5.9 years for gas.

He said Ecopetrol would advance both conventional and unconventional projects from now on. La Republica quoted him promising responsible fracking and continued exploration of offshore fields.

El Heraldo published a longer passage from the same speech on Saturday. He said he was taking charge of the company at a moment of crisis with no room for half measures.

What Ecopetrol does. Ecopetrol S.A. operates as an integrated energy company. It operates through four segments: Exploration and Production; Transport and Logistics; Refining and Petrochemicals; and Energy transmission and Toll Roads Concessions. The Exploration and Production segment engages in the exploration and production of oil and gas. The Transport and Logistics segment is involved in…

Why the Reserve Numbers Matter

Reserve life is a blunt measure with a simple meaning that foreign readers can follow. It divides what a country can prove is underground by what it takes out in a year.

A gas reserve life of 5.9 years does not mean the taps run dry in 2032. It means Colombia has to find more gas, or buy it abroad, well before then.

The country is already buying. Colombia began importing liquefied natural gas in December 2024, after more than four decades of supplying itself.

Production is falling as well as reserves. Ecopetrol pumped 705,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day in the second quarter, its lowest level in four years, ABC Economia reported.

The Fracking Reversal at Home

Fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, pumps water and sand underground at pressure to crack rock and free the oil or gas inside. It is routine in shale fields and contested wherever water is scarce.

Colombia has never fracked commercially, whatever its politicians have promised. Ecopetrol had two pilot projects, named Kale and Platero, near Puerto Wilches on the Magdalena River.

Both were suspended in 2022, after a court order and a request from Ecopetrol itself. Semana reported at the time that the company acted in the face of the incoming government’s position.

The Goldman Environmental Prize honoured a Puerto Wilches campaigner, Yuvelis Morales Blanco, this year for her work against those wells. Its citation says the Constitutional Court ruled in 2024 that the pilot projects breached community rights.

The Fracking Ecopetrol Already Does Abroad

Ecopetrol fracks outside Colombia, which is the part of this argument that Colombians know best. It holds a position in the Permian Basin of Texas, where shale wells are fractured as a matter of routine.

That business is shrinking rather than growing. Permian output fell to 80,800 barrels a day in the second quarter, from a peak of 115,000 in 2025, ABC Economia reported.

The previous government wanted the company out of it altogether. Semana reported that President Gustavo Petro asked Ecopetrol in February 2025 to sell its American fracking assets.

He had already blocked a much larger deal in the same basin. The magazine put the vetoed purchase at about US$3.6 billion and said two board members resigned over the decision.

What Offshore Means for the Caribbean Coast

Offshore drilling is the least contested part of the new plan. The prize is Sirius, a deepwater gas discovery that Ecopetrol runs with Brazil’s state oil company Petrobras.

The well sits about 77 kilometres off Santa Marta, in water 830 metres deep. Testing confirmed more than six trillion cubic feet of gas in place there, Colombia One reported.

That volume could roughly triple national gas reserves if it is developed. None of it arrives soon, with production planned for the end of 2029 and about US$2.9 billion set aside for the work.

Gutierrez named Sirius in his speech, La Republica reported, calling it key to supplying the country. He also announced a second Ecopetrol headquarters in Barranquilla, on the same Caribbean coast, El Heraldo reported.

The Argument, and What Happens Next

The government side of the argument is unambiguous. De la Espriella told the same ceremony that his administration reopens exploration and the signing of new contracts, including fracking, El Heraldo reported.

He framed imported energy as the real danger to the country. El Pais of Cali quoted him saying that dependence on imports is not a transition, and promising what he called energy sovereignty.

The case against is older and plainer than the case for. Infobae quoted Gustavo Petro, who was president until August, calling fracking the worst foolishness and saying water is worth more than gold.

Ecopetrol’s main union has been guarded rather than hostile, and its president Martin Ravelo told Infobae that the first task is to recover trust. Neither Gutierrez nor the government has published a timetable for a first new well.

World.title: Brazil’s Nubank in Talks to Buy Britain’s Monzo, Sky News Reports
World.content:
BRAZIL · BANKING

Key Facts — What happened. Sky News reported this weekend that Britain’s Monzo is in talks over a sale to Brazil’s Nubank. — The price. The report puts Monzo at between £8 billion and £10 billion, about US$10.6 billion to US$13.2 billion. — The buyer. Nubank is Latin America’s largest digital bank, with more than 110 million customers and a New York listing. — The target. Monzo had 15.2 million customers and £25.7 billion (about US$34 billion) of deposits in its 2026 accounts. — The catch. Neither bank has confirmed the talks, and no deal has been announced or filed with any regulator. — Why it matters. A Brazilian bank buying a British one would reverse the usual direction of travel in banking takeovers. — What comes next. Any deal would need approval from Britain’s banking regulators and from Monzo’s own shareholders.

Brazil’s Nubank is in talks to buy Monzo, the British digital bank, Sky News reported this weekend. The report values Monzo at between £8 billion and £10 billion, about US$10.6 billion to US$13.2 billion.

Neither bank has confirmed the talks, and no agreement has been announced. If one were struck, it would be the largest purchase of a British bank by a Latin American company.

Nubank co-founder and chief executive David Vélez, who built the bank in São Paulo from 2013 (Photo: Nubank, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Was Reported

Sky News said the two digital banks have held talks about a deal that would take Monzo into Nubank’s hands. The broadcaster gave a price range rather than an agreed figure, which is normal at this stage.

Talks at this stage often end without a transaction. Neither Nubank nor Monzo commented publicly on the report, and no filing has appeared on either side of the Atlantic.

The range is roughly double Monzo’s last disclosed valuation. An employee share sale in October 2024 valued the bank at £4.5 billion, about US$5.9 billion at the time, Bloomberg reported then.

What Nu Holdings does. Nu Holdings Ltd. provides digital banking platform in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, the Cayman Islands, and the United States. The company provides spending solutions comprising Nu credit and prepaid card, a digitally enabled card that acts as a credit and a prepaid card; Nubank+ Tier, an evolution of the Nu experience; Ultraviolet credit…

Who Monzo Is

Monzo is a London bank without branches, founded in 2015 and known for its coral-coloured cards. Its accounts for the year to February 2026 showed 15.2 million customers and £25.7 billion of deposits, about US$34 billion.

The bank reported gross profit of £1.0 billion, about US$1.3 billion, and adjusted pre-tax profit of £172.6 million, about US$229 million. On a statutory basis, pre-tax profit was £87.3 million, roughly US$116 million.

Monzo closed its United States operation this year to concentrate on Britain and continental Europe. It has also been preparing for a stock-market listing, which a sale would replace.

Why Nubank Would Want It

Nubank began in São Paulo in 2013 as a credit-card company for customers the big Brazilian banks treated poorly. It now serves more than 110 million people in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia.

Its shares closed on Friday at US$13.59 in New York, which values the company at roughly US$65 billion. That is about five times the top of the range reported for Monzo.

The Brazilian bank has been pushing outside Latin America. It began offering accounts in the United States this year through a partner bank, while it waits on its own American licence application.

Buying Monzo would give it a British banking licence, a European customer base and a brand that does not need translating. It would also remove a competitor in the market for app-only banking.

What Would Have to Happen

A takeover of a British bank needs the blessing of the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. Regulators examine the buyer’s capital, its owners and its plans for depositors.

Monzo’s shareholders would also have to agree. They include the venture funds Accel and Passion Capital, and CapitalG, the growth-investment arm of Google’s parent company.

Thousands of customers also hold small stakes from the bank’s crowdfunding rounds. They would be asked to vote on any sale, as they were on earlier fundraisings.

Brazilian regulators would take an interest too, because Nubank’s holding company answers to the central bank in Brasília. None of these steps happens quickly, and any of them can stop a deal.

The Direction of Travel

For most of the past century, European banks bought Latin American ones rather than the other way round. Spain’s Santander and Britain’s HSBC built large regional networks that way.

A Nubank purchase of Monzo would point the other way, with Brazilian money buying a British lender. Latin American companies rarely attempt takeovers of that size in Europe.

The region does have precedents in other industries. Brazil’s JBS bought meat plants across Europe and the United States, and 3G Capital took control of Burger King.

Banking is harder, because regulators judge owners as well as prices. That is why the British approval process matters more here than the money does.

What to Watch

The first thing to watch is whether either bank confirms the talks or denies them. A denial would settle the matter for now, while silence usually means the conversation continues.

The second is Monzo’s listing plan, which had pointed to a valuation near £10 billion, about US$13.2 billion. A sale at that level would tell investors what private buyers think the business is worth.

The third is Nubank’s American licence application. Owning a regulated British bank would change how supervisors in Washington read the company’s ambitions.

The fourth is price. Monzo’s board has to weigh a cash exit now against a listing later, and its early backers have waited a decade for either.

World.title: US Navy Has No Carrier Near Venezuela as Caribbean Strikes Pass 220 Deaths
World.content:
CARIBBEAN · SECURITY

Key Facts — The carrier. The USS Gerald R Ford left the Caribbean for the Middle East in February, Reuters and the New York Times reported. — Since then. The USS Nimitz spent under a month in the Caribbean and ended its deployment on 17 June, leaving no carrier behind. — The mission. Operation Southern Spear, named by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in November 2025, targets boats Washington says carry drugs. — The toll. Human Rights Watch counts 69 strikes and 227 people killed since September 2025; other tallies differ slightly. — The dispute. The UN special rapporteur Ben Saul says the strikes break international law; Washington calls them self-defence. — The force. The Associated Press counted about 15,000 American personnel and 11 warships in the region in December 2025. — Why it matters. Washington is pressing Cuba and Venezuela while the Navy’s heaviest ships sit on the other side of the world.

No United States aircraft carrier has been reported in the Caribbean since June, even as American forces keep striking boats off Venezuela. The carrier that was there sailed for the Middle East in February, and none has replaced it.

That leaves the American campaign against drug boats in the Caribbean running without its heaviest ship. The war with Iran has pulled the Navy’s carriers to the Gulf and kept them there.

The USS Gerald R Ford, which spent three months in the Caribbean before sailing for the Middle East in February (Photo: U.S. Navy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Reports Say

A report that the Pentagon is moving an aircraft carrier out of the Caribbean and into the Middle East has been widely republished. The original is a Reuters dispatch dated 13 February 2026, carried since by energy and shipping websites.

Reuters named two American officials and identified the ship as the USS Gerald R Ford. It said the carrier would take at least a week to reach the Middle East and would join the USS Abraham Lincoln.

The New York Times had reported the decision a day earlier, on 12 February. USNI News, the journal of the United States Naval Institute, said an American official confirmed it.

Where the Carrier Went

The Ford had arrived in the Caribbean in November 2025, after deploying in June of that year. By the time it left, it had been at sea for about eight months.

It was on station in early January, when American forces captured Nicolás Maduro in an overnight raid in Caracas. USNI News noted that an extended deployment risked breaking the post-Vietnam record of 294 days.

The new orders came before the fighting with Iran started at the end of February. The USS Abraham Lincoln had gone to the Middle East in January, and the Ford made a second carrier there.

The Ford left the Middle East in early May and reached Norfolk on 16 May, after 326 days at sea. That was the longest American carrier deployment since the Cold War ended, and the ship entered a shipyard in July.

What Replaced It

Southern Command, the American military headquarters for Latin America, did get another carrier later. The USS Nimitz reached the Caribbean on 20 May, with Carrier Air Wing 17, the destroyer USS Gridley and the oiler USNS Patuxent.

That visit was short. The Nimitz ended its Southern Seas deployment on 17 June, after port calls in Brazil, Chile, Jamaica and Panama.

Rear Admiral Carlos Sardiello, who commands United States Naval Forces Southern Command, said the strike group had worked with 14 countries. No American aircraft carrier has been reported in the Caribbean since.

The Campaign That Continues

The strikes on boats have not stopped. Southern Command said a strike on 20 September killed four people on a vessel it described as carrying drugs, the Hill reported.

The campaign began on 2 September 2025 and was named Operation Southern Spear by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that November. Human Rights Watch counts 69 strikes and 227 people killed to date.

Counts differ because they use different cut-off dates and methods. CBC put the toll at at least 231 deaths across 69 strikes on 21 September.

A United Nations report counted 68 vessels struck and at least 223 people killed to August. Southern Command has said it cannot give a public accounting of every strike and interdiction.

The Argument Over Legality

Washington says the strikes are self-defence against armed groups it has designated as terrorist organisations. It relies on an opinion from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel that it has not published.

Ben Saul, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights and counter-terrorism, disagrees. He found that drug trafficking is not an armed attack, so the self-defence claim does not hold.

Human Rights Watch calls the campaign a year of extrajudicial killings at sea. Southern Command says its task is to counter illicit activities and malign actors in the Western Hemisphere.

The administration has not identified everyone killed in the strikes. Trinidad and Tobago has supported the operations, while other governments in the Caribbean Community bloc have voiced concern.

What to Watch

The first thing to watch is whether the Pentagon sends another carrier south. The Navy has eleven, and maintenance and training usually leave only about three at sea at once.

The second is the war with Iran, which is holding the Navy’s heavy ships in the Gulf. Iran offered this week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, and Washington has not accepted.

The third is the pace of the boat strikes, which slowed through 2026. Eleven were recorded in December 2025 alone, against roughly five a month over the first half of this year.

The fourth is Cuba, where Washington has raised the pressure this month. President Trump told the UN General Assembly that the island’s government would fall.

World.title: Iran’s Seven-Day Hormuz Plan and What US$104 Oil Does to Latin America
World.content:
LATIN AMERICA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, offered a seven-day plan in New York to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. — The terms. Iran wants the fighting stopped, the American naval blockade lifted, oil sanctions waived and frozen funds released. — The answer. The Wall Street Journal reported that President Trump rejected the plan, while the State Department said its channels stay open. — The price. Brent crude settled at US$104.37 a barrel on Friday, against about US$70 before the war began. — The importers. Chile, Peru, Central America and the Caribbean buy nearly all their fuel abroad and carry the higher bill. — The exporters. Brazil, Guyana, Venezuela and Colombia are selling more crude, at better prices, than at any point this decade. — Why it matters. A reopening would lower pump prices across the region and end the windfall its oil producers are banking.

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States meets a list of conditions. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, set out the plan to reporters in New York during the UN General Assembly.

The offer matters far from the Gulf, because the strait has been shut since February and oil still costs about US$104 a barrel. Latin America is split by that price, between the countries that buy fuel and the ones that sell it.

The Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman seen at night from orbit, with the Musandam Peninsula dividing the two (Photo: NASA/Tim Kopra, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Iran Has Offered

Araghchi said Qatar passed the plan to Washington, according to the Anadolu Agency, Turkey’s state news agency. The clock would start the day after the United States accepted it.

Under the plan, fighting would stop on every front, including Lebanon, and the American naval blockade of Iranian ports would end. Washington would also waive sanctions on Iranian oil exports and release frozen Iranian funds, Al Jazeera reported.

The United States would take those steps over the first five days, and the strait would open on the sixth or seventh. Talks on a wider settlement would begin on the seventh day.

“The moment they accept this plan, from the next day, this timetable can start,” Araghchi said. He added that reopening the waterway would not mean concessions on Iran’s nuclear programme.

Washington’s Answer

President Donald Trump has rejected the seven-day offer, the Wall Street Journal reported, and expects American bombing to resume after the midterm elections. The White House has not confirmed that account.

In public the State Department has not closed the door. Its spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said it was not the United States that had stopped talks from happening.

A United States official told CBS News that the discussions were positive and constructive, but that Washington was in no hurry. The official said America held the stronger position.

Iran’s reading is the opposite. Araghchi said the choice now rested with the United States, and that Iran would not surrender sovereign rights under pressure.

Why the Strait Is Shut

The Strait of Hormuz is the channel between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of the world’s oil normally moves. Iran closed it on 28 February, after American and Israeli air strikes began the war.

A ceasefire in June briefly eased the blockage, but it broke down in July. The United States reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July, and the waterway has stayed effectively shut.

Traffic through the strait has fallen from about 20 million barrels a day to fewer than four million, the International Energy Agency estimates. American Central Command says it has turned back 122 commercial ships heading for Iranian ports.

Brent crude, the benchmark that prices most traded oil, settled at US$104.37 a barrel on Friday, down 2.09%. It cost about US$70 before the war and touched roughly US$150 in the first weeks of it.

The Bill for the Importers

Most of Latin America buys its fuel rather than making it. Chile, Peru, the Central American republics and the Caribbean islands import almost everything they burn, so a Gulf shortage lands on their pumps.

OLADE, the intergovernmental energy body for Latin America and the Caribbean, measured the damage done in March. Petrol prices across the region rose 15% that month, diesel prices 21%, and regional energy inflation reached 1.42%.

Chile shows what that costs a treasury, which was spending about US$140 million a week to hold pump prices down. In March the government let go, and petrol rose 44% and diesel 54% in a single week.

The Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, a UN body, expects energy to cost at least 25% more this year. It calculates that the trade balance of Central America, Haiti and the Dominican Republic could worsen by 0.9% of their output.

The Windfall for the Exporters

The other half of the region is selling into the shortage. Latin America pumped 11% of the world’s crude last year against 30% from the Middle East, and is filling part of the gap.

Brazil passed four million barrels a day this year and set a monthly production record in June. The Americas Society and Council of the Americas put its crude sales to China up 87% in the first five months.

Guyana, a country of about 800,000 people on South America’s north coast, has gained most in proportion. Its government raised its 2026 petroleum revenue forecast to about US$6.5 billion, more than double the budget figure.

Venezuela sold more than 1.25 million barrels a day in May, its best month in over seven years. Colombia’s Ecopetrol rose 1.28% on Friday to US$16.58 in New York, the only regional oil share to gain.

What to Watch

The first question is whether Washington answers the offer at all. A rejection reported by one newspaper is not a formal refusal, and Iran has said its timetable stays available.

The second is the oil price, which has swung with each diplomatic signal. Brent lost about 2% on Friday on talk of a deal, having gained 3.4% the day before on talk of a wider war.

The third is what happens to the region’s fuel subsidies if prices stay high into 2027. Chile has already stopped paying, and other governments are weighing the same choice.

The fourth is Latin America’s own diplomatic position, which has hardened. Colombia severed relations with Iran this month over alleged links to armed groups, and Tehran called the accusation baseless.

World.title: ExxonMobil Says AI Cuts Guyana Oil Field Analysis From Months to Days
World.content:
GUYANA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What was said. ExxonMobil’s exploration chief says artificial intelligence now turns seismic interpretation around in days rather than months. — Who and where. John Ardill, vice-president of exploration, spoke at the Offshore Technology Conference in Houston in May, Reuters reported. — The result claimed. The company later said the tools had flagged four new exploration opportunities in the Stabroek block offshore Guyana. — The block. ExxonMobil operates Stabroek with 45 percent, Hess holds 30 percent for Chevron and China’s CNOOC 25 percent. — Output. Guyana produced more than 900,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026 from four floating production vessels. — The money for Guyana. The country’s oil fund received about US$2 billion in the first six months of 2026. — The caveat. ExxonMobil has published no figures for cost or drilling time saved, and a prospect is only proven by drilling.

ExxonMobil says artificial intelligence has cut the time it needs to read seismic data from Guyana’s offshore oil fields. Work that once took months now takes days, the company’s head of exploration told an industry conference.

The claim matters because Guyana has become one of the fastest-growing oil producers on earth in six years. What the company has not published is any figure for money or drilling days saved.

Vessels of this type lift Guyana’s oil; four work the Stabroek block, with a fifth due to start (Photo: K. Krallis – SV1XV, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Said It, and Where

The statement came from John Ardill, ExxonMobil’s vice-president of exploration. He spoke on Tuesday 6 May at the Offshore Technology Conference in Houston, and Reuters reported his remarks.

Ardill described the methods in plain terms as deep learning, classification and reinforcement learning. His point was about speed rather than about replacing people.

Ardill said “we can turn those tools around in just a few days” at the Houston conference. The interpreter then receives “a prioritized list of anomalies to go effectively validate”, he added.

Reuters also reported that ExxonMobil plans to apply the same approach to a block it holds offshore Trinidad and Tobago. Ardill said the technique lets the company look at prospects that were harder to evaluate before.

What the Tools Are Doing

Three different jobs are bundled inside the word artificial intelligence here. The first is seismic imaging and interpretation, the reading of sound-wave surveys that map rock thousands of metres below the seabed.

The second is reservoir monitoring, which watches how oil moves underground once a field is producing. ExxonMobil describes combining that with four-dimensional seismic imaging, meaning repeated surveys of the same rock over time.

The third is drilling itself. At the same conference he said one Guyana well was drilled through the reservoir section with no driller touching the controls.

ExxonMobil said the automated system placed the well better than conventional methods did. It has not published the well’s name, its depth or how long it took.

What It Has Found So Far

The concrete claim arrived in August. The trade publication World Oil reported that ExxonMobil had used the tools to identify four new exploration opportunities in the Stabroek block.

The company fed historical discoveries, drilling results and subsurface data into deep learning and machine learning models. High-performance computing and advanced seismic imaging did the rest.

The Guyanese outlet Fueled traced the disclosure to ExxonMobil’s second-quarter earnings presentation in early August. That presentation credited advanced subsurface technologies with more than US$2 billion of added project value through better reservoir management and recovery.

That figure covers the whole toolkit, not artificial intelligence alone. Four opportunities identified is also not four discoveries, because only a drill bit settles whether oil is there.

Why It Matters for Guyana

Guyana is a country of fewer than a million people that pumped almost nothing until 2019. Gross output from the Stabroek block averaged more than 900,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026.

Four floating production vessels do that work, named Liza Destiny, Liza Unity, Prosperity and One Guyana. A fifth, Errea Wittu, is due to start on the Uaru field and would add about 250,000 barrels a day.

ExxonMobil operates the block with 45 percent, Hess holds 30 percent as a Chevron subsidiary, and the Chinese state company CNOOC holds 25 percent. Guyana’s own take is a 2 percent royalty on all oil plus half the profit oil.

That produced about US$2 billion for the country’s Natural Resource Fund between January and June, of which US$218.4 million was royalty. Faster exploration means more of that, sooner, which is why Georgetown listens when Exxon talks about speed.

The Sceptical Reading

None of this has been independently measured. ExxonMobil has published no before-and-after processing times, no drilling-cycle reduction in days, and no cost saving attributable to the software.

Nor has it named the system or shown that any commercial barrel was found by a machine. The claims that exploration gets faster and cheaper are the company’s own, repeated by industry publications.

The industry’s own technical literature is more careful. The seismic contractor Fairfield Geotechnologies argues that algorithms excel at pattern recognition, while geological context is still needed to validate what they produce.

That is also what Ardill described, a ranked list handed to a person to check. The honest version of the story is a faster shortlist, not a machine that finds oil.

What to Watch

The first thing to watch is whether any of the four opportunities becomes a well. Exploration wells offshore Guyana are drilled in batches, and results are usually disclosed with the quarterly figures.

The second is the production path. ExxonMobil has said it expects capacity of about 1.7 million oil-equivalent barrels a day by 2030 from eight developments.

The third is Chevron, which now owns the Hess stake and has its own view on how fast to drill. Partners that pay 55 percent of the bill have a say in what the operator accelerates.

The fourth is Guyana itself, where the speed of drilling is already contested at home. Critics of the government have argued for years that regulation has not kept pace with the industry it oversees.

World.title: Cuba Informal Exchange Rate Hits New Highs of 730 Pesos to the US Dollar
World.content:
CUBA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The rate. The independent tracker elTOQUE put the informal rate at 730 pesos to the US dollar on Saturday morning. — The euro. The euro reached 840 pesos on the same reading, the highest level the tracker has recorded. — The official rate. The Central Bank’s floating rate stood at about 678 pesos to the US dollar, some 50 pesos below the street. — The year. The informal dollar has risen from 460 pesos in early January, a gain of about 59% in under nine months. — The wage. Cuba’s average state wage of 6,930 pesos a month is worth about US$9.50 at the informal rate. — The government. Granma, the Communist Party daily, accuses elTOQUE of manipulating the rate and driving what it calls induced inflation. — Why it matters. Almost every private price in Cuba is set against the informal rate rather than the official one.

Cuba’s informal exchange rate reached new highs this week, with the US dollar quoted at 730 pesos and the euro at 840. The figures come from elTOQUE, an independent outlet that tracks street offers and publishes a daily rate.

That is not an official rate, and no Cuban bank will sell dollars at it. It is the price Cubans actually pay, and almost every private price on the island moves with it.

A street in Centro Habana, where almost every private price is set against the informal exchange rate (Photo: Antonio Schubert, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Rate Is Now

The elTOQUE reading on Saturday morning put the dollar at 730 pesos, the euro at 840 and the MLC at 474.95. The MLC is a Cuban digital currency used in state shops that sell imported goods.

CiberCuba, a Cuban news site that runs its own index, had the dollar at 733 pesos on Friday. Both trackers have the dollar and the euro at or near the highest levels they have recorded.

The Central Bank of Cuba runs a floating rate of its own, which stood at about 678 pesos to the dollar on Friday. State banks and the CADECA exchange houses were selling dollars at between 677 and 692 pesos.

What an Informal Rate Is

Cuba has not had a single exchange rate for years. The state keeps 24 pesos to the dollar for companies and 120 pesos for individuals, far below what the currency fetches.

Because the official windows rarely have dollars to sell, Cubans buy and sell them privately, through messaging groups and word of mouth. That market is where importers, private restaurants and families getting money from abroad actually trade.

The elTOQUE tracker was built for that market, using software that reads buy and sell offers posted in social media groups. It takes the median, strips out odd offers and publishes a representative rate through the day.

The economist Pavel Vidal, who teaches monetary policy, oversees the method. Cuban state media dispute the result, and the outlet says the calculation runs without human intervention.

How Far It Has Moved This Year

On 10 January the same tracker had the dollar at 460 pesos and the euro at 500. The dollar has therefore gained about 59% against the Cuban peso in under nine months.

The climb has been quick in September. The dollar passed 700 pesos for the first time on 17 September, then 715 on the 21st and 722 on the 23rd.

Reuters reported this week that the peso has lost roughly nine-tenths of its value against the dollar since 2021. Cuba’s economy has shrunk for several years, and the country earns far less foreign currency than it spends.

Remittances through official channels have also thinned. Formal transfers are running about 70% below their 2019 level, when Cuba received more than US$2 billion.

What It Does to Wages and Prices

Cuba’s average state wage was 6,930 pesos a month in 2025, according to the national statistics office. At Saturday’s informal rate that is about US$9.50.

The government raised the minimum wage in state-funded jobs from 2,100 to 3,210 pesos in July. At the current rate the new floor is worth about US$4.40 a month.

The economist Omar Everleny Pérez has estimated that a couple needs about 45,401 pesos a month for basics. That is roughly US$62 at the informal rate, or more than six average wages.

Official figures put inflation at 14% in 2025, while the independent economist Pavel Vidal estimated the real rate near 70%. State statistics also show prices multiplying 4.6 times between 2021 and 2025.

What the Government Says

The Central Bank added a third official rate on 18 December 2025, floating and set daily, starting at 410 pesos to the dollar. Its president, Juana Lilia Delgado Portal, said the step recognised the gap between official rates and the currency’s real scarcity.

She argued that moving gradually avoided a sharp devaluation and a deeper loss of purchasing power. That rate has since climbed from 410 pesos to about 678, chasing the street.

Granma, the Communist Party daily, has run a series of articles accusing elTOQUE of manipulating the rate. It described the published figure as induced inflation and a tool of economic warfare against Cuba.

Not all the criticism comes from outside the island. The Cuban economist Pedro Monreal has written that the new floating rate confirms Cuba’s monetary problems rather than correcting them.

What to Watch

The first thing to watch is the gap between the two rates. It has hovered near 50 pesos, and the Central Bank has been moving its rate up rather than letting the gap widen.

The second is dollarisation, which is spreading through the retail economy. Cuba began letting private businesses charge customers in US dollar cash this month.

That deepens the split between Cubans who receive money from abroad and those who do not. Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernández de Cossio has said the government does not know where the reforms will end.

The third is whether the promised official exchange market ever opens. The government said it would create one, and Cubans are still trading in messaging groups instead.

World.title: Ecuador Economy Grew 2.1% in the Second Quarter, Central Bank Says
World.content:
ECUADOR · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened. Ecuador’s central bank said on 25 September that the economy grew 2.1% year on year in the second quarter. — The quarterly fall. Output was 1.3% lower than in the first quarter of 2026, the bank’s own figures show. — What drove it. Household spending rose 3.5% and investment rose 10% against the same quarter a year earlier. — The strongest branches. Financial and insurance activities grew 12.5%, and electricity and water supply grew 12.6%. — What shrank. Fishing and shrimp farming fell 5.8%, and oil and mining extraction fell 2.2%. — The same figure twice. The first quarter of 2026 also grew 2.1%, in a separate release published in June. — Why it matters. The pace is slower than the 3.5% the bank reported for the same quarter of 2025.

Ecuador’s economy grew 2.1% in the second quarter of 2026 against the same period a year earlier, the central bank said. The bank also reported that output was 1.3% lower than in the first three months of the year.

Household spending and investment carried the annual figure, while oil output and shrimp farming shrank. No government minister commented publicly on the numbers on the day they appeared.

The Banco Central del Ecuador publishes the quarterly national accounts that measure the country’s output (Photo: PLACEHOLDER)

What the Central Bank Reported

The Banco Central del Ecuador publishes quarterly national accounts, the official measure of the country’s economic output. Its report for the second quarter of 2026 appeared on 25 September.

The bank said gross domestic product rose 2.1% between April and June, measured against the same months of 2025. It added that fifteen of the twenty industries it tracks grew over that period.

Ecuador uses the US dollar as its currency, so these figures carry no exchange-rate distortion. That makes the quarterly series easier to read than in most neighbouring countries.

The bank publishes the series roughly three months after each quarter ends. The second-quarter report therefore covers a period that closed at the end of June.

The Quarter That Went Backwards

The annual comparison was positive, but the quarterly one was not. Output between April and June was 1.3% below the level of January to March.

Two things pulled it down, according to the bank’s own breakdown. Investment fell 4.0% from the previous quarter, and household spending fell 0.9%.

Exports were the exception, rising 0.7% over the three months. El Universo, the Guayaquil daily, reported that eleven of the twenty industries grew on that quarterly measure.

Quarterly movements in a small economy swing more than annual ones. A single weak harvest or a maintenance shutdown at an oil field can move the figure.

What Drove the Annual Growth

Households did most of the work. Their spending rose 3.5% against the second quarter of 2025, contributing about 2.2 points of the annual growth.

Investment rose 10% on the same comparison, adding about two points. El Comercio, the Quito newspaper, reported that spending on machinery, works and equipment led that increase.

Financial and insurance activities grew 12.5%, which the bank singled out as a main driver. Electricity and water supply rose 12.6%, and manufacturing outside food and drink rose 6.4%.

Hotels and restaurants grew 5.7% and commerce grew 2.4%, according to El Comercio. Construction rose 2.2% on the same annual measure.

What Shrank

Five of the twenty industries did not grow over the year. Fishing and shrimp farming fell 5.8%, the largest decline on the list.

Oil and mining extraction fell 2.2%, and agriculture and livestock fell 1.4%. Public administration fell 2.7%, and government spending overall was down 3.4% on the year.

Shrimp and crude oil are two of Ecuador’s largest exports. Weakness in both limits how much the headline figure tells a reader about the country’s export earnings.

The fall in oil and mining matters because crude is Ecuador’s single biggest export earner. On the bank’s figures the sector subtracted from growth rather than adding to it.

The Same Number Twice

The first quarter of 2026 also grew 2.1% year on year. That figure came in a separate release the central bank published in June.

The match is a coincidence of rounding rather than a repeat of one announcement. Two different quarters were measured, each against its own quarter a year before.

The two identical annual rates also sit on top of a quarterly decline. A reader looking only at the headline would miss that the economy shrank between March and June.

Rounded figures can also hide real differences between quarters. The unrounded rates for the two periods need not be identical, even though both print as 2.1%.

Forecasts and What to Watch

The central bank raised its own forecast for 2026 on 15 September, ten days before the quarterly report. It now expects growth of 2.7% for the year, up from 2.5%.

The International Monetary Fund is less optimistic, projecting 2.5% for 2026 in its August programme document. That paper put Ecuador’s growth for the whole of 2025 at 3.7%.

Both forecasts sit above the 2.1% recorded in each of the first two quarters. Reaching either would need a stronger second half of the year.

Early evidence points that way, with the bank’s monthly activity index up 7.9% in July from a year earlier. Cumulative growth for January to July reached 2.9%.
