World.title: Russia strikes Ukraine as Putin denies plans to attack Europe amid growing tensions
World.content:
At least six people were killed and multiple people were injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities.

 

In Zaporizhzhia Oblast in southeastern Ukraine, two women died and seven people were injured following attacks on the region, regional governor Ivan Fedorov reported on Saturday morning.

"A total of 86 reports were received of damage to infrastructure, residential buildings, and vehicles," he wrote in a post on Telegram.

Two people were also killed and eight were injured in Donetsk in eastern Ukraine, governor Vadym Filashkin said, with 1,121 people evacuated from the front lines.

In Kherson Oblast, Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, reported that another person was killed and three people were injured in attacks across the region.

"Russian forces struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging five private homes in particular. The occupiers also destroyed private vehicles," Prokudin said.

A 69-year-old man was also killed in a drone strike on the Sumy region in the north of the country, according to local authorities. A further 10 people were wounded in a guided aerial bomb attack on the region.

Russian forces also carried out another wave of strikes on the Ukrainian capital overnight, injuring five people, per Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

The Ukrainian air force said early Saturday that Russia had launched 173 attack drones at Ukraine overnight.

"According to preliminary data, as of 7:30 am, air defense forces have shot down or neutralised 134 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerber types, as well as other types of drones," the force said, adding that strikes were recorded at 19 locations.

On Saturday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia had also carried out a "double strike" attack on a logistics facility serving fast-food chain McDonald’s.

"Relentless attacks disrupt Ukrainians’ daily lives, damage businesses, threaten jobs, and undermine international investment," he wrote in a post on social media, while also sharing video footage appearing to show the aftermath of the strikes.

Putin denies plans for conflict with Europe amid rising tensions

It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin told reporters in Saint Petersburg that Moscow was not preparing for conflict with Europe, despite warnings from European officials amid an increasing number of suspected Russian hybrid attacks.

"We are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe," the Russian leader said. "There is no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe, no matter what anyone says, no matter who says it, including in the Baltic states".

Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are particularly vulnerable to security threats stemming from Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In recent months, the three Baltic states have seen a rapidly growing number of drone incursions and related incidents, raising fresh concerns over airspace security and prompting Brussels to step up efforts to coordinate Europe's response.

World.title: Baku's week of F1 racing, global security, and record investments
World.content:
The Azerbaijan International Investment Forum (AIIF) completes a full week of high-level events in Baku, which include the Baku Security Forum, where over 100 countries attended to discuss new-age threats and Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, which has seen the city transform into the biggest motorsport event of the year.

 

It is one of the busiest weeks in the country’s calendar, and many industries are reaping the rewards.

The week concluded with a shift in focus to international finance and investment as the Second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum opened on 25 September at the Baku Convention Centre.

The two-day event aimed to redefine the global investment architecture and strengthen the South Caucasus as a pillar of connectivity.

Keyu Jin, Professor of Finance, Chair of the Centre for Macro-Finance and Geo-economics at the Hong Kong University of Science & Technology, China, was one of the attendees at AIIF.

She said she was "remarkably impressed" by the city and the organisation of all the events "from the Formula One to the security conference to the AIIF conference really bring a flow of people around the world and really placing Azerbaijan on the global map".

She told Euronews that "it is inherent forward-looking towards the future, but fused with this savouring of the past is really what makes this place really special".

Mikayil Jabbarov, Minister of Economу of Azerbaijan Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, September 2026

Major deals at the investment forum

Azerbaijan’s Minister of Economy, Mikayil Jabbarov, said in his address that "reliability of partners and the resilience of supply chains carry even greater weight in economic decision-making" and that long-term partnerships were continuing to grow and "generate new investment and reinvestment".

"Most foreign companies operating in our country choose to reinvest their profits back here and especially along with traditional energy production also to renewable one," he added.

Azerbaijan’s new pitch for international capital is not simply to invest in the country, but also to use it as a gateway to a much bigger market.

There are reasons why the country is attracting global investors.

A growing focus on what connects Asia to Europe and a push towards diversification seems to be very attractive to some, including the Ministry of Economy, which partnered with Vietnam's ROX Group on construction and development, while also signing a memorandum of understanding with Microsoft to advance the national digital economy.

In renewable energy, the Ministry of Energy teamed up with energy subsidiaries of ROX Group to evaluate utility-scale solar and wind projects.

The Azerbaijan Business Development Fund signed agreements with Slovakia's Saneca Pharmaceuticals for drug manufacturing, Turkey's VETAL for veterinary vaccine production, and the Czech Republic's AGROFERT alongside Agro Dairy for the Aghdam Poultry Project.

Azerbaijan Investment Holding and the Oman Investment Authority signed a term sheet regarding the Azerbaijan-Oman Direct Investment Fund, while SOCAR, the Azerbaijan State Water Reserves Agency, and UAE-based Esyasoft Technologies established a tripartite agreement to assess local water meter manufacturing.

Nouriel Roubini, CEO of Rubini Macro Associates, believes Azerbaijan is going from "strength to strength".

He cites several reasons, including its energy resources, saying "we live in a world in which the demand for energy is really important".

When referring to Azerbaijan, he underlines his belief that the country has "good governance, good macroeconomic policies, and they have also a vision about how they can integrate their own economy into a broader regional economy and trade and investment links between East and West".

These new contracts build directly upon the massive capital influx initiated during the inaugural forum. The first Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September 2025 resulted in the signing of investment agreements worth over $10 billion (approximately €8,8 billion)

Significantly, more than $7 billion (€6,1 billion) of those initial commitments went to the non-oil sector, setting a strong precedent for this week's deals.

Panel discussions Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, September 2026

Attracting cross-border partnerships

The pull of the Middle Corridor, which is increasingly being considered a real logistical alternative route for trade and energy, is certainly becoming a draw.

The World Bank estimates that, with sufficient investment and greater efficiency, trade flows along the route could triple by 2030, while journey times could be cut in half.

"We see the Middle Corridor as an efficient alternative transport route for our export-import operations," Uzbekistan's Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade, Laziz Kudratov, explained.

He noted that bilateral trade has reached "almost $1 billion (approximately €877 million)," with a firm target set to "double our trade".

The logistical impact is already measurable, as Kudratov disclosed that "over the past three years, the shipment of goods via Azerbaijan has more than doubled" and growth sits "above 30% these six months of this year".

To support this volume, the two governments are establishing a joint transport and logistics venture to invest in new ferries and infrastructure through the Nakhchivan and Zangezur corridors.

"For Montenegro, Azerbaijan, it is a really special and important country," Mirjana Koic, Director of the Montenegrin Investment Agency, said, pointing to major existing Azerbaijani investments on the Montenegrin coast from Azmont and ongoing dialogues with Sea Breeze.

She highlighted the strategic importance of energy connectivity, noting Montenegro's undersea cable whose "first phase finished with Italy," framing it as a vital link connecting the region to Europe.

Having worked in the artificial intelligence sector for "over four decades," Kai-Fu Lee, CEO of ZeroOne.ai, expressed strong optimism for the region's technological landscape.

"I believe it is extremely secure, and also I can see a lot of very favourable policies on tax and other issues," he observed, confirming his company's intention to set up operations in Azerbaijan to help train a "new army of AI engineers and also AI entrepreneurs".

Azerbaijan F1 Grand Prix in Baku, Azerbaijan Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Formulating the Grand Prix

The country is celebrating its 10th anniversary of hosting Formula 1's Grand Prix, attracting tourists and visitors alike, and is currently dominating the city's hospitality and tourism sectors.

This year, the weekend runs an accelerated Thursday-to-Saturday schedule to accommodate Remembrance Day observances on Sunday, 27 September, but the race goes on.

CEO of the European House Ambalzetti TEHA Group, Valerio De Molli, who attended AIIF, reflected on how the F1 Grand Prix helps to communicate Baku as one of the "modern, active, fast cities in the world".

"That is important," he told Euronews.

"Secondly, you need to identify the specific sectors of opportunities and spot those specific investors, again, in renewable energies, transport, and digital innovation spaces," he added.

This compressed timeline has aided the central service infrastructure, which has operated continuously to support the massive influx of international motorsport fans and corporate delegations around the Baku City Circuit.

Panel discussions Azerbaijan International Investment Forum, September 2026

Looking ahead to defence and technology

At the beginning of the week, the State Security Service hosted the 4th Baku Security Forum, bringing together nearly 600 high-ranking representatives and special service agencies from over 100 countries to discuss transboundary infrastructure protection and global security architecture.

The intense pace of international arrivals will continue directly into next week. As the motorsport and financial forums end, the events continue.

Next, the city’s focus will shift to the 6th Azerbaijan International Defence Exhibition (ADEX), scheduled to begin on 30 September at the Baku Expo Centre.

The exhibition will draw global defence delegations to review advancements in unmanned systems and electronic warfare, extending the capital's high-level economic momentum straight into October.

When reflecting on the past week, one may describe the week as a "business boom in Baku," and looking ahead to this F1 weekend might well prove to be its most economically successful yet.

World.title: Lourdes: Everything you need to know about Pope Leo XIV's visit
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV is set to travel to the shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes on Saturday as part of his official visit to France this week.

 

Nestled in the Pyrenees near the Spanish border, the small town of Lourdes draws millions of pilgrims every year. Here is everything you need to know about the pope's visit, the town, and the shrine.

Pope Leo XIV waves after a prayer vigil with young people at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis near Paris, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Leo XIV will be the first pontiff to set foot in Lourdes since Benedict XVI, who visited in September 2008 to mark the 150th anniversary of the Virgin's apparitions to Bernadette Soubirous.

Now one of the world's foremost Catholic pilgrimage sites, Lourdes owes its fame to Soubirous.

A young girl from a modest background, she said she witnessed 18 apparitions of a lady dressed in white in the Massabielle grotto, near Lourdes, between February and July 1858.

Believers say that during the ninth apparition, Bernadette heard the words: "Go and drink at the spring and wash yourself there."

In 1862, the Catholic Church officially recognised that the apparitions were those of the Virgin Mary and later built a shrine on the site. Millions of pilgrims from around the world have since flocked to the Massabielle grotto.

A street in Lourdes, in south-west France, Tuesday 8 September 2026. (Photo AP/Fred Scheiber)

These days, Lourdes welcomes around three million pilgrims a year. According to the town hall, it is the fourth most visited Catholic pilgrimage site in the world, after the Vatican, the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City and the Basilica of Our Lady of Aparecida in Brazil.

Although Lourdes has a population of just 13,000 residents, it has almost 10,000 hotel rooms and around 21,200 beds to accommodate the many visitors.

Finding affordable accommodation during Pope Leo's visit, however, has proved challenging, with huge crowds expected to gather for the event and some hotels charging more than €2,000 euros per night.

According to the latest figures released by the authorities, close to 200,000 people are expected to converge on Lourdes over two days, including around 150,000 who have registered to take part in the celebrations at the shrine.

Leo XIV's visit comes at a time when the number of baptisms in France is rising sharply.

Over the past five years, the number of adults being baptised has risen by 28%, while the number of teenagers baptised has increased by 10%. A total of 21,386 baptisms were recorded in 2026 - more than three times the figure from a decade ago.

Worshippers enter the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary in Lourdes, in south-west France, Tuesday 8 September 2026. AP Photo/Fred Scheiber, File

After spending two days in Paris, Leo XIV is set to land at Tarbes Lourdes Pyrénées airport on Saturday evening. He will then begin his visit to Lourdes with Mass at the Massabielle grotto.

The pope is also due to hold private talks with seven victims of sexual abuse.

The visit comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Catholic Church in France. In 2021, the Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church estimated that 216,000 minors had been sexually abused by priests or members of religious orders between 1950 and 2020. That figure rose to around 330,000 when laypeople working in Church-related institutions were included.

World.title: The secret behind the Sagrada Familia's final towers: Stone, steel and 21st-century glue
World.content:
Some projects defy the passage of time. And then there is the Sagrada Família. In the heart of Barcelona, Antoni Gaudí's masterpiece has been under construction for more than 140 years. That prospect did not seem to trouble the architect, who was fond of saying, "My client is not in a hurry" — a reference to God.

 

This year, however, after accidents, delays, a pandemic and countless other setbacks, the basilica could finally emerge from its now-familiar scaffolding.

The moment coincides with two remarkable milestones: the centenary of Gaudí's death, after he was struck by a tram in 1926, and the completion of the Tower of Jesus Christ, which has taken the basilica to a height of 172.5 metres, surpassing Germany's Ulm Minster as the world's tallest church.

Behind that achievement lies one of the most fascinating aspects of the Sagrada Família's construction: the convergence of Gaudí's 19th-century geometric vision with 21st-century engineering and materials science. It is a combination that would surely have fascinated an architect who always knew that future generations would have to complete his greatest work.

Façade of the Sagrada Familia. María Muñoz Morillo

Mysticism carved in stone

The Sagrada Familia is not simply something to be seen; it is a building to be experienced and deciphered. Gaudí, a devout Catholic who is in the process of beatification, did not merely design a church; he conceived a Bible in stone, one that speaks through organic forms and layers of symbolism. The building has 12 towers representing the 12 apostles, while its floor plan evokes the body of Christ and each façade depicts different episodes in the life of Jesus, from the Nativity to the Passion.

Look closely at the Passion Façade and you can find a tribute to the Catalan architect himself: his face is immortalised in one of its figures.

Higher up, the depiction of the crucified Christ departs from traditional iconography. Christ appears naked, while his head is replaced by the geometric form of an open book - a striking symbol in a building Gaudí conceived as a "stone catechism", a book through which the faithful could read the Christian story.

Rear façade of the Sagrada Familia showing a crucified Christ. Bottom left, an image of Gaudí and a soldier who inspired 'Star Wars'. María Muñoz Morillo

Gaudí, who devoted 43 years of his life to the project, used real people as models for his sculptures. During the final 12 years of his life, he devoted himself entirely to the Sagrada Familia, turning down other commissions and seeking private funding. The temple received no public money; its construction was financed by donations from the faithful.

'Star Wars' and the legend of Saint George and the dragon

The temple's blend of Gothic and naturalistic elements - its interior evokes a forest, with coloured light filtering through the stained-glass windows and bathing the columns - has proved so captivating that its influence has even reached popular culture.

The basilica's guides point to a curious connection between Gaudí, Barcelona and 'Star Wars'. According to a story they tell visitors, George Lucas found inspiration for the helmets of his iconic Stormtroopers in the figure of a Roman soldier depicted on the façade.

Helicoidal forms are infinite, rising endlessly towards the sky, like the eternity and spiritual life of the souls that contemplate God, the infinite Being. Such will be the columns of the Sagrada Familia Antoni Gaudí

Another curiosity within the basilica evokes the legend of Saint George and the dragon. Inside, a figure of the saint stands beneath a white structure whose twisting form suggests the body of the dragon.

Saint George inside the Sagrada Familia; the white waves around him depict the dragon of the legend. María Muñoz Morillo.

The basilica's latest milestone, however, is one that has transformed Barcelona's skyline. Last week, Pope Leo XIV visited the city to bless the imposing Tower of Jesus Christ, the central and tallest tower of the Sagrada Familia.

Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass at the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona, Spain, on Wednesday 10 June 2026. AP/Bernat Armangue

The clergy gather around the Basilica of the Sagrada Familia, designed by Antoni Gaudí, as Pope Leo XIV blesses the Central Tower of Jesus Christ on 10 June 2026. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti

Inside the tower is a striking sight: a glass lamb created by Italian artist Andrea Mastrovito, through which the warm Mediterranean light filters into the space. From 2027, the tower is expected to open to the public, offering a walkable viewing platform at the highest vantage point in the Catalan capital.

Image of the glass lamb inside the Tower of Jesus in the Sagrada Familia. Sagrada Familia

A titanic puzzle: stone, steel and invisible chemistry

Gaudí knew that he would not live to complete the monumental work he had envisioned for Barcelona. He therefore left behind models and instructions, trusting future generations to carry on the construction of the Sagrada Familia.

In 1926, at the age of 73, Gaudí was struck by a tram. Contemporary accounts describe how, as he attempted to cross the Gran Via, he avoided one tram only to be hit by another. He died from his injuries a few days later, leaving the project in the hands of his closest collaborators.

Since his death, generations of architects have taken up the challenge of continuing Gaudí's vision while inevitably leaving their own mark on one of the world's most iconic buildings. Among the greatest structural challenges has been the construction of the six central towers: complex, hyperbolic structures designed to withstand wind, seismic forces and immense loads. The most ambitious of them is the Tower of Jesus Christ, crowned by a monumental 17-metre cross.

Detail of the Tower of Jesus in the Sagrada Familia. Jesús Maturana

How has a seemingly endless process been sped up?

The answer lies partly in modern engineering: a structural adhesive developed by Henkel after a decade of research and testing.

Step 1: Modular construction

Instead of placing individual stones hundreds of metres above the ground, the towers were divided into a giant puzzle of 826 modular panels incorporating more than 2,100 stone pieces, which are pre-assembled at the quarry.

Step 2: Bonding stone and steel

To make the stone and steel work together as a single structural unit, engineers apply Loctite EA 9497, a two-component epoxy adhesive developed by German manufacturer Henkel and produced at its factory in Montornès del Vallès. Around 30 kilograms of epoxy resin are used for each panel.

Step 3: Controlled curing

The panels undergo a 24-hour curing process under controlled temperature conditions. As the adhesive cures, it fills the microscopic gaps between the materials, creating a durable bond between the steel and stone.

Step 4: Final lifting

The completed panels were transported to the basilica, lifted into position and assembled level by level with millimetre precision, like building blocks on a monumental scale.

Image of the adhesive used in the construction of the Tower of Jesus in the Sagrada Familia. Jesús Maturana.

This modular approach has allowed construction to progress up to ten times faster than with traditional methods. According to project manager Begoña Cantera, work completed in barely eight years would have taken between 50 and 60 years using conventional construction techniques. That leap in efficiency has helped bring the central towers to completion in time for the centenary of Gaudí's death.

Designed to withstand time and the city

The structure stands out not only for its architectural complexity, but also for the engineering designed to protect it from the stresses of its urban and coastal environment. In total, 24 tonnes of adhesive have been used in a structure exposed to a demanding combination of environmental conditions:

Marine environment: located just 2.5 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, the basilica is exposed to salt-laden air, which can accelerate the corrosion of steel.

located just 2.5 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, the basilica is exposed to salt-laden air, which can accelerate the corrosion of steel. High humidity: relative humidity levels of between 65% and 75% place additional demands on the materials over time.

relative humidity levels of between 65% and 75% place additional demands on the materials over time. Thermal cycles: temperatures ranging from around 5°C in winter to more than 30°C in summer cause repeated expansion and contraction of the materials.

temperatures ranging from around 5°C in winter to more than 30°C in summer cause repeated expansion and contraction of the materials. Urban vibrations: two metro lines pass beneath the basilica, generating vibrations that must also be taken into account in the structural design.

The resin used in the project is designed to accommodate small movements between the steel and stone without cracking. According to the project team, the bonded structure can withstand loads equivalent to the weight of around 100,000 people per square metre - roughly the combined weight of a capacity crowd at FC Barcelona's stadium. That strength is particularly important for supporting the monumental cross that crowns the Tower of Jesus Christ.

Antoni Gaudí did not live to see his masterpiece completed, but today he rests in the crypt of the basilica to which he devoted the final years of his life.

Gaudí designed the Sagrada Familia with the height of Montjuïc in mind, believing that the work of man should not surpass the work of nature.

Today, at 172.5 metres, the basilica has become the tallest church in the world. It has reached that height not through the construction methods of Gaudí's time alone, but through a combination of his original vision and technologies developed generations after his death.

More than a century later, stone, glass, steel and modern engineering are bringing a project once thought almost impossible closer to completion.

World.title: Are you in pain?  In some cases, exercising may be as good as painkillers
World.content:
Whether you often suffer from migraines, period cramps or chronic pain, exercise could help ease the symptoms in a similar way to common painkillers.

 

Across a wide range of conditions, exercise can significantly reduce acute and chronic pain, a new study by Adelaide University has found after analysing 157 systematic reviews encompassing 2,736 randomised controlled trials and over 220,000 participants.

“At a time when we’re looking for safe and effective ways to manage pain beyond medication, these findings provide strong evidence for making exercise a more routine part of pain care,” said Carol Maher, senior researcher at Adelaide University.

The researchers examined how the type, intensity and duration of exercise influenced pain relief.

Overall, exercise reduced pain by around 1.1 points on a zero-to-10 scale – a reduction roughly 60% larger than the average relief reported for common medications in separate chronic pain trials.

Low-intensity exercise produced greater pain relief than moderate-to-vigorous activity and shorter programs, of around 12 weeks, showed larger effects than longer ones.

“Importantly, we found that more exercise wasn’t necessarily better. In fact, shorter-duration and lower-intensity programs showed greater reductions in pain, suggesting people may not need to exercise harder or for longer to experience meaningful benefits,” said lead researcher Ben Singh.

Programmes under 120 minutes per week were more effective than higher weekly-duration ones that can feel unattainable for people living with chronic pain, the researchers wrote.

“When we exercise, our body releases chemicals including endorphins and serotonin that can help reduce how strongly we feel pain and increase our pain tolerance,” said Singh, adding that exercising helps calm inflammation and change the way the brain responds to pain, while also improving mood.

Despite these findings, the study noted that exercise remains underused as a treatment for pain: it is not yet routine practice and is rarely prescribed with the same precision as medication.

“Instead, people experiencing pain may be told to ‘stay active’, rather than being given a specific, evidence-based exercise program that considers what type of exercise to do, how hard to work and for how long,” added Singh.

Healthcare providers need definitive guidance, not just whether exercise helps, but which exercises work for which patients, and how to prescribe them effectively, the authors added.

Yet, they warn that exercise should not be considered a universal solution or expected to eliminate pain, as its effects depend on individual factors such as the condition causing the pain, a person's level of fitness, and adherence to the programme.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Deadly blast rips through Athens building, near Acropolis
World.content:
Several foreign tourists remain missing after an explosion brought down a building in Athens' tourist area of Plaka, with the city's mayor calling it an "incredible disaster."

Rescuers have recovered the body of a young woman following a building collapse in Plaka, in central Athens, a Greek fire brigade official said Saturday.

Later, Greek public broadcaster ERT said a man's body was also recovered from the rubble.

The building was brought down by a large blast which injured three other people and damaged shops and cars near the site.

"The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building," said Athens Mayor Haris Doukas. "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

Several people, believed to be foreign nationals, remain missing.

On Saturday, Greek news agency ANA reported that the female victim whose body was retrieved was an American tourist, sharing the holiday rental with her husband and another couple.

Cause of the blast still uncertain

Authorities suspect a gas leak caused the Friday blast, but the sequence of events was not immediately clear.

"Something went terribly wrong," Doukas said.

Local media reported the missing people included a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor, and four American tourists staying on the first floor.

While their nationalities have not been officially confirmed, a police official said the group of tourists had been expected to check in for a flight from Athens on early Friday afternoon.

Excavators on the scene

Rescuers were using sniffer dogs and thermal cameras to search for possible survivors. According to ANA, dozens of firefighters and six vehicles have been deployed to help with the search, including two specialized rescue vehicles.

Excavators were also deployed to clear the rubble, according to photos from the scene.

Plaka is close to many Athens most visited sites, including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus.

World.title: Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown
World.content:
09/26/2026 September 26, 2026 Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Merkel was Germany’s chancellor from 2005 to 2021 Image: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, received one of the highest honors of the Catholic Church's social welfare charity in Germany.

The 72-year-old was awarded the Elisabeth Prize by the Catholic Caritas Association at an event in the southern city of Augsburg on Friday evening.

The prize is named after Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, who lived from 1207 to 1231 and who helped people in need. She is the patron saint of Caritas.

The honor recognized Merkel's commitment to social cohesion, with Caritas President Eva Welskop-Deffaa paying tribute to the "inner compass with which she [Merkel] successfully steered the country's fortunes."

The former chancellor told the roughly 400 guests that "there will always be a need for people to be there for one another."

Once seen by some as Mutti — Germany’s reassuring mother figure — Merkel has become an increasingly divisive figure because of her 2015 decision to open the borders to more than a million refugees.

Critics say Merkel’s decision fueled years of backlash that helped turn the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from a fringe protest party into a force that now leads most national polls.

World.title: India news: New Delhi, Islamabad trade accusations at UN General Assembly
World.content:
09/26/2026 September 26, 2026 Jammu and Kashmir assembly seeks restoration of statehood, BJP protests

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday moved a resolution in the legislative assembly seeking the immediate restoration of full statehood to the region leading to chaos in the assembly, media reports said.

"We have been waiting. In public and private meetings and every forum, we made the government of India remember that you had made a promise with the people of J&K but it is not being fulfilled," Abdullah said in the assembly of the Union Territory.

Describing it as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's promise, Abdullah said that it should now be fulfilled, adding that the central government had promised to restore it after delimitation and elections.

He also cited administrative difficulties arising from J&K's status as a Union Territory.

The resolution was supported by the ruling National Conference, as well as other parties, but triggered an uproar from Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) legislators who objected to seeking greater autonomy for J&K.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP government in 2019 had revoked Kashmir's special status, known as Article 370, which had allowed Jammu and Kashmir to have its own constitution and a degree of internal autonomy.

Under locally approved laws, this meant that only local Kashmiris could vote, own land, and apply for government jobs.

A land ownership provision, called Article 35A, was also scrapped, leading to accusations of being a move by the BJP to engineer a demographic change in the Muslim-majority region.

World.title: Thailand: Bangkok flooding triggers disaster declaration
World.content:
Rainfall over the past three days has caused heavy flooding in the Thai capital. A state of disaster has been declared in all 50 districts in Bangkok.

Authorities in Bangkok on Saturday declared a disaster across 50 districts in Thailand's capital after days of heavy rainfall caused severe flooding.

Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the eastern parts of the city were impacted most.

By Saturday afternoon, Chadchart said the situation had "stabilized" and added: "If more rainwater doesn't fall in the area, it will be solved."

"If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater," he said in an update on social media.

Bangkok's governor urges residents to move cars to higher ground Image: AP Video/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Situation in brief

Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the situation has "stabilized"

Emergency ​advisory for ⁠people living near canals to move possessions to ​higher ground

Bangkok city officials open shelter for evacuees

More rain forecast into Sunday

More rain in Bangkok forecast

Chadchart said almost 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) of rain had fallen since Thursday afternoon and warned that more rain was expected.

"The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full," the governor said on social media and advised residents to move their possessions to higher ground.

"The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled," he said.

Chadchart urged bedridden patients dependent on life-saving medical equipment to consider a temporary stay in hospital.

Thai authorities said more than 84,000 people in 21 provinces nationwide have been impacted by flooding as of Saturday, especially in the central region.

Thailand's Meteorological Department warned the heavy rain would persist in most parts of the country through Sunday Image: Alex Ogle/AFP

Floods evoke memories of deadly 2011 deluge

"The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now," local vendor Somkid Pheuk-ngam, told the AFP news agency.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now," she told AFP, adding that while she often gets flooded, "I think this time is worse than the 2011 flood."

Flooding across Thailand in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

Thailand's Meteorological Department warned the heavy rain would persist in most parts of the country through Sunday and pointed to a strong low-pressure system dominating the central region and strengthening monsoon conditions.

World.title: OpenAI tools post user images from ChatGPT online
World.content:
OpenAI said it found 53 cases in which user-uploaded image links on ChatGPT were shared with third-party websites. The company said it had removed most of these links.

Artificial intelligence giant OpenAI on Friday acknowledged that its AI tools had posted images users provided to ChatGPT on online sites, without the company's knowledge, in yet another example of AI agents operating outside of their confines.

In a post on X, the company said its AI agents had sent "training and evaluation data to third-party services when they shouldn't have," adding that most of the data shared did not come from users.

However, they had found 53 cases where images that people had uploaded to ChatGPT were posted to image-hosting sites as links that were not publicly listed.

"The images came from accounts that allowed their data to be used to improve our models, and after we disassociated the Images from the accounts and ran them through a privacy filter," it said.

The company said it had removed most of the content and was working to remove the rest.

Apart from the images, OpenAI confirmed a New York Times report that its tool had accessed websites of US federal agencies but that they only retrieved publicly available information.

Tech giant OpenAI heads for Wall Street To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising fear of rogue AI

The latest disclosure comes amid heightened global concerns about AI systems escaping human control and hacking into external websites, as well as industry calls for a slowdown on AI development — a move which OpenAI said it supports.

Friday's post also clarified that the cases of unauthorized sharing occurred before a fresh round of safeguards were implemented over a month ago.

In July, OpenAI had said internal cybersecurity evaluations showed that its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Friday said it was "still the most severe event we've seen."

"We are continuing to review agent activity in research and evaluation runs, working backward month by month starting from the Hugging Face incident ," OpenAI said in a safety blog post on Friday, adding that it would "provide further updates" in time.

How US, China could end the AI race To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Investigation finds OpenAI agents attempting hacks

AI evaluator and research lab Transluce on Friday said that it also found that AI agents, appearing to originate from OpenAI, attempted a rudimentary hack on the US Department of Education website for the department's civil rights office. The agents did not succeed, according to the independent investigation.

The company said it found "additional rogue activities," some of which were not directly attributable to OpenAI, targeting other government agencies, including the Justice Department and the Commerce Department, as well as some state government websites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York.

World.title: White House bars CNN from covering upcoming Trump trip, broadcaster says
World.content:
CNN said its journalists have been barred from accompanying President Donald Trump on his upcoming trip to Tennessee. The episode marks the Trump administration's latest salvo against the major cable news network.

American news broadcaster CNN said its journalists were not allowed to board Air Force One for a planned trip with President Donald Trump on Saturday.

CNN was scheduled to travel on Air Force One to Knoxville, Tennessee, where Trump was expected to watch a college football game.

The news organization was to be the representative of the TV press pool for the weekend, meaning that it would cover the president and share video and information with the four other big networks that are part of the press pool.

CNN was replaced by Real America's Voice News, a conservative network, the Associated Press reported.

The episode represents the latest showdown between the Trump administration and media networks that the president believes to be unfavorable in their coverage.

Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House

Trump earlier this week barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House after he said the networks report "fiction and lies."

Major TV networks, including DW, then cut off their pooled coverage of the president in solidarity.

A federal judge temporarily struck down the ban in a ruling on Thursday after the outlets filed a lawsuit.

But the order from the judge addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties.

World.title: TikTok agrees to settle with Alabama state over teen safety
World.content:
The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.

Short-form content sharing platform TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance reached a settlement with Alabama, the southeastern US state said on Friday, days ahead of what would have been a revealing trial over teen safety and its impact on their mental health.

As part of the deal, TikTok agreed to pay $100 million (€87.7 million) to the state of Alabama and enact measures for teens including a two-hour daily use limit, restricted access for children and pauses after 15 minutes of use.

However, the payout could rise to $300 million if 40 other states sign similar agreements with the company within a stipulated time period, the document said.

What have TikTok and Alabama state said after the settlement?

"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually ​enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok's US operations said in a statement.

Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the social media giant last year.

At least 27 other states and Washington DC have brought similar lawsuits. Apart from these, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its impact on teen mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet's YouTube are also defendants in many of these ​cases.

"This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Marshall said in a press release.

With this, the company has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.

What were the allegations against TikTok?

The state of Alabama had argued that TikTok's endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive of social media platforms and that its algorithm specifically pushes young users toward content about violence and self harm.

The state held the app partially responsible for a teen mental health crisis and a significant increase in emergency room visits.

The lawsuit also accused TikTok of falsely claiming that it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have the app rated as 'safe for teens' on app stores.

It said that TikTok asks users to self-report their ages but also allows them to evade questions by viewing videos without creating an account.

That still earns the company data on viewing habits. Being able to scroll videos without signing in makes 'Kids Mode' an entirely useless feature, the lawsuit said.

France debates social media ban for teenagers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What measures will TikTok take?

As per the settlement, TikTok has to implement a series of safety measures, including:

Two-hour daily limit

Additional parental control limiting time on platform

'Productive pauses' interrupting continuous scrolling after 15 minutes, 60 minutes and 90 minutes

Restrict children access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.

Restrictions on push notifications during night and school hours

Robust measures to verify user age

Limits on discoverability of teen accounts by adults

Sending parents notifications of suspicious interactions between teen users and adults

Blanket ban on use of cosmetic filters by teens

Non-personalized feed for teens

Last month, Meta agreed to pay a massive $17 billion to 47 US states and territories in a similar case while agreeing to make changes to teens' access to its platforms, Facebook and Instagram.

It did not admit wrongdoing and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube's adoption of the same terms. TikTok has not commented publicly about that deal.

World.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
World.content:
Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.

The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.

What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.

He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.

Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.

"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.

The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.
