Prosecutors have ended a decade-long case in which former president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa was accused of falsely claiming not to have authored documents relating to his alleged cooperation with the communist authorities. Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that helped bring down the communist regime in the 1980s, has always denied longstanding claims that, in the 1970s, he acted as an informant to the communist security services. The case has become highly politicised, with right-wing figures – especially from the Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 – critical of Wałęsa. By contrast, the former president, who turns 83 next week, enjoys good relations with the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Waldemar Żurek, Tusk’s justice minister and prosecutor general, welcomed the decision to drop the case against Wałęsa, saying that, under PiS, “a politicised state apparatus hounded the legend of Solidarity, deliberately ignoring facts and basic logic”. Now, “truth has triumphed over an attempt to rewrite history”. Prokuratura ostatecznie umorzyła śledztwo przeciwko Lechowi Wałęsie. Przez lata upolityczniony aparat państwa ścigał legendę „Solidarności”, celowo ignorując fakty i elementarną logikę. Zignorowano bezsporny fakt historyczny – SB masowo fałszowała dokumenty i podpisy Wałęsy w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 24, 2026 The case in question stems from statements made by Wałęsa in 2016 during an investigation by the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that also has prosecutorial powers. Those proceedings, in which the former Polish president testified as a witness, were launched after documents apparently carrying his signature were found in the home archives of former communist interior minister Czesław Kiszczak. The files indicated that Wałęsa, working under the code name TW Bolek, signed a commitment to collaborate with the communist Security Service (SB). They also included payslips and informant’s notes. The former president had told the media at the time when the documents were discovered that they had been forged. When speaking to IPN investigators, he also denied having drafted or signed all but one of the documents. However, prosecutors subsequently claimed that – after comparing the documents from Kiszczak’s file with others they said had been written and signed by Wałęsa, as well as consulting forensic handwriting experts – Wałęsa’s testimony was false in the case of over 50 of the documents. In 2021, the former president was charged with giving false testimony. Then, in 2023, he was indicted, meaning the case was sent to court. However, in 2024, after Tusk’s government had taken power from PiS, prosecutors asked that the case be returned to them by the court, which agreed to the request. Now, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw has announced that it is discontinuing the case entirely, after finding that there are no grounds for Wałęsa to be prosecuted. Lech Wałęsa will face trial accused of falsely testifying not to have signed documents of cooperation with the communist authorities. If convicted, he can be jailed for up to 3 years. He calls the claims against him "terrible insults and monstrous lies" https://t.co/X0eb4e5ahm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2023 In a statement explaining the decision, prosecutors claimed that there had been significant “methodological errors” made previously in attributing handwritten texts to Wałęsa and in handwriting comparisons between them. “There was no evidence to assume with 100% certainty that the comparative material actually came from Lech Wałęsa,” they wrote. In fact, “the evidence collected clearly indicated that Lech Wałęsa did not write long manuscripts during his life, and especially not in the 1970s”. “Some witnesses explicitly stated that, at that time, he was a secondary illiterate,” meaning someone who has lost their ability to read and write, said the prosecutors. “He was not able to write and could barely read.” This, along with other concerns over how the case was previously conducted, “led to the conclusion that there was no certain basis to assume that Lech Wałęsa was the author of the documents disclosed in the ‘Kiszczak files’, and therefore there was no evidence that he lied during the interrogation”. Hit! Ekipa Tuska ogłosiła Wałęsę analfabetą by wybronić go przed Bolkiem! To się nie dzieje! To niemożliwe! pic.twitter.com/PQnOn5XDb0 — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 Prosecutors also said that “the testimony of numerous witnesses proves that the files of TW Bolek, discovered in the possession of General Kiszczak’s widow, were most likely fabricated. Finally, they argued that, even if Wałęsa had given false testimony, he was protected by the constitutional right against self-incrimination while being interviewed as a witness. “The prosecution found that Lech Wałęsa could have feared that if he admitted to having prepared or signed the documents from the ‘Kiszczak files’…all his testimonies in which he denied being secret collaborator “Bolek” in previous proceedings…would be deemed false and would lead to his being held criminally liable.” Lech Wałęsa, Angela Merkel and Volodymyr Zelensky have been named the first distinguished members of the European Order of Merit. The award was created by the European Parliament to "honour those who did not simply believe in Europe, but helped build it" https://t.co/inosiiRQkW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 11, 2026 In response to the announcement, Wałęsa shared on his Facebook page the post by Żurek praising the prosecutors’ decision. Wałęsa then added a comment claiming that Jarosław and Lech Kaczyński, the founders of PiS, had ordered a right-wing historian, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, to fake the Kiszczak files. Cenckiewicz has written extensively about Wałęsa, including about his alleged collaboration with the communist security services. He also recently served as national security advisor to current Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS. In a series of social media posts on Thursday, Cenkiewicz said that he had “never read a bigger lie” than the prosecutors’ statement justifying dropping the case. He also ridiculed the idea that Wałęsa could have led the Solidarity movement in the 1980s and served as president in the 1990s if he was a “secondary illiterate”. Większego kłamstwa przebranego w wymiar sprawiedliwości RP nigdy nie czytałem! To większe kłamstwo niż skandaliczny wyrok Kapińskiego i spółki z 2000 r.! Reżim Tuska uznał, że Wałęsa nie był Bolkiem, a Instytut Sehna niczego kategorycznie nie ustalił! I powtórzyli brednie… — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) September 24, 2026 The accusations of communist collaboration have tarnished Wałęsa’s reputation among some Poles. In 2017, shortly after the Kiszczak files were uncovered, a poll by IBRiS for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 28% believed Wałęsa was not a national hero. However, 62% said that he was. Earlier this year, Wałęsa was named as one of the first three distinguished members of the European Order of Merit, a new initiative launched by the European Parliament, alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and former German Chancellor Angela Merkel. World.title: Poland issues guidance on responding to air attacks and warns of Russia threat
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has launched an information campaign on how to respond in the event of an air strike. It has also announced that 85,000 shelters are to be marked with clear signs across Poland and an evacuation plan is being developed. The moves come amid growing concerns over Russia strikes in Ukraine near the Polish border. The prime minister and foreign minister have warned that Russia could be planning “something big” this year, without specifying what that might involve. 🟡 KOMUNIKAT | MSWiA publikuje instrukcję reagowania podczas zagrożenia atakiem z powietrza. 📄 Ministerstwo Spraw Wewnętrznych i Administracji udostępnia nową instrukcję postępowania na wypadek ataku z powietrza. To rozwinięcie treści zawartych w „Poradniku Bezpieczeństwa”,… pic.twitter.com/aw3h07mdeF — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 25, 2026 On Friday, Poland’s interior ministry published information on how to respond to the threat of an air attack, expanding on a safety handbook sent to all 17 million households in the country earlier this year. The new guidelines explain where to seek cover during an air raid, how to prepare homes and what to do if an attack occurs while people are at home, at work, outdoors or in a car. They advise people to seek a shelter point, take a prepared evacuation backpack and any necessary medication, and use only stairs. If reaching a shelter would require spending a long time outdoors, people are advised to remain inside and move to a central room without windows. Separately, the ministry has prepared guidelines for schools after some were criticised last week for evacuating children outside school buildings during alarms in the eastern province of Lublin. W całej Polsce mają pojawić się obowiązkowe oznaczenia Punktów Schronienia. Specjalna aplikacja pokaże ich lokalizacje, a nowe oznakowanie ma ułatwić mieszkańcom znalezienie bezpiecznego miejsca w sytuacji zagrożenia. Materiał 🎥 Michał Niewodowski pic.twitter.com/HVoo3ypETT — 19.30 TVP (@1930_tvp) September 21, 2026 To make shelter points easier to identify, the interior ministry has prepared a draft regulation requiring local authorities and managers of designated sites to mark them clearly by the end of the year with a blue triangle on an orange background, as well as a green sign saying “Punkt schronienia” (“Shelter point”). The locations can also be found using a mobile application launched last year. According to the ministry’s own data, Poland currently has about 85,000 shelter points, which could host 23.7 million people, or 64% of the country’s population. A national plan is also being developed to coordinate potential evacuation as a result of war, a threat of war or a natural disaster. The plan is intended to establish evacuation routes and reception areas in advance, including how many people may need to be moved and where they could be accommodated. “When a threat arises, we warn the Polish people and defend our security. It is only natural that we prepare for worst-case scenarios, while deeply believing that they will never come to pass,” interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told the Rzeczpospolita newspaper. “Evacuation plans are being prepared…These plans rely heavily on the strength of the entire crisis response system. The more we strengthen that system, the more precise the plans will be,” Kierwiński added. Poland has launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in times of war or other emergencies https://t.co/YE3rsltCj5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The evacuation plans have become the subject of false claims circulating on social media. These posts allege that the government is preparing to forcibly displace Poles and ultimately eliminate the Polish nation, with some linking the alleged plan to an agreement between Berlin and Kyiv, reports the Onet news service. They claim that evacuees would never be allowed to return, allegations the government quickly moved to debunk. 📢 STOP FAKE NEWS! W sieci krążą fałszywe informacje, jakoby przygotowywany Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji miał oznaczać masowe wysiedlenie mieszkańców Polski ‼️To nieprawda‼️ 🔎 FAKT: Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji określa procedury na wypadek wojny, zagrożenia wojną lub klęski żywiołowej.… pic.twitter.com/YNEqXF3StJ — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 18, 2026 The measures are part of a broader effort to strengthen Poland’s civil protection system. Last week, Kierwiński said Poland plans to triple the current number of warning sirens in Lublin province to more than 1,000 by the end of 2026. This follows a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation comes after several incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. Those warnings were echoed yesterday by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who said that multiple sources suggested that “Russia is planning something big this year.” “I think Putin needs a pretext for mobilisation, so they might carry out a false-flag attack to tell the Russians, ‘We are under attack, and that is why we must mobilise,’” he added. World.title: Zelensky condemns knife attack by Ukrainian at Polish abbey that left priest dead and others injured
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has expressed his horror at an “evil” knife attack carried out today by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland, which left one priest dead and others seriously injured. The incident has caused shock in Poland, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledging that the perpetrator, who is in police custody, will face the “full severity of Polish law”. W Opactwie Sióstr Benedyktynek w Jarosławiu obywatel Ukrainy dopuścił się straszliwej zbrodni. Jesteśmy wstrząśnięci tym złem. Według dotychczasowych informacji zginął ksiądz katolicki, a kilka innych osób zostało rannych. Składamy najgłębsze kondolencje rodzinie i bliskim… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 24, 2026 The attack took place on Thursday morning on the grounds of a Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław in southeast Poland. Local police reported that a 31-year-old Ukrainian man had stabbed four male victims and one female. Three were members of the clergy and two laypeople. Authorities later confirmed that one of the men, a priest, had died of his injuries in hospital and that two others were in serious condition. The cathedral in the nearby city of Rzeszów named the deceased as Stanisław Zbojnowicz. The superior of the Benedictine Sisters Monastery, Barbara Dendor, told news website Interia that Zbojnowicz had been in a confessional when the attack began. He had rushed out to attempt to close the gates and protect other people, but was stabbed by the assailant before he could do so. In its initial social media post announcing Zbojnowicz’s death, the cathedral also said that a second priest, Marek Pieńkowski, had died. However, a few minutes later it deleted that claim, blaming the “enormous information chaos surrounding today’s tragic event”. One person was killed and four were injured in a knife attack at a Catholic convent in Poland this morning, with clergy among the victims. Police have detained a 31-year-old Ukrainian man on suspicion of carrying out the attack. The motive remains unknown https://t.co/93nbqpwnIA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, prosecutors revealed that the suspect, who has not been named, had entered Poland from Germany in the early hours of Thursday and “was heading to the border crossing [with Ukraine] in Korczowa”, which is around 30km (18.6 miles) from Jarosław. However, he ultimately did not cross the border and, for unknown reasons, ended up in Jarosław, where he entered the grounds of the abbey and began his attack, using a knife taken from the kitchen. Prosecutors said that doctors would assess the suspect’s condition before he was interrogated. Blood samples were also taken to be tested for the presence of narcotics and alcohol. The motive for the attack remains unknown. Dendor told news website Wirtualna Polska that the perpetrator was unknown to them. “He looked like a madman, in shorts and a T-shirt, even though it was cold today,” she said. Wirtualna Polska reports, based on the accounts of unnamed witnesses, that the Ukrainian man had earlier in the day knocked on the gates of the abbey and asked for financial assistance. However, he was turned away due to the suspicion that he was drunk or under the influence of drugs and was asked to come back later. That is standard practice for places that offer aid, reports the news service. The man “flew into a rage when he didn’t get help and allegedly threatened priests”, said one of the unnamed sources. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk expressed his sympathy for the loved ones of the victims of the attack and pledged that the perpetrator “will be punished with the full severity of Polish law”. President Karol Nawrocki likewise expressed his condolences and called on the authorities to “quickly and thoroughly clarify all the circumstances of this tragedy”. Later on Thursday afternoon, Zelensky also extended his condolences in a social media post published in Polish. “We are shocked by this evil,” he wrote. “The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the applicable law.” Morderca z Jarosławia jest w rękach Polskiej Policji. Trwają czynności. Sprawca to obywatel Ukrainy. Będzie ukarany z całą surowością polskiego prawa. Łączę się w bólu z bliskimi ofiar tego brutalnego ataku. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 24, 2026 Earlier, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw had “condemned the brutal attack” in Jarosław. However, it also appealed for people “not to allow pain to turn into hatred or further violence”, saying that “accountability for the crime must be based solely on the law”. Polish-Ukrainian relations have been tense in recent months, amid rising anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland and anger at Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. There has been a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland this year. Marcin Piotrowski, a board member of the Folkowisko Foundation, which provides aid to Ukrainian refugees, told newspaper Rzeczpospolita today that the tragedy in Jarosław was already being exploited on social media. He expressed fear that “we are almost on the verge of lynchings”. 🔴Jesteśmy na granicy nastrojów linczowych. World.title: Polish constitutional court officials charged with preventing entry of new judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further, after prosecutors charged two senior TK officials over their role in preventing new judges from taking up their positions on the court. Those judges were chosen by the government’s majority in parliament but rejected by President Karol Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, both of whom are aligned with the right-wing opposition. Following news of the charges, Święczkowski announced that he has initiated proceedings of his own against three other new judges who were admitted to the court this year after being chosen by the ruling coalition. That could result in them being expelled from their positions. Zarzuty w śledztwie dotyczącym niedopuszczenia sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego do orzekania: ⬇️https://t.co/MPiKCEqGBs — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 After coming to power in December 2023, the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk refused to recognise the TK, which was stacked with judges appointed by the former Law and Justice administration. It argued that, because some of those judges were unlawfully appointed, the TK itself was illegitimate. Earlier this year, Tusk’s majority in parliament finally began the process of appointing new judges to the TK to fill the growing number of vacancies. Normally, 15 judges sit on the tribunal, but many seats were empty after incumbents’ nine-year terms had expired and the government had previously refused to fill them. However, under Polish law, new TK judges must take an oath “before the president” in order to take up their position. Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, has refused to swear in four of the six judges chosen by parliament in March. Nawrocki argues that there were legal doubts surrounding their election. The government rejects this, as do the judges themselves, who organised their own swearing-in ceremony before a notary and then submitted the documents to the presidential chancellery. Afterwards, the four judges attempted to take up their positions at the TK. However, Święczkowski, who served in the PiS government before becoming a TK judge, refused to admit them, arguing that they had not taken the necessary oath before the president. The judges took their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which in May issued an interim order requiring that they be allowed to take up their positions. But Święczkowski has refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the competence to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 While Święczkowski himself is protected from prosecution by legal immunity, two senior TK officials have now been charged over their role in refusing entry to the four judges. One of the two suspects, who can be named only as Zofia H. under Polish privacy law, is the director of the TK’s chancellery; the other, Piotr P., is the commander of the TK’s security service. They have been charged with abuse of power by a public official, which is punishable by up to three years in prison, and “maliciously and persistently” violating the employment rights of the judges, an offence that carries a sentence of up to two years. Prosecutors say that the officials’ actions were “to the detriment of the private interests of judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and the public interest in the proper functioning of the judiciary in Poland”. Both of the accused have been questioned and pleaded not guilty. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The decision to bring charges was welcomed by Waldemar Żurek, who serves as justice minister in Tusk’s government as well as prosecutor general. “In a building that should stand guard over the constitution, unlawful blockades were organised, humiliating inspections were conducted, and malicious bullying was directed at legally elected judges,” he wrote on social media. “A state official has no right to place themselves above the law, and the gates of the tribunal are not the gates of a private fortress,” he continued. “Anyone who carries out unlawful political orders and destroys the foundations of the rule of law must reckon with criminal liability.” W budynku, który powinien stać na straży Konstytucji, urządzono bezprawne blokady, upokarzające kontrole i złośliwy mobbing wobec legalnie wybranych sędziów. Urzędnik państwowy nie ma prawa stawiać się ponad prawem, a bramy Trybunału nie są bramami prywatnej twierdzy.… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 23, 2026 The TK itself, however, condemned prosecutors’ actions, calling them “unlawful” and a “tool of personal pressure and a form of intimidation”. “The director of the chancellery and all other employees of the TK have performed and continue to perform their duties and official orders in accordance with the applicable law,” wrote the tribunal on its official X account. It argued that it would, in fact, have been a criminal abuse of power to have “allowed persons who have not taken the oath before the President to assume the office of a TK judge”. W dniu dzisiejszym @PK_GOV_PL przedstawiła Pani Dyrektor Kancelarii Trybunału Konstytucyjnego absurdalne zarzuty z art. 231 § 1 i 218 § 3 Kodeksu karnego, które od początku do końca są oparte na wymyślonych podstawach prawnych. Działanie to stanowi kolejną próbę wywarcia wpływu… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 On Thursday, the day after the charges were announced, the TK issued a further statement saying that Święczkowski had initiated proceedings against three new TK judges who were chosen by parliament this year and sworn in by Nawrocki (two in March, the other in June). The TK said that it was assessing complaints that two of those judges filed against tribunal employees, as well as their refusal to participate in sessions of the TK’s general assembly. Those three judges have shown solidarity with their four excluded colleagues by refusing to participate. “These proceedings may conclude with the most severe ruling of the disciplinary court in the form of removal from office of the aforementioned TK judges,” wrote the TK. Prezes @TK_GOV_PL Bogdan Święczkowski, działając na wniosek jednego z sędziów, wszczął dzisiaj postępowanie mogące się zakończyć zarzutami dyscyplinarnymi wobec trojga sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego: Magdaleny Bentkowskiej, Dariusza Szostka oraz Sławomira Patyry.… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 24, 2026 An eighth new TK judge chosen this year, Maciej Berek, who was elected by parliament earlier this month, has also not yet been sworn in by Nawrocki. Berek’s appointment has been particularly controversial, given that he served in the government until being nominated to the TK. Tusk described Berek as his “right-hand man”. Even some MPs from Tusk’s ruling coalition voted against Berek’s appointment, arguing that it contradicted the government’s own efforts to “depoliticise” the judiciary, including by banning recently serving politicians from sitting on the TK. The presidential chancellery has so far refused to swear in Berek based on a technicality, arguing that there is no evidence he has previously served for at least ten years as a legal counsel, which is a requirement to sit on the TK. Berek says that he has presented such evidence. World.title: Starlink ground station in Poland hit by fire in suspected arson attack
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gawkowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gawkowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Poland and Belarus seek thaw in relations as foreign ministers meet for first time in a decade
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. The foreign ministers of Poland and Belarus have met for the first time in a decade, as both sides indicated that they are open to thawing their long-frosty relations. The two countries have regularly clashed in recent years, in particular over Minsk’s alliance with Moscow, the migration crisis Belarus has engineered on the Polish border, and the persecution of Belarus’s ethnic Polish minority. Warsaw, meanwhile, has supported the Belarusian democratic opposition. However, on Tuesday this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed to reporters that he had met with his Belarusian counterpart, Maxim Ryzhenkov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Sikorski said that the initiative had come from the Belarusian side. “When a neighbour wants to unfreeze and improve relations, Poland is the first to reach an agreement,” said Sikorski, quoted by broadcaster RMF. “This is a first, introductory meeting, but meetings with other ministries and at other levels are also taking place,” he added, noting that Poland will also “soon be opening a new embassy building in Minsk”. When asked what topics had been discussed, Sikorski said that they had included the border situation and regional security. Asked if he had requested that Belarus not allow Russia to fly drones and missiles through its territory, he said that this was discussed “among other things”. The last known time that the Polish and Belarusian foreign ministers met was in October 2016, when Belarus’s Vladimir Makei visited Witold Waszczykowski in Warsaw. Sikorski said that this week’s meeting with Ryzhenkov had been possible because the situation on their shared border – where Belarus has since 2021 encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to cross into Poland – is now “more normalised”. Poland has installed physical and electronic barriers along the border, sent thousands of armed officers to guard it, and has banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly. Following those measures, the number of attempted crossings has fallen dramatically this year. Sikorski also noted that relations have been improved by Belarus’s recent decisions to release political prisoners, including Polish ones. Most prominent among them is Andrzej Poczobut, a leader of the Polish community in Belarus, who had been imprisoned on trumped-up charges for five years. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Minsk’s recent actions have provided “more freedom and greater reasons to try to stabilise relations”, said Sikorski. “A snowdrop can bloom if the weather is favorable.” Belarus’s foreign ministry continued that metaphor in a post on social media on Wednesday, sharing a photo of Sikorski meeting with Ryzhenkov and writing that “snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart”. “But we’re in it for the harvest,” added the ministry. “Let’s plant an orchard – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host.” Last year, Belarus called for “dialogue” with Poland in order to “reduce the risk of armed clashes” amid a military build-up around the border. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace on Wednesday morning, the operational command of Poland’s armed forces has announced. The incident is the latest in a series of airspace violations by Russia, which have also involved drones and, most recently, a missile. It follows recent warnings by the Polish government that Moscow has been planning further “provocations” intended to test NATO’s defences and unity. ❗️ Informujemy, że 23 września br. o godz. 11.08, na północ od miejscowości Braniewo, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia przestrzeni powietrznej Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej przez śmigłowiec Mi-8 Sił Zbrojnych Federacji Rosyjskiej. Śmigłowiec wykonywał lot z Obwodu Królewieckiego.… pic.twitter.com/afULQdSeTc — Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) September 23, 2026 On Wednesday afternoon, Polish operational command announced that, shortly after 11:00 a.m. that day, an Mi-8 helicopter belonging to the Russian armed forces had briefly entered Polish airspace near the town of Braniewo, after crossing from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The helicopter did not travel further than 300 metres into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. In response, the Polish military scrambled fighter jets and placed ground forces on standby. “The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defences,” wrote operational command. At the time of writing, Russia has not commented on the incident. Today’s violation appears to be the first publicly reported instance of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. Last year, in two separate incidents, a Russian Su-24 bomber and a naval helicopter flew over Poland’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. In 2023, two helicopters belonging to the armed forces of Belarus, a close ally of Russia, briefly entered Polish airspace before crossing back over the border. On one night in September last year, around 20 Russian drones entered Poland over its eastern borders amid Russian attacks on Ukraine. Polish and allied forces shot down some of them, while others hit the ground without causing casualties. In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The object that crashed in the Lublin region on Thursday was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a "significant amount" of explosive material. The missile was "potentially very dangerous,” Poland's defence ministry confirmedhttps://t.co/NoqZwIcaWp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 In recent months, Poland and other NATO countries have been warning of Russian plans to carry out further “provocations” intended to test the alliance’s defences and unity, saying that they could include border and airspace violations. In the last few weeks, Poland has regularly intercepted Russian aircraft that have flown close to Polish territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. This month, Russian drones have repeatedly hit targets in Ukraine near to the Polish border, including a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw. Just last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
World.content:
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.

For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?



Where you can shop on September 28

Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.

The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.

Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.

Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.

Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day

The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.

Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.

His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.

Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.

The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.

See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle

September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.

The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.

The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.

Government buildings open to visitors

Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.

Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.

The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.

The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.

Museums and other attractions

The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.

The Postal Museum will also be open.

For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.

Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.

The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation: The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy: A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance: The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: Prague Taxi Drivers Could Be Tested on Czech and Local Geography
World.content:
Prague taxi drivers could soon be required to demonstrate their knowledge of Czech and the city’s geography.

The Chamber of Deputies approved the change on Wednesday as part of an amendment to the Road Traffic Act. The legislation does not automatically introduce testing in Prague or other Czech cities. Instead, it would give municipalities the authority to impose such requirements.



Under the amendment, municipalities could test taxi drivers on their legal rights and obligations, their Czech language skills to the extent necessary for the job, and their knowledge of locations within the municipality that are relevant to taxi services.

The bill now goes to the Senate.

What the new rules could mean for taxi drivers

The issue has been debated in Prague for some time, particularly as the taxi industry has changed with the rapid growth of app-based services.

Pirate Party leader Zdeněk Hřib introduced a more detailed proposal in May. That version included specific provisions defining what drivers could be required to know and what would fall outside the scope of the tests.

For example, the proposal said drivers should not be expected to demonstrate encyclopedic knowledge of Prague’s landmarks. Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik of the SPD, however, argued that the Pirate Party’s proposal had legal shortcomings.

A shorter amendment submitted by ANO MP Patrik Nacher ultimately became the version approved by the Chamber of Deputies.

Supporters of the change say taxi driving has increasingly become a profession with few formal qualification requirements beyond holding a driving licence.

The explanatory report accompanying the legislation argues that the sector has attracted foreign workers who may have limited knowledge of Czech, local traffic rules and the city in which they operate.

Critics, meanwhile, have raised concerns about the potential impact on fares. They argue that additional requirements could increase the cost of entering the profession and eventually lead to higher prices for passengers.

No English requirement in the legislation

The approved amendment refers specifically to knowledge of the Czech language. It does not introduce an English-language requirement, even though some taxi drivers in Prague also have limited English skills.

The legislation would apply to taxi drivers regardless of whether they operate independently or through digital platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

Foreign nationals make up roughly half of Prague’s registered taxi drivers, reflecting the sector’s long-standing reliance on foreign workers and recently arrived migrants.

World.title: While flying, Hungarian minister opens up about father lost in national airline tragedy
World.content:
For Hungary’s economy and energy minister, flying carries an unusually personal meaning. Asked about aviation while travelling on board a plane, István Kapitány recalled his father, a Malév chief pilot who died in a crash near Paris when the future minister was not yet one year old. Decades later, aviation would unexpectedly become a constant part of Kapitány’s own life as well.

“The first thing that usually comes to mind is my father, who was a chief pilot at Malév and flew a great deal,” Kapitány said.

His father was a professional pilot for Malév, Hungary’s former national airline. Kapitány said that despite choosing an entirely different profession himself, flying ultimately became a major part of his own life as well.

Working for a large international company meant travelling constantly. According to the minister, he visited 85 countries by air over the course of his career.

“I chose a job in which I ended up flying more in my life than my father did,” he said.

His father, also named István Kapitány, was the captain of Malév Flight 355, one of the most serious accidents in the history of Hungary’s former national airline.

From turboprops to giant Airbuses

Kapitány described an unusually wide range of flying experiences accumulated over several decades. He recalled travelling on everything from small turboprop aircraft to large Airbus and Boeing jets.

Yet despite spending so much time in airports and aircraft cabins, he said flying never became something he simply endured as part of the job. He continues to enjoy not only aircraft themselves, but also the social side of travelling: meeting new people, discovering different cultures and striking up conversations during flights.

“I love the whole atmosphere,” he said.

He summed up his enthusiasm with a characteristically Hungarian comparison, saying he likes aircraft at least as much as Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy likes trains and buses.

If you missed it: Hungary’s energy minister shares when the country could leave Russian gas

A plain tragedy near Paris

Behind Kapitány’s enthusiasm for flying lies a deeply personal family history. His father, István Kapitány Sr, was a Malév chief pilot who died in an air crash when Kapitány was less than a year old.

On 23 November 1962, Malév Flight 355 was travelling from Budapest to Paris, with a stop in Frankfurt.The aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-18V registered as HA-MOD, crashed while approaching Paris-Le Bourget Airport near Roissy-en-France.

A Malév Ilyushin Il-18 photographed in April 1972. Photo: Lars Söderström / Wikimedia Commons

All 21 people on board – 13 passengers and eight crew members – were deceased. István Kapitány Sr was the aircraft’s captain. Aviation accident records show that he had accumulated more than 10,000 flying hours by the time of the crash.

Kapitány was born in December 1961, meaning he was not yet one year old when his father died. French, Hungarian and Soviet experts tried to determine the exact cause of the crash, but were unable to reach a definitive conclusion.

Despite losing his father in an aviation disaster, Kapitány himself became fascinated with flying. He has previously recalled that he wanted to follow in his father’s footsteps and become a pilot. Ultimately, however, he chose a different career, partly at the request of his family.

World.title: Births fall sharply in Hungary – could the population really drop to 5 million by 2100?
World.content:
Hungary has recorded another sharp fall in the number of births, while deaths slightly increased in August compared with a year earlier. The latest figures add to a long-running demographic trend that has seen the country’s population decline for decades, even as fewer deaths have somewhat moderated the natural population loss so far this year.

According to preliminary data released by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) and reported by MTI on Friday, 5,922 children were born in Hungary in August 2026, while 9,452 people died.

The number of births was 7.4% lower than in August 2025, representing 475 fewer newborns. Meanwhile, deaths increased by 0.9%, or 87 people, year on year. As a result, Hungary recorded a natural population decrease of 3,530 people in August, compared with 2,968 in the same month last year.

The August decline is part of a much longer demographic trend: Hungary’s population has been shrinking for decades, while the number of births has continued to fall in recent years.

Fewer children born in Hungary

Between January and August, 46,497 children were born, 3.5% or 1,663 fewer than during the same period in 2025.

Births fell by 3.4% between January and March and by 4.7% between May and August compared with the corresponding periods of last year. April was the only exception, when the number of births rose by 1.8% year on year.

Hungary’s estimated total fertility rate also declined, from 1.31 to 1.29 children per woman. The indicator estimates how many children a woman would have over her lifetime if the fertility patterns observed during the period remained unchanged.

The difference between births and deaths produced a natural decrease of 34,900 people between January and August. That was slightly smaller than the 35,374 recorded a year earlier, primarily because fewer people died. Birth numbers, however, continued to decline.

More than 51,000 more deaths than births in 12 months

Between September 2025 and August 2026, 70,354 children were born in Hungary, 5.1% fewer than during the preceding 12 months. Over the same period, 122,056 people died, which means the number of deaths exceeded the number of births by 51,702.

Natural population decrease should not be confused with the total change in Hungary’s population, as immigration and emigration also affect the number of people living in the country. The latest figures nevertheless fit into a demographic decline that has been underway for decades.

What about the warning that Hungary could have only 5.2 million people by 2100?

The latest KSH data come only weeks after a separate long-term demographic forecast attracted considerable attention in Hungary.

As we previously reported, demographer Pál Péter Tóth warned at the 64th Annual Meeting of the Hungarian Economic Association that, if current demographic trends continue, Hungary’s population could fall to around 5.2 million by 2100.

The KSH’s own forecasts are also scenarios rather than predictions of an inevitable future. Under its medium scenario, Hungary’s population could also fall significantly, to around 6.8 million by 2076.

What the latest data do show is that the immediate trend has not reversed: fewer children are being born, and Hungary continues to record substantially more deaths than births.

If you missed it: Shocking warning by demographer: Hungary could have just 5 million people by 2100

Marriages also fell sharply in August

The KSH figures also showed a significant decline in marriages during the month. A total of 5,633 couples married in August, 12% or 739 fewer than in August 2025.

Across the first eight months of the year, however, the picture was slightly different. A total of 31,287 couples married between January and August, 1% more than during the same period last year. The KSH also stressed that the latest 2026 vital statistics are preliminary.

World.title: Germany and Hungary revive defence ties – Leopard tanks, joint exercises and Ukraine on agenda
World.content:
Germany and Hungary plan to significantly deepen their defence cooperation, with training, logistics, joint military exercises and German-made weapon systems among the areas identified for closer coordination. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius made the announcement after talks with his Hungarian counterpart, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi.

The meeting marked a renewed push to strengthen defence relations between Berlin and Budapest after a period of limited high-level contacts. According to Ruszin-Szendi, a German defence minister had last visited Hungary in 2020, MTI reported.

“Berlin and Budapest will work more closely together again,” Pistorius said, arguing that stronger cooperation would benefit Hungary, Germany and NATO as a whole.

Leopard tanks and artillery among key areas of cooperation

The two ministers said they had identified several areas where military cooperation could be expanded, including logistics, training and joint exercises.

Pistorius also highlighted the possibility of Germany sharing expertise related to weapon systems already used by the Hungarian Armed Forces, including the Leopard family of tanks and the Panzerhaubitze 2000 self-propelled howitzer.

Hungary has relied heavily on German defence technology during the modernisation of its armed forces. Ruszin-Szendi said German equipment had played an important role in the development of Hungary’s military capabilities and its NATO heavy brigade.

A Lithuanian PzH 2000 self-propelled howitzer during a military exercise. Photo: Lithuanian Armed Forces / Wikimedia Commons

The Hungarian defence minister added that cooperation could now be extended further, including into military mobility, logistics and the space industry. Budapest would also like to see more Hungarian companies integrated into defence-industry supply chains.

Ruszin-Szendi said the two sides wanted to make greater use of existing agreements and demonstrate that Hungary could be a reliable partner for its allies.

If you missed it: Peace at last between Hungary and Ukraine? Budapest signs major declaration backing Kyiv

Pistorius warns of growing threat from Russia

The German defence minister said closer European defence cooperation had become increasingly important because of what he described as a growing threat from Russia.

Pistorius argued that Moscow was increasingly testing NATO countries through hybrid operations and provocations, while stressing that the alliance had both the capabilities and determination to defend itself.

His remarks are consistent with comments he made in the German Bundestag on 23 September, when he said the security threat posed by Russia had intensified in recent weeks. The German government has pointed to incidents involving drones, attacks near NATO territory and suspected hybrid operations as signs of a deteriorating security environment.

Pistorius also reiterated Germany’s support for Ukraine, particularly in the field of air defence and preparations for the winter. At the same time, he said NATO’s response was designed to strengthen deterrence without escalating the conflict.

Hungary says it will not block Ukraine’s EU accession process

Ruszin-Szendi also addressed Hungary’s policy towards Ukraine. He said the Hungarian government would continue its policy of not sending troops or lethal military equipment to the war, while humanitarian and energy assistance would continue.

However, the minister also announced a notable development in Budapest’s position on Ukraine’s European integration.

According to Ruszin-Szendi, recent talks with Kyiv had produced progress on the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. As a result, he said Hungary had decided not to continue blocking Ukraine’s EU accession procedure.

Budapest had still been blocking progress on parts of Ukraine’s accession negotiations earlier in September, linking its approval to guarantees concerning minority rights.

The Hungarian government nevertheless continues to oppose an accelerated accession process. Ruszin-Szendi said Ukraine should not be allowed to move ahead of candidate countries that have already spent years waiting to join the European Union.

“Thank you for coming back”

Referring to Hungary’s political changes following the April parliamentary election, Pistorius welcomed the renewed cooperation and said developments in Hungary could encourage people living under authoritarian or similar political systems.

“Thank you from the bottom of my heart for coming back,” the German minister said.

Ruszin-Szendi described the meeting as evidence that relations between Hungary and Germany were being rebuilt not only in defence policy but at a broader political level.

The Hungarian minister also stressed that Budapest remains committed to NATO and European defence cooperation, arguing that the country’s security depends both on a strong Hungarian military and on close cooperation with its allies.
