Was Wharfie Time a mistake? Another of the great unknowns about this game. It's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful.

What is also certain is that the Lions fed off it, saw it as a sign the Dockers had an eye on celebrations when five decisive minutes remained on the clock.

These Lions, of course, need no invitation. The self-belief and composure and character required to win this premiership — a journey that extended well beyond those final five minutes or this grand final or even the start of the season — is the envy of the entire AFL.

The Lions enjoy the three-peat spoils. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

One problem with dynastic greatness in sport is you can sometimes run out of things to talk about. Once you've ascended to the peak and set up camp, the story of how you got there can lose its lustre.

They'll tell this story forever. The day the Lions won the unwinnable, the day the world collapsed upon the Dockers, among the greatest and most horrible days footy has ever seen.

World.title: Quick hits: Lions use 'Wharfie Time' to energise, Treacy misses a sitter
World.content:
It was one of the greatest grand finals in history as the Brisbane Lions used "Wharfie Time" to their own advantage to claim their third flag in a row.

From a controversial call on the siren to an absolute sitter missed on the goal-line, these are the quick hits from a stunning grand final.

1. Neale booed from the moment he takes the field

If you weren't aware that Fremantle fans were none too pleased that Lachie Neale was playing in this grand final before the match, the Purple Haze left no doubt as their former favourite son ran onto the field.

Neale, who played for the Dockers in their only other grand final appearance in 2013, was controversially freed to play in this grand final after originally being handed a one-week ban for a gut punch on Jack Ginnivan in the prelim final.

Starting on the bench, Neale ran onto the field to a chorus of booing at the MCG as Dockers fans showed that they weren't fully on board with the "good bloke" provision that had allowed the dual Brownlow Medallist to play.

Later, Neale had a shot at goal as the 'G hummed with a long "boooo" that turned quickly to a joyous "ayyyy" as his shot flew wide.

2. Dockers controversially denied a shot on quarter time

With the seconds counting down to quarter time and the Lions leading by a point, the Dockers made a last-ditch attack that saw Neil Erasmus take a mark just outside 50.

Erasmus turned casually and laid a perfect little pass out in front of the leading Josh Treacy.

The problem was that it was just a little too little.

The umpire called play on for the kick not going 15 metres, Treacy was tackled, a ball up was called, and the quarter ended.

If Dockers fans hadn't had enough of the old boo for Neale, they were well rewarded with another opportunity to unleash on the umpire.

To the eye, it looked like it was a 15m kick, and commentators and spectators alike were blindsided by the call as it happened.

On replay, it was certainly close, but you'd want to be sure making that call in a grand final.

3. McKenna kicks another goal of the year

Goals kicked in the finals aren't considered for the goal of the year, but if they were, Conor McKenna might have won it.

I mean, he did win it for his regular-season pearler, but he probably would have won it again for this dribbler.

Down by five points early in the second quarter, the Sherrin spilled to a static McKenna who barely had enough space to get any leverage behind his boot.

But with what seemed like millimetres between his hand and his foot, McKenna managed to get the pill to his foot, dribbling it through to take the lead.

4. Dockers skipper crumples to the ground

Hearts were in mouths in the third quarter as Dockers skipper Alex Pearce crumpled to the ground while chasing the ball on the wing.

It wasn't a grab at a hamstring, or pull of a calf, or a twist of the knee, but a straight fall to the turf that signalled something pretty serious.

Carried from the ground, shots of Pearce on the bench later on would show a big bag of ice strapped to his Achilles.

It was day done, and it was a costly loss of a key defender that would come back to haunt Freo.

5. Young's double special

The Norm Smith Medal was up for grabs in the third quarter, and Dockers star Hayden Young figured he'd put his hand up for a shot at the title.

His first act was a very Hayden Young-like goal, streaking through the 50m arc on the run and launching long for a major.

His next was a goal that mimicked his stunner in the preliminary final against the Swans, but from the opposite pocket, curling a beauty around to give the Dockers the break.

6. Treacy misses an absolute sitter

With the Dockers on a burst and looking to put what felt like a game-winning break on the Lions, Josh Treacy got on the end of ball that spilled into his hands in the goal square.

The key forward was all but 2m from the goal as he looked to launch a big hoof into the Sherrin and send it into the third tier.

But as he did, Lions defender Ryan Lester just got a hand to Treacy's bottom, ever so slightly putting him off balance, with the kick somehow flying wide.

Not hitting the post flush, not even scraping the side — just completely missing.

While Patrick Voss would go on to kick a goal not long after and get the break anyway, it was an incredible blunder at a crucial moment.

7. Where's Wharfie Time?

Whenever Wharfie Time isn't in the room, people should be asking "where's Wharfie Time?"

And that was the case as Fremantle made their break, with commentators questioning why the Dockers hadn't pushed the button yet for the iconic tolling of the bells.

Well, they did after the Voss goal — and it might go down in history as the "Wharfie Curse" for what happened next.

8. Charlie and Zac snap absolute rippers

Lions football manager Danny Daly told the ABC Sport broadcast team before the game that coach Chris Fagan had played "Wharfie Time" to his players in their Friday team meeting.

But the Lions players after the game revealed just how much that session had impacted them, saying they were told to use it to energise them if they were feeling flat.

With the Dockers up by 17 and the bells still ringing in Lions' ears, the pill hammered forward twice in the blink of an eye, the first attack finishing in a Charlie Cameron snap, the next in a Zac Bailey goal.

The Lions were in touch.

9. Morris grabs an absolute ripper

And in mere moments, the Lions had the lead.

This time it was Logan Morris clunking a big grab in the forward 50, directly in front.

Morris converted.

Fremantle hearts broke.

And the Brisbane Lions became just the second team in VFL/AFL history to claim two three-peat victories, doing so in one of the greatest grand finals you're ever likely to see.

World.title: Surprised Docker wins Norm Smith Medal in losing grand final team
World.content:
Fremantle's Shai Bolton has become the first player in 21 years to win the Norm Smith Medal in a losing grand final team.

Minutes after the heartbreaking 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) defeat to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG, where the Dockers were overrun in the closing stages, Bolton was as surprised as anyone to hear his name called.

Stunning Lions comeback breaks Freo hearts The Brisbane Lions launch an incredible fightback late in the grand final to edge Fremantle by seven points and win a third consecutive premiership.

Bolton polled 10 votes from the selection panel, edging out Lions pair Dayne Zorko and Will Ashcroft (six votes each).

He is one of only five players to be named best on ground in a losing grand final team.

Chris Judd was the most recent, doing so for West Coast in 2005 against the Sydney Swans.

Nathan Buckley (2002), Gary Ablett Snr (1989) and Maurice Rioli (1982) were the others.

"To our boys, heads up, we'll be back better and stronger," Bolton said after 2009 winner Paul Chapman presented the medal.

On paper, Bolton had an excellent match, with 26 disposals, 686 metres gained and nine score involvements.

Shai Bolton had helped put the Dockers in front during the grand final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Ashcroft had a case for a third Norm Smith Medal in as many grand finals after a fourth-quarter masterclass.

When Patrick Voss put Fremantle up by 17 points and the 'Wharfie Time' rev-up activation sounded around the MCG, it was Ashcroft who helped orchestrate the Lions' remarkable fightback.

Ashcroft recorded 12 disposals and four clearances in the final term, finishing the match with 31 and nine, as the Lions responded with goals to Charlie Cameron, Zac Bailey and Logan Morris to hit the front.

Lions captain Harris Andrews was also superb, along with Zorko (28 disposals).

Fremantle's Caleb Serong was arguably the most impressive midfielder across the day, with 24 disposals and 13 clearances.

Serong finished fourth in the Norm Smith Medal standings, collecting four votes.

AAP

World.title: 'Lost love of my life': Family visits crash site of young officer's death
World.content:
The partner of Constable Mia Lay says he has lost the love of his life a day after she was killed in a police car crash.

Daniel Vasquez, who is also a member of the NSW Police Force, was among the family and friends who placed flowers at the location in Redfern where the 20-year-old died.

Constable Lay died in a car crash in the early hours of Friday morning. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Her father planted bright yellow flowers at the site.

"She was the happiest girl I've met when she was with me, when she was at work," Mr Vasquez said on behalf of the family.

"And I've asked for everyone to remember how stunning and beautiful she was.

" I know myself, she will always be in my heart. I've just lost the love of my life. "

Constable Lay's father at the scene where his daughter died. (ABC News)

Just 16 months into her policing career, Constable Lay was responding to reports of a stolen car in the nearby suburb of Glebe.

She was sitting in the passenger seat of a marked police vehicle travelling along Gibbons Street, when it hit a tree near the intersection of Regent Street in the early hours of Friday morning.

She died at the scene. The 24-year-old driver suffered facial injuries, and was taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, but has since been discharged.

Constable Lay died at the scene. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Mr Vasquez said that Constable Lay's mother, Tamara, wanted everyone to know how much her daughter had loved her work.

"She was happy in the police, she was good at her job and how loved she was by everyone in the community.

"She was a kind-hearted person and gave so much love to everyone that she cared about."

Constable Lay's mother, Tamara (centre in red), wanted people to know how much her daughter loved her job. (ABC News)

'Thank you for your courage'

It was a sentiment shared by Redfern resident Tim Cochran.

He recalls thinking, after Constable Lay responded to an incident earlier this year, that she was the kind of person "that brings a lot of good into the world", and says her untimely death has "hit him pretty hard".

In January, Mr Cochran called Triple Zero when he found a man unresponsive in a park.

The young officer was only 16 months into her policing career. (ABC News)

She took control when she arrived, he said, as he "watched her do her thing", leaving him in awe.

"She got the guy moving and responding," he said.

"She just struck me as an incredibly confident and competent, and reassuring person for someone her age.

"I just remember thinking to myself 'This young woman, half my age and is pulling this off' … It felt good, she made me feel better, and I wasn't the one in need."

While he did not know her, he added, she came across as someone who was "clearly doing the thing that she was meant to do".

"If somebody like that can leave an impression on me from just a few minutes of interaction, I just can only imagine how much it would hurt for the people who actually know her," he said.

Constable Lay is being remembered as a kind-hearted, loving and competent person. (ABC News)

On Friday, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said she had shown "exceptional promise" in the short time she had been in the Force.

"To Mia 'Thank you for your courage, thank you for choosing to join the NSW Police Force, and thank you for serving the community of New South Wales, you will not be forgotten'," he said.

The investigation into the critical incident is ongoing and is being assisted by the Crash Investigations Unit.

"It will be a complex investigation, but we will get answers out of that, we have assured the family members of that," Commissioner Lanyon said.

World.title: 40yo man critically injured in house fire in Adelaide's south-west
World.content:
A man is in a critical condition after a fire broke out inside a home in Adelaide's south-western suburbs.

Emergency services were called to a house on George Street, at Marion, about 6.30am after reports of a fire.

A 40-year-old man was rushed to hospital with serious burns where he remains in a life-threatening condition.

Metropolitan Fire Service crews were able to extinguish the blaze which was contained to the bathroom.

Fire cause investigators have attended the scene and investigations are ongoing.

Police say they do not believe the fire is suspicious but have urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Melbourne family holds fears for son missing on Peru hiking trip
World.content:
A Melbourne family holds grave fears for their son, who is missing after embarking on a solo hiking trip in a remote part of Peru.

Vinh Dao said he had not heard from his son Jordan Yap since the 30-year-old attempted to complete a hike in the remote Huayhuash region earlier this month.

"Before the 10-day hike in the Huayhuash region, he sent the last message to us saying that he's going to be off grid for the next 10 days," Mr Dao said.

Peru's remote Huayhuash mountain range is a popular destination for hikers. (Unsplash: Wolfgang Lutz)

Having left a hostel in the town of Huaraz on September 14, Mr Yap was due to check into a hotel on the 23rd before catching a flight from Lima to Cusco the following day.

"So he failed to check in at the hotel and he missed his flight as well, so that's when the panic and the concern kicked in," Mr Dao said.

Mr Dao said his son was an experienced hiker, but that the trip to Peru was one of his first solo trips.

The family has since contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) in an attempt to liaise with local police in Peru, without success.

In a statement, a DFAT spokesperson said it was providing consular assistance to the family.

As they wait for a response from local authorities, the family has engaged a local private mountain rescue team to search for their son.

Mr Dao said the company assembled a search team last night at about 3am Melbourne time.

"They've completed the first day and they got some positive identification of Jordan on day two," he said.

"So that was a while ago … there were people who came across Jordan on the second day and that was it."

The rescue team plans to expand its search area over the coming days, with the 30-year-old's family now preparing to travel to Peru if necessary.

"We're very anxious. We just can't imagine that he's there, lost somewhere," Mr Dao said.

World.title: AFL grand final LIVE: Lions surge late for third flag in a row, breaking Docker hearts

Grand final hero Logan Morris played through a stress fracture in his back and barely trained in recent months as he became the first AFL footballer to win a premiership in each of his first three seasons.

Morris’ injury revelation followed a star turn in the final quarter, when he kicked all three of his goals, including slotting the go-ahead major with 64 seconds left after brilliantly out-marking Oscar McDonald just inside 50.

Match winner: Logan Morris kicked the goal that put Brisbane in front for the final time. Justin McManus

“I think throughout the game I was getting under them [when the ball was kicked to him], and wasn’t marking ones that I would have liked,” Morris said.

“[Development coach and ex-AFL player] Liam Jones came up to me at half-time and just said, ‘Be patient with your marking, don’t release too early’, and that last one, I think I did it perfectly and released at a perfect time and was able to mark it and then obviously go back and kick it.

I knew that this kick was to put us up in a grand final. I was nervous, but I just went back to what I do in training … and I was super stoked to kick it.” Morris started poorly early with an errant set shot that went out on the full late in the opening quarter, but his afternoon transformed after Alex Pearce suffered a game-ending Achilles injury while he and Morris were chasing after the loose Sherrin. “It was obviously shattering for him,” Morris said. “They were probably a bit smaller [in defence after that], so we wanted to isolate whoever had a better match-up. It’s shattering for him, but it probably worked out better for us.



“I didn’t have the start that I wanted, but in a grand final – a high-pressure game – I knew that my moment was going to come. I had a quiet three quarters, and I was a bit flat with myself … [but] I knew that it would open up late in the game, and I just got my chances, and took them.” Morris has kicked 149 goals in his first three seasons – 72 of them this year while earning his maiden All-Australian selection – to go with his history-making premierships, and he finished this year under great duress. The Lions’ medical staff nursed him through to the grand final, with a weekly regimen where he didn’t train early in the week. “I can probably say it now. I’ve had a stress fracture to the left side of my back for probably the back half of the year,” he said.

“Will Ashcroft and Levi Ashcroft’s old man, [Lions premiership star] Marcus, came up to me after the game and said, ‘Enjoy this one, but you’ve got to go again’. World.title: The Dockers had one hand on the premiership cup. Then came four minutes that turned the grand final
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL grand final The Dockers had one hand on the premiership cup. Then came four minutes that turned the grand final Andrew Wu September 26, 2026 — 8:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories .

When the bells tolled for Wharfie Time with just over four minutes left in this epic grand final, few, if any, of the 100,023 crammed into the MCG could have imagined what they would see next. Fremantle’s Patrick Voss, a hero to the purple army, had bolted on the victory run to end all victory runs towards bays of despondent Brisbane Lions fans in the Ponsford Stand after showing nerves of steel to first run down the clock, then convert from 20 metres out. Charlie Cameron celebrates a goal. Joe Armao Up by a game-high 17 points, with the finish line tantalisingly close, the Dockers had never been closer to the premiership in their 11,502 days in the AFL. What happened after the cacophony bellowing around this famous stadium had reached its climax will be etched into the minds of the millions around the globe who love this game.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final Honoured, but surprised: Why Shai Bolton took off his medal right after winning the Norm Smith For the Fremantle faithful, who came across the Nullarbor and had visions of a hobbled Alex Pearce lifting the cup with Justin Longmuir, they will be memories they may never exorcise. Of the premierships in Brisbane’s second three-peat, none have forced Chris Fagan’s immortals to show more skill, tenacity and bloody-mindedness. They needed all this – and more than a slice of good fortune – to turn back-to-back flags into a dynasty. This grand final victory, a wire-to-wire test of character and resilience, played in testing conditions – was a worthy sequel to last week’s nerve-jangling goalfest between Hawthorn and the Lions, dubbed by many to be one of the greatest games played. Both could not be greater s for the sport. Champions possess an almost mystical capability to win from hopeless positions, but in this case, there is a rational explanation.



The Lions, like all great teams, have different ways to win. Shootouts like last week? We’ll back ourselves to score more. Arm wrestles? We have more midfield muscle. This was a game that, for all bar the final minutes, was played on Fremantle’s terms. The Dockers dominated at clearance, had the game played for long periods in their forward half but could not land the knockout blow. Josh Treacy, who missed from a few feet out when all he had to do was toe poke the ball over the goal line rather than blast it into the stands, will have trouble sleeping. Wharfie Time is supposed to propel the Dockers to another level. Instead, it served as a rally cry for the unshakable Lions, who, nearly to a man, revealed it had been a source of motivation.



Beaten in the clinches all game, the Lions’ midfield gritted their teeth and willed the ball forward with every sinew in their aching bodies. Sam Draper, recruited to the club for games like this, had been shaded by Luke Jackson but knocked the ball forward to Will Ashcroft, whose perfectly imperfect kick inside 50 gave Charlie Cameron the ideal platform to pounce, turn and curl it through on his right foot. No sooner had the strains of Take Me Home, Country Roads subsided, the Dockers’ defence was under siege again. This time, Zac Bailey bounced off a tackle from Caleb Serong that had been sticking in the previous two hours, to snap in heavier traffic than peak hour on Punt Road.



Amid the chaos, the Dockers, through a clutch mark to Treacy and another contested-ball win by him at half-forward, composed themselves sufficiently to send the ball forward, but the defensive integrity that has defined their game all year crumbled at the most important moment. Jarrod Berry found Lachie Neale, who was only playing due to a successful 11th hour appeal, in space. Resoundingly booed by all but the Lions fans for each of his 20 disposals, he landed the ideal kick for Hugh McCluggage to gather and send deep to Logan Morris, who no longer had to contend with Pearce’s strength and wiles. This is where the footy gods smiled on the Lions, and taunted the Dockers, whose fans will wonder what may have been if Pearce’s Achilles had not given way on the MCC members’ wing early in the third term. Morris also had little influence against Oscar McDonald, but came up trumps when the stakes were at their highest, out-marking the man who would not have played had Brennan Cox was fit.



The day did not belong to Morris, but he owned the moment. From 45 metres out, he showed temperament beyond his three seasons in the big time to put the Lions in front. So sweetly did he make connection, he launched into celebrations from the moment the ball left his boot. Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals With 64 seconds left, the Dockers had a final chance to reclaim a game they had led for all but a few minutes since quarter time. Any one of five Dockers could have gathered possession as the Sherrin ricocheted like a pinball deep in Fremantle’s forward line after Shai Bolton’s clean takeaway, but it was Ryan Lester’s number that won the lotto, sending the ball out of danger. As the ball pinged around again on the wing, it was the Lions who got what they wanted; first a boundary throw-in, then a clearance and regather from Will Ashcroft, who, as he did last week, scythed his way forward to set up the clinching goal.



Related Article AFL grand final Match-winning Lion reveals he’s been playing with fractured back As far as grand final losses, few could be as cruel as the fate which befell the Dockers. A shattered Justin Longmuir had his head in his hands. Karl Worner played out the remaining seconds with tears blurring his vision. A surprise Norm Smith winner with only 58 per cent efficiency from his 26 disposals, Bolton’s medal stayed on his neck not much longer than Nathan Buckley’s 24 years ago in the opening act of the Lions’ first three-peat. When the siren rang, the 18 Dockers on the field collapsed to the turf almost simultaneously, stunned how the cup they had one hand on – plus several fingers on the other – had been ripped away from them. No position in a game will ever feel unassailable again. In September, Fagan’s Lions do not die. In each of their premierships, they have taken the long way home. Only once has a club won four flags in a row. If a club stops them next year, they will have to go the distance. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: The note that helped Patrick Voss after grand final heartbreak
World.content:
SportAFLAFL grand final The note that helped Patrick Voss after grand final heartbreak Danny Russell September 26, 2026 — 8:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories .

For most of this season, excitable Fremantle forward Patrick Voss played the pantomime villain. Late on Saturday afternoon, he became the unexpected shoulder of comfort amid a flood of Fremantle despair. It was by design, he said, in the painful aftermath of a seven-point loss. He had penned himself a note during the week to remind himself to be a good person. Patrick Voss speaks to the media after Fremantle’s grand final loss. AFL Photos That was why he kept his feet after the cruellest of grand final losses and instead offered solace to his devastated teammates. First he lifted Jye Amiss from the MCG turf and then Josh Treacy before giving them both a hug. “I wrote on a card before today the things I’m proud of myself for, and I sort of said to myself, ‘whatever happens today, I’m not going to be defined by being a premiership player or not’,” he said.



“I feel like I’m a good person, and I feel like my 22 brothers on the field are all good people, and they’re not going to be defined by this loss. So, yeah, I wanted to show my love and support to them.” Voss, almost more than any other Fremantle player on the day, typified the vast contrast between winning and losing. He pranced with delight around the boundary after his third goal gave the Dockers a 17-point lead deep in the final term, setting off the deafening roar of Wharfie Time. Voss lived up to his “Prancing Pony” nickname earlier in the match. Eddie Jim Few thought his team could be denied their fate so late in the game before Brisbane willed themselves to victory. In the space of five minutes, his glee had been transformed to desolation.



Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals Voss fought back tears in the Fremantle rooms, his voice one of the rare sounds in a funereal-like room that had been pervaded by pockets of silence. Players staggered around the room in trances, looking for loved ones and unable to speak of their pain. Captain Alex Pearce supported himself on crutches, his towering presence reduced in height and potency, while Treacy leant back on a wall, his hand across his head in utter disbelief. Both had been central to pivotal moments in the game.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented Lions hero Logan Morris kicked three last-quarter goals after Pearce crashed to the ground and out of the match seven minutes into the third term with a ruptured Achilles. Treacy missed what seemed a certain goal during the final term when he was dragged to the ground by Ryan Lester and the ball skewed off his boot. But neither moment could be blamed for costing the Dockers their first premiership, according to Voss. “Alex is a great player and a great leader, but I thought Oscar McDonald, Luke Ryan, Heath Chapman, Judd McVee, Karl Worner and Jordan Clark all stepped up and performed really well, and we didn’t notice his absence at all,” Voss said.



He might have been overplaying the team-first mentality. Sometimes players cannot be replaced. Sometimes squandered opportunities cannot be understated. Not in grand finals, and not against the Lions. “Everyone will have moments that they’re going to replay in their head for the next six months and want back, and I’m no different,” Voss said. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir and his players after the loss. Getty Images “But we win together as a team. We lose together as a team.” The Fremantle players filed down the race and into the rooms after the game barely able to contain their tears.



Ryan was first, followed by Clark and then the skipper on his crutches. Mason Cox folded his arms into his jumper and ambled past deep in thought. He had been here before with Collingwood in 2018. Once again so close, but so far. Amiss and Andrew Brayshaw brought up the rear of a sad and sorry conga line, walking arm in arm with their partners, and reluctantly parting ways as they filed off to a backroom for a debrief with coach Justin Longmuir. The loyal Fremantle fans clapped as their brave team ambled in, careful not to overdo their appreciation for what most certainly classified as an honorable loss. Voss said Longmuir was “extremely disappointed, but extremely proud”. “More than anything, he told us to be easy on ourselves.”



But not being hard on yourself after what could have easily been a historic victory was easier said than done. Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Dockers had one hand on the premiership cup. Then came four minutes that turned the grand final “I’m replaying moments in my head right now that I’d love to have back,” he said. “But that’s sport. I heard [Hawthorn coach] Sam Mitchell say after their loss last week, to feel the greatest achievement, greatest accomplishment, you have got to be willing to be heartbroken and lose like we’ve lost today. “So we are disappointed and heartbroken. But I think it’s the hardships and the hard losses that bring the group together and will make it all the sweeter when we manage to win one.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL grand final Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals Jake Niall September 26, 2026 — 8:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories . Loading

Seemingly beaten with barely four minutes left when trailing by 17 points, the Brisbane Lions have conjured one of the greatest time-on miracles in AFL history to snatch the premiership from a luckless Fremantle in an extraordinary grand final that completed their premiership three-peat under Chris Fagan and stunned a disbelieving Dockers nation. In a grand final that arguably surpassed even the Hawthorn-Brisbane Lions preliminary final for drama, courage and unexpected twists, the Dockers squandered numerous opportunities and dominance of territory to be swept aside and beaten by an inspired Brisbane. The Lions’ surge was piloted by their young champion Will Ashcroft and mercurial forwards Charlie Cameron, Zac Bailey and 21-year-old Logan Morris, who put the Lions ahead with 64 seconds left and then confirmed the improbable victory with a right foot snap in the final seconds. Loading It was a game that the Lions should not have won on the numbers – a reality so graciously acknowledged by Fagan in his podium speech. “You guys probably deserved to win the game today,” said the beloved triple premiership coach, who entered the game saying he did not know if he would continue to coach this astonishing team that he had transformed since his appointment 10 years ago.



The Dockers owned most of the statistical categories, as their midfield – propelled by their hyper-athletic ruckman Luke Jackson – held sway in the clearances and ensured that the ball was in their scoring territory more often. But they did not nail their chances, a familiar story for teams vanquished in tight finals, with Josh Treacy’s unexplainable miss from the goal square with six-and-a-half minutes left the hardest to comprehend. And they were badly affected by the loss of their skipper and anchor in defence, Alex Pearce, who hurt his Achilles early in the third quarter and was on crutches when he took to the stage for a concession speech that was as classy as Fagan’s. Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan and co-captains Hugh McCluggage, Josh Dunkley and Harris Andrews with the premiership cup. AFL Photos The AFL had permitted the deployment of Fremantle’s “Wharfie Time” for the grand final – a decision that Fremantle might not wish repeated in neutral grand finals given what transpired with those four minutes and eighteen seconds left when AC/DC’s Hell’s Bells sounded. Patrick Voss had just slotted his third goal from 15 metres out and set off at full pace on his patented exuberant celebration. The Docker faithful, who had the Lions’ share, so to speak, of the 100,023 behind them (half of the AFL’s corporate packages were bought from Perth), erupted.



They – and the bulk of the millions watching this epic grand final – felt that Fremantle had at least one hand on the cup. Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented But whatever millions thought at that moment, there were 23 people who would not yield, each of them wearing Brisbane Lions jumpers. “My guys have a stack of heart,” said Fagan, whose feat in guiding Brisbane to a treble of flags from four consecutive grand finals matched the achievements of his friend and Lions’ board member Leigh Matthews more than two decades earlier, and his colleague at Hawthorn, Alastair Clarkson in 2015. It is hard to know whether the Dockers believed they had won – it is doubtful they would ever say so – or if they did not believe enough to survive the forthcoming onslaught by the road-tested and composed Lions.



Post match, their coach Justin Longmuir said he did not feel Wharfie Time influenced the result, but it was a common talking point among the victorious Lions players. “We thought when they hit that trigger, that’s when we go up a notch,” said Brisbane ruckman Sam Draper, who reaped his first premiership, as did ex-West Coast skipper Oscar Allen, after leaving his lowly team as a free agent to join Fagan’s heroes. Brisbane coach Chris Fagan consoles his opposite number, Justin Longmuir, after the siren. via Getty Images To borrow from the pre-game’s premier performer Kylie Minogue, it is a defeat that Fremantle people will find hard to get out their heads. The footy gods were capricious for Fremantle. They had almost gift-wrapped them a grand final berth, despite a bad qualifying final loss to the Hawks in Perth, by handing them the scandal-depleted Swans in the preliminary final, in which they rattled home and won unconvincingly.



But the same footy gods – in the form of the AFL appeals tribunal – had reversed the suspension of Lions champion Lachie Neale, and then saw that Pearce was injured mid-game. Neale’s final game for the Lions before his passage to Collingwood, following a season of self-inflicted personal travails, was solid rather than as spectacular as his second half in 2025, when he came off the bench and was instrumental in a demolition of Geelong. Logan Morris stepped up when the Lions needed him most. via Getty Images It is among the many astounding features of this grand final that Neale will leave the Lions after a third flag on end and that it is conceivable that Fagan will finish with the club, too. We will know soon enough. “I have to clear my head,” said the victorious coach, on his future.



The choice of Shai Bolton as Norm Smith medallist, the fifth from a losing team, was surprising. Will Ashcroft’s efforts in the denouement – when he had critical clearances and then ran on the members’ wing, bouncing the ball to find Morris for the sealer – might have given him the nod for a third Norm Smith (he had 31 disposals over the game and nine clearances). While he was unfortunate to not match Dustin Martin as a three-time winner of the medal for best afield in the grand final, he must realise how blessed he was to land at Brisbane in 2022. Loading Hayden Young, who was a major influence in Fremantle’s third quarter dominance, was another contender, as was the grand final’s oldest player, Dayne Zorko, and indefatigable Fremantle midfielder Caleb Serong, whose 13 clearances were important. Brisbane decisively lost the territorial battle (48-62 in entries), the clearances (31-45 and 9-17 at centre ball-ups) and were edged in the contest.



But nearly all of their 23 had been on this stage before. At the end, the chaotic surge from the midfield created half-chances. Charlie Cameron grabbed one with a snap, Bailey followed within seconds with a ludicrous finish in a confined space, and then – as a Fremantle parry forward was rebounded, Morris took a textbook contested mark in front of Oscar McDonald, stretching his endless arms and holding on before calming slotting the goal that changed the lead. Again. The scoreboard says that Brisbane prevailed by seven points, which is misleading considering there was only a minute left when Morris recaptured the lead. In terms of famed comebacks, this grand final now rivals Carlton’s mythic victory over Collingwood in 1970, when the Blues triumphed despite a 44-point half-time deficit. Pitting clubs from the footy state of Western Australia and the Queensland frontier, the grand final capped off a storied finals series, in which four finals – counting the new wildcards – were determined in the final minutes (or after the siren, as in the Bulldogs v Collingwood game).



The Hawthorn v Brisbane preliminary had entered the popular imagination instantly as a claimant for “best game in history” – a shootout that ended in controversy and was replete with individual highlights and abrupt momentum shifts. Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Lion who scored a perfect 10 – and the Docker who scored just one: AFL grand final player ratings This grand final, by dint of the slippery ball and Fremantle’s more defensive method, was less freewheeling and less pristine, but the pressure on the man with the football was greater and all were afforded less time and space in which to execute skills. Like last year’s grand final, the teams were locked on the same score at half-time – 6.7 (43). Then, the Dockers owned the third quarter. Wharfie Time chimed too soon. Even without Neale and potentially Fagan, the Lions’ time is not concluded either.

World.title: ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented Jon Pierik Updated September 26, 2026 — 7:55pm ,first published 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories . Loading

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan admitted it was the Dockers who deserved to win, but when “Wharfie Time” rang out across the MCG on Saturday, it was the reigning premiers who lifted most – they’d prepared for that exact moment. In the aftermath of the seven-point triumph – 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) – Lions great Lachie Neale confirmed he was leaving the club, while Fagan admitted he could still walk away from the job on the highest of highs as a triple-premiership coach, saying “it overtakes your life, and I don’t know whether I want to keep doing that or I don’t”. Lions matchwinner Logan Morris. AFL Photos In cold, initially wet conditions before 100,023 supporters, the Lions left their loudest roar until the closing minutes after they trailed by 17 points with four minutes to play. But there was another surprise post-match when Dockers star Shai Bolton won the Norm Smith Medal, given Lions midfielder and two-time Norm Smith medallist Will Ashcroft was arguably best afield yet again. Bolton is only the fifth man to claim the medal in a losing grand final side.



Neale, who has been linked with a move to Collingwood, confirmed to Channel Seven he was leaving the Lions after they cemented their legacy as one of the all-time great sides. The dual Brownlow medallist and four-time Lions best and fairest said this remarkable victory was a fitting end to his time up north. Related Article Live

Sponsored

AFL grand final AFL grand final LIVE: Lions surge late for third flag in a row, breaking Docker hearts “I have absolutely loved my time at this football club,” the 33-year-old told Seven. “It’s been an incredible ride. To finish with three premierships is a dream.” Lions co-captain Josh Dunkley said his team had been inspired by the Dockers’ “Wharfie Time”, as they booted the final four goals after a burst of music and energy from the Dockers’ supporters to post one of the greatest premiership victories.



“We talked about taking energy from ‘Wharfie Time’ … we grew another leg,” Dunkley said. With a minute remaining, a clutch set shot from Logan Morris put the Lions up by just a point, and Fagan’s men then held on for dear life. Morris capped the comeback with just eight seconds left after a brilliant run by Ashcroft – leaving a distraught Dockers coach Justin Longmuir with his head in his hands, and his players devastated and slumped on the turf. This was a meltdown for the ages. View post on X Speaking after the game, Longmuir admitted just how devastated he was – despite maintaining his typical composure in his press conference.



“We’re devastated, there’s no sugarcoating it. Like we, like I said to them after the game, I have never felt so disappointed,” he said. “But I had this massive sense of pride in the group. We came to play, we executed the plan, created so many opportunities for ourselves, [and] I thought we competed our backsides off all day. “At times, when we got challenged throughout the game, we responded, and yeah, [we] put ourselves in such a great position to go on and win it, and we just didn’t quite play out the 120 minutes. What a contrast: The Lions celebrate, while the Dockers were in disbelief after a meltdown for the ages late in the grand final. Getty Images “Clearly, we’re playing against one of the better teams of all time, in their fourth grand final, they have won three in a row, playing one of the best teams of all time. They just found something, and we just didn’t have an answer for their run-on late. But yeah, just so proud of the way we competed all day.”



Fagan said the Dockers deserved to win but praised his team’s heart and fight, having also had to come from behind to pinch victory against Hawthorn in the preliminary final. “That’s probably the most amazing comeback, three-or-four minute comeback, I’ve ever seen,” he said post-match. “I must admit, sitting there on the bench, I thought, ‘Well, we’ve put a lot of good campaigns together, and maybe today’s the day that we just weren’t going to be good enough’. Chris Fagan (right) arm-in-arm with fellow triple-premiership Lions coach, and great mate, Leigh Matthews. AFL Photos “But I also hadn’t given up hope because, you know, we practice those scenarios to try and get back in and win games, and you know this group has built up over the last eight years a tremendous amount of resilience, and I knew they wouldn’t give up easily, but I just thought that might have been a bridge too far.”



Fagan also spoke about how he prepared his side for “Wharfie Time”. Related Article Opinion

AFL grand final Neale has behaved selfishly, but he’s worth the angst. He owes the Lions one last hurrah Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age “We hadn’t heard it before, so I wanted the players to sort of hear it first of all [during the week’s build-up], and understand what it meant, and then just to say to them, ‘Well, if they do play it, then maybe we can use it as a sign for us to get cracking’,” Fagan said. “It just so happened it turned out that way. That’s a little bit of a fluke, but I’m not taking the credit for that idea because the bloke who suggested it is our backline coach, Dale Morris. He already had audio of ‘Wharfie Time’, so we displayed that at our meeting, and yeah, that story’s got out.” Fagan was determined not to make grand final week – and the big day itself – all about him, but in the aftermath of the game he admitted that this could have been his final game at the Lions’ helm.



“I’ll still have that conversation [with club bosses] – I’ve been coaching the club for 10 years now, and I’ve got to work out whether it’s the right thing to continue on, which might sound a strange thing for me to say after we’ve just won a premiership, but I don’t really want to be that guy that hangs around until we fail, and there’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away when the team’s on top,” he explained. What a day: Logan Morris was a star up forward for the Lions on a day of drama. Getty Images “I’ve got to be honest; it’s sort of the dream way to finish in many ways because, for most coaches, unfortunately, it ends in tragedy. Usually, you’ve been given the boot.” Dockers skipper Alex Pearce tore his Achilles tendon in the third term, finishing the game on crutches. Pearce later spoke of the pride he had in his team. While Hayden Young, Bolton, Caleb Serong, Murphy Reid, Luke Jackson and Sam Switkowski (in his final game) were all outstanding for the Dockers, it was a typically even team contribution for the Lions that got the job done.



Ashcroft had 32 touches, including nine clearances, while Morris finished with three goals. Dunkley was also superb, recording 12 tackles, including a pair that stopped a goal, and another which directly led to a goal. This Lions side joined their 2001-03 brethren in capturing a three-peat of flags, ensuring their place in history as one of the greatest-ever teams. Loading On a day of drama, the Lions led by a point at the first change, each side booting three goals. They made the curious move to start Neale on the bench, but the robust ball winner was soon in the thick of the action after a late reprieve by the AFL’s appeals board to allow him to take his spot for the decider.



Charlie Cameron delivered the first goal with a delightful left-foot snap, ensuring an early rendition of Take Me Home, Country Roads. The Dockers steadied through a long set shot from Josh Treacy, and had the lead when Isaiah Dudley accepted a handball and converted. The Dockers looked to go long down the line, while the Lions were keen to ignite their gameplan based on uncontested football. Dunkley had the job on star Docker Serong, while forward Patrick Voss, also playing a defensive role, held intercept king Harris Andrews possessionless in the opening term. Reid had a team-high nine touches for the Dockers to that point, while Dayne Zorko also had nine for the Lions. The arm-wrestle continued in the second, each side having momentum at stages, only for the other to respond.



Loading Conor McKenna delivered yet another freakish goal when he scooped up a loose ball on a tight angle and dribbled it through. Voss booted two goals for the term, and continued to ensure Andrews was a non-factor in defence. The Ashcroft brothers got busy, as did Dunkley, who delivered successive smothers within seconds on Bolton and Serong to stop what seemed certain goals. Neale, who played for Fremantle in the 2013 grand final, heard the jeers of the Dockers supporters when he marked and lined up for goal, and then the cheers when his shot was wayward. With nine lead changes to half-time, this was as tight and tough a grand final as anyone could have wanted. Victorious yet again: Harris Andrews and the Brisbane Lions. Eddie Jim



The drama went to a new level after the main break when Pearce injured his right leg chasing a loose ball on the wing, his afternoon over and requiring crutches to move. His absence forced fellow defender Heath Chapman to play as a tall on the threatening Oscar Allen. The Dockers dominated early, but squandered several opportunities before a brilliant Dudley goal, having somehow managed to avoid a collision with McKenna, gave them a 15-point buffer - the biggest lead of the game to that point. However, the Lions responded as the great team they are. Three goals in less than eight minutes regained the lead, their speed of ball movement something to behold. But two late goals by Young, the second a set-shot snap on the left foot from right on the right boundary, gave the Dockers a 10-point lead at the final change, before a remarkable final quarter. Morris’ injury revelation followed a star turn in the final quarter, when he kicked all three of his goals, including slotting the go-ahead major with 64 seconds left after brilliantly out-marking Oscar McDonald just inside 50.

Match winner: Logan Morris kicked the goal that put Brisbane in front for the final time. Justin McManus

“I think throughout the game I was getting under them [when the ball was kicked to him], and wasn’t marking ones that I would have liked,” Morris said.

“[Development coach and ex-AFL player] Liam Jones came up to me at half-time and just said, ‘Be patient with your marking, don’t release too early’, and that last one, I think I did it perfectly and released at a perfect time and was able to mark it and then obviously go back and kick it.

World.content:
SportAFLAFL grand final Match-winning Lion reveals he’s been playing with fractured back Marc McGowan September 26, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A
